## How to use these files
- Pick the card that fits the question from the list below, open the file named above it, and read the card's Bottom line first, then its Rules and Gotchas.
- Every legal statement carries a claim id (M- plus four digits in square brackets). The claims a card cites follow that card in the same file, each with its source, pinpoint and verbatim quote.
- A claim tagged (unverified) was not confirmed against its source. Say so when relying on it.
- If these files do not answer a question, say "not in my files" instead of guessing.
- A pending bill is not law. Name the jurisdiction (US federal, a state, a circuit, UK or EU) before answering.

# Music law knowledge pack: Rights and licensing
- File: 01-rights-and-licensing.md, part of the music law knowledge pack (remix edition).
- Contains: M01 Composition and master; M02 Exclusive rights and the 114 limits; M03 Mechanicals, 115, the MLC, MMA; M04 CRB rates and proceedings (Phonorecords, Web, NSS); M05 PROs and consent decrees; M06 SoundExchange, 114 and 112; M07 Sync and master use licensing for video. Each card is followed by the claims it cites, with source, pinpoint and verbatim quote.
- Law last checked: 2026-11-10.
- Research tool, not legal advice. Have a licensed music attorney confirm anything before you act on it.
- Claim ids are M- plus four digits in square brackets. VERIFIED claims were checked against the saved source text. Claims tagged (unverified) were not confirmed; say so when you rely on one.

## M01 Composition and master
- Law last checked: 2026-11-10. Volatility: low.
- Use for questions like: What are the two copyrights in a recorded song; Who usually owns the composition and who owns the master; Is the audio of a mix posted with video a sound recording; Does a sound recording copyright cover the song underneath; Which exclusive rights attach to a composition versus a master; Can one party license only part of a copyright

### Bottom line
- In the US (federal), a recorded song carries two separate copyrights: the musical work (composition) and the sound recording (master) [M-0028, M-0029, M-0025].
- Owning or licensing one never gives you the other. Different people usually control them, and any use in a video needs permission from each owner (analysis).
- The statute defines "sound recordings" to exclude sounds accompanying an audiovisual work [M-0030, M-0337, M-0508]. That carve-out is why a track placed in a video needs direct sync and master use licences (analysis).
- Nothing on this card says any song is cleared. Name the missing licence and who grants it.

### Rules
#### Two works
- 17 U.S.C. 102(a) lists musical works, including any accompanying words, as copyrightable [M-0028]. It lists sound recordings as their own category [M-0029, M-0105].
- The Copyright Office says a sound recording is a separate work from the composition, and a sound recording copyright is not a substitute for copyright in the underlying composition (regulator guidance, Circular 56A) [M-0025].
- The Office treats a sound recording as a derivative work of the underlying composition (regulator guidance, not statute) [M-0026]. Section 101 defines a derivative work as one based on preexisting works, such as a sound recording or musical arrangement [M-0035].
- Authors of the composition are composers, lyricists and songwriters. Authors of the recording are performers, producers and sound engineers, as the circular chart lists them [M-0027].

#### Definitions that matter for video
- A "sound recording" results from fixing a series of sounds, but not including the sounds accompanying a motion picture or other audiovisual work [M-0030, M-0337, M-0508].
- "Phonorecords" are material objects fixing sounds, other than sounds accompanying an audiovisual work [M-0031, M-0338, M-0119].
- "Copies" are material objects other than phonorecords in which a work is fixed [M-0033]. The statute does not say how that applies to a video file with music in it.
- Reading of the definition (unverified): the audio track of a short video is not itself a sound recording, but a commercial track inside it keeps its own sound recording and composition copyrights [M-0032]. This is an inference, not statutory text.
- The 114 and 115 statutory licences are not a route for music placed in a video. Sync (composition) and master use (recording) are direct licences (analysis) [M-0030].

#### Rights that attach
- Reproduction (106(1)): both musical works and sound recordings carry it, subject to sections 107 to 122 [M-0108, M-0334].
- Public performance of a musical work (106(4)) is an exclusive right of the composition owner [M-0106, M-0335, M-0183].
- Sound recordings have a public performance right only by digital audio transmission (106(6)) [M-0107, M-0336].
- Performance societies license public performance of nondramatic musical works for owners. That is the performance leg only [M-0341].
- The performance right is separate from reproduction, distribution and sync (analysis) [M-0183].

#### Ownership and splitting rights
- Copyright vests first in the author. Authors of a joint work are co-owners [M-0037]. A joint work is prepared by two or more authors intending their contributions to merge into inseparable or interdependent parts of a unitary whole [M-0036].
- Ownership can be transferred in whole or in part by any conveyance or by operation of law [M-0038].
- Any exclusive right, and any subdivision of it, can be transferred and owned separately [M-0039]. So one right (for example sync) can sit with a different party from another (for example performance).
- A transfer of ownership includes an assignment or exclusive licence but not a nonexclusive licence [M-0034].
- Work made for hire: an employee's work within the scope of employment, or a commissioned work in a listed category with a signed written agreement [M-0045, M-0046]. The employer or commissioning party is then the author and owner unless a signed writing says otherwise [M-0048].
- The listed categories do not name sound recordings. Whether a master is made for hire turns on the employee prong or fitting a category such as compilation or part of an audiovisual work (analysis, unsettled) [M-0047]. Detail is in M13.

### Gotchas
- "I bought or streamed the song" gives a listener right, not a sync or master use licence (analysis).
- A master copyright does not cover the song, and a composition licence does not cover the recording [M-0025].
- Section 101 excludes video audio from "sound recording", but that does not strip the embedded song of protection (unverified) inference [M-0032]. Do not read the carve-out as "music in videos is free".
- Statutory 114 and 115 licences are not a shortcut for videos [M-0030].
- The M-0047 "unsettled" point is analysis. Source support beyond section 101 was not checked on the ledger.
- Circular 56A is regulator guidance, not statute [M-0025, M-0026]. The author chart flattens in the saved text, so lists are as given in the circular [M-0027].
- Statute text is as saved 2026-11-10. Check for amendment before relying on it.

### Open questions for counsel
- US federal: for a short video with a commercial track baked into the audio, do you read the section 101 definitions to leave the track's own sound recording copyright intact, and is there case law supporting that (M-0032 is only an inference, unverified)?
- US federal: does a platform re-encoding a creator's uploaded audio need its own licence, or can it rely on the creator's licence and a terms of service allocation?
- US federal: is a live stream performing a licensed song a performance by the platform, the creator or both, and which PRO or direct licences must exist?
- US federal: for a commissioned track used in creator videos, is a master "made for hire" under the audiovisual or compilation category in the current case law (M-0047)?
- Which counsel should draft the creator terms that require creators to hold both composition and master permissions?

## M02 Exclusive rights and the 114 limits
- Law last checked: 2026-11-10. Volatility: low.
- Use for questions like: Do I need a licence from the label if I already have the songwriter's; Does the statutory webcasting licence cover an app that streams user mixes; Can a sound-alike recording avoid the master owner; Does a PRO licence cover a platform copying and processing user audio; Does the MLC blanket licence cover songs in a user mix; Why does a sound recording have no general performance right

### Bottom line
- US federal law: a song is two copyrights. The composition (words and music) and the sound recording (the recorded performance) are separate works with separate owners [M-0025, M-0028, M-0029].
- The statutory licences in 112, 114 and 115 do not cover music placed in a video. A platform that hosts music in user videos needs direct licences: sync from the composition owner and master use from the recording owner [M-0112, M-0340, M-0179, M-0180].
- Re-encoding is still copying the sounds [M-0108, M-0110]. (analysis) Blurring or muting is not a licence either. This card is not legal advice; see the counsel section.

### Rules
#### Two works
- A sound recording is a separate work from the composition. Owning one is not a substitute for the other (regulator guidance, Circular 56A) [M-0025].
- The Copyright Office treats a sound recording as a derivative work of the composition (regulator guidance) [M-0026].
- Authors of the composition are composers, lyricists and songwriters. Authors of the recording are performers, producers and sound engineers [M-0027].
- 17 U.S.C. 102(a) lists musical works with any accompanying words [M-0028] and sound recordings [M-0029, M-0105] as separate categories.

#### Rights under 106
- Both works carry the reproduction right (copies or phonorecords) [M-0108, M-0334], subject to sections 107 through 122 [M-0334].
- The composition owner has an exclusive public performance right [M-0106, M-0335, M-0183].
- A sound recording owner has only the 106(1), (2), (3) and (6) rights [M-0296]. The performance right is only by digital audio transmission [M-0107, M-0336]. There is no general public performance right under 106(4) [M-0109].

#### The 114(b) limit and sound-alikes
- The recording's reproduction right covers only duplication that recaptures the actual sounds [M-0110].
- An independent sound-alike fixation does not infringe the recording copyright [M-0111]. The composition is a separate copyright, so (analysis) a sound-alike still needs a composition licence [M-0111].

#### The 114 statutory licence
- 114(d)(2) covers subscription digital audio transmissions, eligible nonsubscription transmissions and preexisting satellite radio transmissions, if conditions are met [M-0114, M-0298].
- The transmission must not be part of an interactive service [M-0115, M-0298]. An interactive service lets a member of the public receive a program made for them or, on request, a particular recording [M-0113, M-0299].
- An eligible nonsubscription transmission is a noninteractive, nonsubscription digital audio transmission made as part of a service providing audio programming [M-0300].
- A "digital audio transmission" does not include transmission of any audiovisual work [M-0112, M-0297]. So the 114(d)(2) licence does not extend to a video with music [M-0112, M-0180, M-0312].
- Rates: the Judges use a willing buyer, willing seller standard [M-0167]. Rates and terms last 5 years unless otherwise agreed and bind affected owners [M-0168]. Specific rates are for M04 and M06.
- An interactive service may not publicly perform a recording unless a licence exists for each musical work in it [M-0301]. (analysis) Even an interactive service would still need a composition performance licence, from a PRO or the owner [M-0313].
- Receipts: 50 percent to the recording owner [M-0302], 45 percent to featured artists [M-0303], distributed by a nonprofit collective the Judges designate [M-0304].

#### The 112 ephemeral copy limit
- 112(e)(1) gives a statutory licence for one ephemeral phonorecord, to a transmitting organization entitled to transmit under 114(d)(1)(C)(iv) or a 114(f) statutory licence, if the listed conditions are met [M-0116].
- The 112(a) ephemeral privilege excludes motion pictures and other audiovisual works [M-0117].
- (analysis) A platform cannot rely on 112 for server copies of video with music [M-0181].

#### The 115 mechanical licence
- Section 115 makes the 106(1) and 106(3) rights to make and distribute phonorecords of nondramatic musical works subject to compulsory licensing [M-0339].
- It is limited to phonorecords whose primary purpose is distribution to the public for private use [M-0120].
- A digital phonorecord delivery does not include digital transmission of sounds accompanying a motion picture or other audiovisual work [M-0340]. The 1976 House Report says the same of sound tracks (legislative history) [M-0121].
- (analysis) So 115 does not license putting a song into a user video. Sync stays a direct licence [M-0179, M-0342].
- The Music Modernization Act blanket licence is issued through the MLC to digital music providers [M-0023, M-0122]. It covers digital phonorecord deliveries including interactive streams [M-0123, M-0124], all musical works available for compulsory licensing, except as provided in subparagraph (C) (voluntary licences and individual download authority) [M-0125], and necessary server and incidental copies [M-0126].
- Blanket licences were available only from the licence availability date [M-0127]. The MLC administers them and collects and distributes royalties [M-0128, M-0129]. Significant nonblanket licensee thresholds: over 5,000 recordings on any day in a month, or $50,000 a month or $500,000 over 12 months [M-0136]. Detail is for M03.

### Gotchas
- "We pay SoundExchange or a PRO, so we are covered": the 114 licence excludes audiovisual transmission [M-0112], and PRO licences address composition performance, not sync (see M05) [M-0088]. Neither is sync or master use.
- "The MLC licence covers songs in videos": it does not [M-0340, M-0179].
- "Muting or editing avoids it": re-encoding is still copying the sounds [M-0108, M-0110]. (analysis) Editing or muting alone is not a licence; removing the audio before publishing is the lawful path.
- "Sound recordings have no performance right": only in the general sense. A digital audio transmission right exists [M-0107].
- Rates, the MLC and the Judges' proceedings change. Check M03, M04 and M06 for 2026 figures. Facts here are statute text as of 2026-11-10.
- (unverified) M-0317 is an inference, not a verified rule.

### Open questions for counsel
- US: does a short video with a licensed library track still need a separate live-room performance licence?
- US: if a platform hosts a creator's upload with a commercial song, is the creator or the platform the direct infringer, and does 512 protect it (see M08)?
- US: does a platform's re-encoding of user audio create a reproduction exposure for the platform as opposed to the user?
- US: is a sound-alike track safe if it copies a recognisable arrangement?
- US: could a tiny live-room audio feed qualify as an interactive service under 114(j)(7)?

## M03 Mechanicals, 115, the MLC, MMA
- Law last checked: 2026-11-10. Volatility: high.
- Use for questions like: Who issues the blanket mechanical licence and since when; Does a mixing platform need a mechanical licence to store or stream songs; What is the current mechanical rate; Does the MLC blanket licence cover songs in a mix posted with video; Is the Phonorecords V settlement final

### Bottom line
- US federal law. The 115 mechanical licence covers the composition only, for phonorecords made mainly for private-use distribution, and it does not reach music placed in a video [M-0120, M-0340, M-0342]. Sync (composition) and master use (recording) need direct licences from the rights holders (analysis) [M-0179].
- The MLC issues the MMA blanket licence to digital music providers for covered activities [M-0023, M-0128]. The Copyright Office continued the MLC designation on June 3, 2026 [M-0131].
- The 2026 rate for physical phonorecords and permanent downloads is 13.1 cents per work or 2.52 cents per minute, whichever is larger, and it is a 2026 rate only [M-0142, M-0143].
- Not legal advice. A licensed music attorney must confirm any claim that a platform needs no licence.

### Rules
#### What 115 covers (17 U.S.C.)
- 115 makes the 106(1) and 106(3) rights to make and distribute phonorecords of nondramatic musical works subject to compulsory licensing [M-0339].
- A person may obtain the compulsory licence only if the primary purpose is distributing phonorecords to the public for private use [M-0120].
- The definition of a digital phonorecord delivery excludes digital transmission of sounds accompanying a motion picture or other audiovisual work [M-0340].
- The 1976 House Report (legislative history, not binding) said the licence does not reach sound tracks accompanying audiovisual works. Clause numbering has since changed, so treat it as history only [M-0121].
- Analysis: 115, including the 115(d) blanket licence, does not license putting a song into a user video. Sync stays a direct licence [M-0179, M-0342].
- The Copyright Office said in 2015 (regulator report, not binding) that consumer audiovisual uses should stay in the free market, and it did not recommend a compulsory licence for them [M-0140]. The MMA did not add audiovisual uses [M-0120].
- "Sync" is an industry term for reproducing a musical work synchronized to visual content [M-0141] (industry practice).

#### The MMA blanket licence and the MLC
- A digital music provider can obtain a blanket mechanical licence through the MLC [M-0023, M-0122]. It covers digital phonorecord deliveries, meaning permanent downloads, limited downloads and interactive streams [M-0123, M-0124].
- It covers all musical works available for compulsory licensing for covered activities, except as provided in subparagraph (C), which covers voluntary licences [M-0125].
- It includes server, intermediate, archival and incidental reproductions reasonable and necessary for covered activities [M-0126].
- The MLC administers blanket licences, including notices of licence and usage reports [M-0128]. It collects and distributes royalties from providers [M-0129].
- A provider obtains the blanket licence by submitting a notice of licence to the MLC (regulation, 37 CFR 210.24) [M-0137].
- Blanket licences were available only from the licence availability date [M-0127]. The MLC says it began administering them on January 1, 2021 (MLC website, volatile) [M-0133].
- A provider may keep or enter voluntary licences with publishers instead of, or alongside, the blanket licence (MLC FAQ) [M-0135].
- A significant nonblanket licensee is one operating under voluntary or individual download licences that offers more than 5,000 different sound recordings on any day in a month, or meets revenue thresholds ($50,000 a month; $500,000 over 12 months) [M-0136].
- The Register designated the MLC and the Digital Licensee Coordinator effective July 8, 2019 [M-0130]. The Office opened a periodic review in 2024 [M-0132] and, in its first review, continued both designations effective June 3, 2026 [M-0007, M-0131].
- The DLC coordinates communication among the providers affected by the MMA (MLC FAQ; the statute is the primary source) [M-0134].

#### Rates (Copyright Royalty Board, regulations)
- Part 385 sets rates only where a 115 compulsory licence is obtained and the exclusive rights are implicated [M-0138]. Voluntary licence rates and terms apply in lieu of part 385 [M-0139].
- 2026 only: the larger of 13.1 cents per work or 2.52 cents per minute of playing time or fraction, for physical phonorecords and permanent downloads [M-0142]. The cost of living notice sets this effective December 1, 2025, applicable January 1 to December 31, 2026 [M-0143], using CPI-U 324.800 against a November 2022 base of 298.012 [M-0144].
- Ringtones: a flat 24 cents per work [M-0145].
- Streaming and limited downloads: the all-in royalty is the greater of a percent of service provider revenue and the TCC prong [M-0147]. The percent runs 15.1 (2023) to 15.35 (2027) [M-0146].
- Phonorecords IV applies from January 1, 2023 through December 31, 2027 [M-0148]. A March 2024 correction fixed capitalization and a late-fee term [M-0149].
- Phonorecords V, for 2028 to 2032, began on December 31, 2025 [M-0150]. Petitions to participate were due January 30, 2026 [M-0151].
- Proposed only: on July 10, 2026 the Judges published a proposed partial settlement that would continue the physical, permanent download, ringtone and bundle rates with only continuing inflation adjustments [M-0152, M-0153]. Comments were due August 10, 2026. Final adoption is unconfirmed as of 2026-11-10. It is not law. The notice does not settle streaming (inference per the row note) [M-0153].

### Gotchas
- "The MLC covers me" is wrong for video. The blanket licence is a 115 licence for phonorecords and digital deliveries, not sync [M-0122, M-0179].
- The 13.1 cent figure is 2026 only and adjusts annually [M-0142, M-0143]. Check the Federal Register for 2027 before quoting a rate.
- Phonorecords V is a proposal as of the July 10, 2026 notice. Do not say the 2028 to 2032 rates are set [M-0152].
- Rates cover composition royalties only, not the master recording.
- The statutory percent table ends with royalty year 2027 [M-0146, M-0148].
- MLC website statements (start date, FAQ answers) are MLC's own words, captured 2026-11-10, and may change [M-0133, M-0135].
- Open source gaps: Phonorecords V final rule is not in the ledger. Do not guess it.

### Open questions for counsel
- US: Does any platform feature, such as a standalone audio or playlist function, make the platform a digital music provider that must file a notice of licence with the MLC?
- US: For user video with licensed library music, what warranties and indemnities should a platform require from the library and from creators?
- US: Does a platform's private re-encode of a user's own audio need any licence, or only the user's rights?
- US: Should a platform watch Phonorecords V for any term change affecting streaming rates after 2027?

## M04 CRB rates and proceedings (Phonorecords, Web, NSS)
- Law last checked: 2026-11-10. Volatility: high.
- Use for questions like: What is the current mechanical rate; Do the CRB webcasting rates cover a platform that streams user mixes; What is Web VI and is there a rate for a mixing app; What is Phonorecords V and is it final; How long do CRB proceedings take and can they be appealed; Can a voluntary licence replace the CRB rate

### Bottom line
- US federal: the Copyright Royalty Judges (CRB) set the rates and terms for the statutory licences in 17 U.S.C. 112(e), 114 and 115 [M-0170]. Section 115 is the mechanical licence for the musical work (composition) [M-0148]. Sections 112(e) and 114 are the digital performance and ephemeral licences for the sound recording (master) [M-0158].
- None of these rates is a price for putting music in a video. Part 385 says it sets rates only where a section 115 compulsory licence is obtained and the exclusive rights are implicated [M-0138]. Sync (composition) and master use (recording) still need direct licences from the rights holders (analysis).
- Rates move by period. The 2026 mechanical rate is 13.1 cents per work or 2.52 cents per minute, whichever is larger, for 2026 only [M-0142, M-0143]. Web V rates are 2025 only. Web VI is not fully codified for a commercial non broadcaster app (unverified) [M-0182]. Phonorecords V is a proposed settlement, not law.

### Rules
#### Who sets rates, and how (17 U.S.C. 801 to 804)
- US federal (statute): the Librarian of Congress appoints three full time Copyright Royalty Judges, one of them Chief [M-0169].
- The Judges determine reasonable terms and rates under sections 112(e), 114, 115, 116, 118, 119 and 1004 [M-0170].
- The Judges may adopt a settlement among some or all participants. They may decline to bind non parties only if a participant objects and the record shows no reasonable basis [M-0171].
- Section 115 (Phonorecords) proceedings recur every fifth calendar year, or at other times agreed under 115(c)(3)(B) to (C) [M-0177].
- Timeline (statute): for section 804(b)(2) proceedings, notice of commencement by January 5 of the year specified [M-0172]. Phonorecords V commenced December 31, 2025 [M-0150]. Petitions to participate are due 30 days after that notice [M-0173]. The voluntary negotiation period is 3 months [M-0174]. The determination is due not later than 11 months after the 21 day settlement conference period ends [M-0175].
- Appeal goes to the D.C. Circuit within 30 days after Federal Register publication [M-0176].
- The Copyright Office opened the periodic review of the MLC designation by notification of inquiry on January 30, 2024 (89 FR 5940) [M-0132].
- Reports of use: preexisting subscription services must deliver them to the designated Collective within 45 days after the close of each month (37 CFR 370.3(b)) [M-0178]. A Collective is an organization designated under a statutory licence by CRB determination [M-0305].

#### Phonorecords: section 115 mechanical rates (37 CFR Part 385)
- Part 385 applies only where the exclusive rights of a copyright owner are implicated and a section 115 compulsory licence is obtained [M-0138].
- Voluntary licence rates and terms apply in lieu of Part 385 [M-0139].
- Phonorecords IV (regulation): applies January 1, 2023 through December 31, 2027 [M-0148]. A March 18, 2024 correction fixed capitalization and a late fee term [M-0149].
- Physical phonorecords and permanent downloads, 2026 only: the larger of 13.1 cents per work or 2.52 cents per minute of playing time or fraction [M-0142]. The December 1, 2025 notice applied the cost of living adjustment for January 1 to December 31, 2026 [M-0143]. It used a CPI-U of 324.800 against a November 2022 base of 298.012 [M-0144]. The rate adjusts each year.
- Ringtones: flat 24 cents per work [M-0145].
- Streaming and limited downloads (Subpart C, 2023 to 2027): the all in royalty is the greater of a percent of service provider revenue and the TCC prong, with Mixed Service Bundles excepted [M-0147]. The revenue percent runs 15.1 (2023) to 15.35 (2027) [M-0146].
- Phonorecords V (2028 to 2032): the Judges announced commencement on December 31, 2025 [M-0150]. Petitions to participate were due January 30, 2026 [M-0151].
- Phonorecords V proposal: on July 10, 2026 the Judges published a proposed partial settlement that would continue the Subpart B rates (physical, permanent downloads, ringtones, music bundles) for 2028 to 2032 with only continuing inflation adjustments to physical and permanent download rates [M-0152]. Comments were due August 10, 2026 [M-0152]. The notice covers Subpart B configurations only [M-0153]. It does not settle streaming (analysis, from M-0153).

#### Webcasting: sections 114 and 112(e) (37 CFR Parts 380, 383)
- Web V (regulation): Part 380 codified rates for January 1, 2021 through December 31, 2025. That period has ended [M-0157, M-0158, M-0306].
- Web V commercial webcaster rates, 2025 only: $0.0032 per performance (subscription) and $0.0025 per performance (nonsubscription) [M-0154, M-0307]. Minimum fee $1,000 per channel or station per year [M-0155]. Royalties are credited 5 percent to ephemeral recordings and 95 percent to section 114 [M-0156].
- Voluntary licence agreements may apply in lieu of the Part 380 rates and terms [M-0306].
- Web VI (2026 to 2030) commenced by Federal Register notice on January 5, 2024 [M-0184]. The Judges adopted four final rules, effective March 10, 2026 [M-0010].
- Web VI commercial broadcasters: $0.0028 per performance in 2026 rising to $0.0032 in 2030 [M-0159]. Minimum fee $1,100 (2026) to $1,250 (2029 and 2030) [M-0160]. The rule came from a SoundExchange and NAB settlement [M-0162], proposed May 16, 2025 (90 FR 20977) [M-0185].
- Web VI Educational Media Foundation: $7,125,000 for 2026, rising to about $8.3 million in 2030, one named licensee [M-0163]. Noncommercial educational webcaster minimum fee starts at $800 in 2026 [M-0164].
- A Commercial Broadcaster is a Commercial Webcaster a material part of whose business is owning and operating FCC licensed terrestrial AM or FM stations. A non broadcaster app is outside that subpart [M-0161].
- Commercial non broadcaster Web VI rule: not published as of 2026-11-10 in the saved set. The saved sources show only the four settlement rules. That absence rests on a search capture, not rule text (unverified) [M-0182].

#### New subscription services: NSS V (37 CFR Part 383)
- NSS V (2026 to 2030) covers digital performances by new subscription services that provide transmissions to residential subscribers as part of a cable or satellite television bundle [M-0166].
- Stand alone contracts: the 2025 base of $0.0234 per subscriber per month, as adjusted by the annual royalty fee adjustment [M-0165]. Bundled contracts: $0.0390 base, same adjustment [M-0507]. The saved text has placeholders for the 2026 amounts, so the 2026 figure is not stated here.

### Gotchas
- "Statutory rate means I can use any song in my video." No. The rates are for the statutory licences only, and Part 385 is limited to compulsory licence use [M-0138].
- The 13.1 cent figure is a 2026 rate only. Check the notice for 2027 when it publishes [M-0142, M-0143]. The saved eCFR file also holds an older Phonorecords III copy (9.1 cents); ignore it [M-0139].
- Web V ($0.0025 and $0.0032) is 2025 only. Do not use it as a 2026 rate [M-0154, M-0307].
- Web VI is not one rule. Four rules are final for broadcasters, EMF and noncommercial educational webcasters [M-0010]. A commercial non broadcaster rule is not published as of 2026-11-10 (unverified) [M-0182]. Never state a Web VI commercial non broadcaster rate.
- Phonorecords V is a proposal. A Federal Register search on 2026-11-10 showed no later final rule for docket 25-CRB-0013-PR, so final adoption is unconfirmed [M-0152]. Not law.
- NSS V 2026 amounts are bracketed in the saved text. Needs source: the December 2025 final rate notice [M-0165].
- Rate periods end on set dates (Phonorecords IV on December 31, 2027 [M-0148]). Expect a new determination or an adopted settlement for 2028 on.
- Treating a CRB rate as a cap on a direct licence quote is wrong. Direct deals are priced by agreement [M-0139].

### Open questions for counsel
- US federal: does any statutory licence (115, 114, 112(e)) apply to a short video app that distributes user videos with licensed or unlicensed music, or is every such use a sync plus master direct licence?
- US federal: if the Judges adopt the Phonorecords V Subpart B settlement, does anything change for an app that is not a phonorecord distributor?
- US federal: is any platform feature (live streams, audio only streams) a digital audio transmission that could fall under Web VI, and which rate class would apply with no commercial non broadcaster rule published?
- US federal: is a platform's audio plan, if any, a new subscription service within NSS V, or outside it?
- US federal: what does the commercial non broadcaster Web VI status mean for exposure today?

## M05 PROs and consent decrees
- Law last checked: 2026-11-10. Volatility: medium.
- Use for questions like: Who are the US performing rights organizations and what do they license; Do the ASCAP and BMI consent decrees give a mixing platform a right to a licence and a rate court; Can a PRO license sync, master or remix rights for a mix; Does a PRO licence cover every co-owner of a song; What if SESAC or GMR will not license; What is different in the EU

### Bottom line
- US federal: a PRO collectively licenses public performance rights in musical works [M-0328, M-0341]. ASCAP's decree bars it from licensing sync (the composition placed in a video) or any right other than public performance [M-0256]. Master use (the recording) is not a composition right at all (analysis). Whether BMI, SESAC and GMR have the same limit is inference (analysis) [M-0311].
- ASCAP's decree gives a music user a right to a licence on written request and a rate court [M-0259, M-0263]. For BMI the rows show a rate court with the fee burden on BMI [M-0266, M-0268]; no BMI row here shows the right to a licence. SESAC is not under a decree [M-0320]. GMR is not under the decrees on the DOJ statement and a commenter's view, not an Office finding [M-0278, M-0293].
- A PRO licence is not a clearance for a video. The platform or the creator still needs direct sync and master licences (analysis) [M-0311].
- Decree law is volatile. The decree texts here are saved editions, and the Copyright Office ran an inquiry in 2025 and delivered a letter on 2025-11-20 with no policy recommendations [M-0283, M-0288, M-0290].

### Rules
#### What a PRO is (US federal)
- A PRO contracts with songwriters and publishers for authority to license public performance rights, then offers collective licences of those rights to users [M-0328].
- The Copyright Office lists ASCAP (1914), SESAC (1931) and BMI (1939) as the established PROs. It says three more formed later: GMR (2013), PRO Music Rights (2018) and AllTrack (2019) [M-0285, M-0329].
- DOJ described GMR in 2016 as a fourth PRO with a collection considerably smaller than ASCAP or BMI [M-0330].

#### ASCAP decree (court decision, Second Amended Final Judgment, S.D.N.Y. 2001, saved 2016 filing edition)
- ASCAP may license only public performance rights in compositions, and only on a nonexclusive basis [M-0256].
- ASCAP members keep the right to license performance rights directly to music users. ASCAP may not interfere [M-0257].
- A blanket licence is a nonexclusive licence to perform ASCAP music at a fee that does not vary with how much ASCAP music the user performs [M-0258].
- ASCAP must grant a nonexclusive licence to all works in its repertory to any music user that asks in writing [M-0259].
- A through-to-the-audience licence covers performances in content a licensee delivers to another music user with whom it has an economic relationship [M-0260].
- ASCAP must issue that licence on request to broadcasters, on-line users and operators of new transmission technologies. It need not cover performances outside the United States [M-0261]. The fee must take into account the value of all performances made under it [M-0262].
- If no fee is agreed within 60 days of the licence request, the music user may apply to the rate court for a reasonable fee [M-0263]. ASCAP carries the burden of proving its fee is reasonable, except that a per-segment licensee carries a tracking burden [M-0264].
- While negotiation or a rate proceeding is pending, either side may ask the court for an interim fee [M-0265].
- Status: no termination found in a 2026-11-10 read-only check of justice.gov [M-0256, M-0257].

#### BMI decree (court decision, Final Judgment as amended 1994, Article XIV only saved)
- In a BMI rate proceeding BMI carries the burden of proving its requested fee is reasonable [M-0266].
- Once the rate court fixes a fee, BMI must offer a comparable fee to similarly situated applicants who later ask [M-0267].
- An applicant or BMI may ask the rate court for an interim fee [M-0268].
- DOJ's 2021 statement says the decrees require ASCAP and BMI to offer the same terms to similarly situated users in the same industry, and to provide through-to-the-audience licences to certain users on request [M-0276, M-0277].

#### Full-work against fractional licensing
- DOJ's 2016 statement closed its review without seeking to change the decrees. It took the view that they require full-work licences [M-0269]. That is DOJ's view only.
- DOJ described a full-work licence as each PRO licensing the work so the user can perform it without infringement risk. It described a fractional licence as each PRO licensing only its own share, so the user needs the other co-owners' PROs too [M-0270, M-0271].
- The S.D.N.Y. held in 2016 that the BMI decree neither bars fractional licensing nor requires full-work licensing [M-0272]. The Second Circuit affirmed on 2017-12-19 by summary order, which has no precedential effect [M-0273].
- DOJ's 2021 statement says the Second Circuit disagreed with its view and that the BMI decree does not require full-work licences. Whether PROs should offer them is still debated [M-0274, M-0275].
- Do not say a PRO must license full works. For BMI the decree does not require full-work licences [M-0275]. ASCAP's treatment is not decided by these rows.

#### Rates and the rate court
- The Second Circuit held in Pandora v. ASCAP (2015) that the ASCAP decree unambiguously precludes partial withdrawals of public performance licensing rights [M-0281].
- It upheld a 1.85 percent of revenue rate for Pandora and ASCAP. The rate period is 2011 to 2015 and it is not a current rate [M-0282].
- The MMA partly repealed the bar on considering sound recording digital performance rates when setting musical work performance rates [M-0279].
- The MMA requires DOJ to notify Congress before moving to terminate a decree [M-0280].

#### Who is not under a decree
- The decrees regulate only ASCAP and BMI. Other PROs are free of the same constraints [M-0278].
- SESAC has never been under an antitrust consent decree [M-0320, M-0333]. A commenter quoted by the Office says SESAC, GMR, Pro Music Rights and AllTrack are not governed by decrees. That is a commenter view, not an Office finding [M-0293].
- The Office says the decrees are an important factor in new PRO formation, because other PROs are not under a decree [M-0292].
- Interested parties disagree. ASCAP says music users must pay SESAC and GMR what their repertories are worth [M-0331]. RMLC and MPA say non-decree PROs can extract disproportionate royalties [M-0332]. These are party positions, not findings.

#### SESAC and the Meredith settlement (court decision, S.D.N.Y. 2015)
- Television stations alleged SESAC's all-or-nothing blanket licence violated Sherman Act section 1 [M-0319]. SESAC agreed to pay $58.5 million into a settlement fund [M-0321].
- SESAC agreed to offer class stations a blanket licence and alternatives, protection from infringement claims while negotiating, and binding arbitration of industry-wide terms [M-0323, M-0324, M-0325]. The restrictions run 2016 to 2035 and cover local commercial television stations in the class [M-0322, M-0326].
- This is the television history, not a radio or digital arrangement [M-0333].

#### Copyright Office PRO inquiry (regulator)
- The Office opened a notice of inquiry on PROs and the public performance right on 2025-02-10 at Congress's request [M-0283, M-0008]. Comments were due 2025-04-11 and replies 2025-05-27 [M-0284].
- Topics included added cost from paying additional PROs and clarity for entities seeking PRO licences [M-0286, M-0287].
- The Office delivered its letter to House Judiciary leaders on 2025-11-20 and received over 5,000 comments [M-0288, M-0289]. The letter summarises commenter views and says these are not Office policy recommendations [M-0290].
- GMR and SESAC have joined BMI and ASCAP in committing to put repertoire data on Songview [M-0291].

#### SoundExchange is not a PRO
- SoundExchange says it is the sole organization designated by the US government to administer the section 114 sound recording licence [M-0294]. It covers the master side digital performance right, not the composition. See M06.
- It says it collects from services such as Pandora, SiriusXM and iHeartRadio [M-0295].

#### EU (foreign law)
- Directive 2014/26/EU Art. 5(2): rightholders may authorise a collective management organisation of their choice for the rights and territories of their choice [M-0308].
- Art. 16(1): organisations and users must negotiate licences in good faith and share necessary information [M-0309].
- Art. 16(2): licensing terms must rest on objective and non-discriminatory criteria [M-0310]. See M19.

### Gotchas
- "We have a blanket licence" does not mean sync or master are cleared [M-0256, M-0311].
- DOJ's full-work view is DOJ's view only. It was rejected for the BMI decree [M-0269, M-0272, M-0273].
- The Second Circuit BMI ruling is a summary order with no precedential effect [M-0273].
- The 1.85 percent Pandora rate is a 2011 to 2015 period rate, not a current rate [M-0282].
- The ASCAP decree text is a saved 2016 filing edition and the BMI row covers Article XIV only. No termination or change was found as of 2026-11-10, but check docket changes.
- The Office's 2025 letter is a summary of views, not a recommendation or a change in law [M-0290].
- A PRO licence for the US does not cover other territories. AFJ2 through-to-the-audience licences need not cover performances outside the United States [M-0261].
- Gap, needs source: RMLC v. GMR and SESAC settlement terms are not in the ledger. Do not describe them.

### Open questions for counsel
- US federal: would a livestream with a performer's background music need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR licences, and would a platform blanket licence cover creators' streams?
- US federal: does the through-to-the-audience licence fit a platform, and how should the request be made under AFJ2 and the BMI decree?
- US federal: for co-owned songs, how should a platform handle fractional licensing across four PROs?
- US federal: is the 2025 Copyright Office PRO inquiry likely to produce legislation that changes decree rights?
- EU: would an EU rollout negotiate with collective management organisations under Directive 2014/26/EU, and which territories?

## M06 SoundExchange, 114 and 112
- Law last checked: 2026-11-10. Volatility: high.
- Use for questions like: Does the 114 statutory licence cover a platform that streams user mixes; Who is SoundExchange and what does it collect; Does the 112 ephemeral copy exemption cover platform server copies; What are the Web VI rates and do they apply to a mixing platform; Does a platform storing or processing user audio need a licence; Is there a performance right in sound recordings for terrestrial radio

### Bottom line
US federal law: the 17 U.S.C. 114 statutory licence is for audio only transmissions of the sound recording (the master). It does not cover a short video with music, because a "digital audio transmission" excludes any audiovisual work [M-0112, M-0297, M-0312]. The 112 ephemeral copy licence does not help either [M-0181]. SoundExchange says it is the designated collective for the 114 royalties, so it is not who clears music for a video platform [M-0294, M-0304]. A video platform needs direct sync (composition) and master use (recording) licences from the rights holders.

### Rules
#### What 114 gives and withholds (US federal statute)
- A sound recording owner has the 106(1), (2), (3) and (6) rights and no general public performance right under 106(4) [M-0109, M-0296].
- The sound recording reproduction right covers only duplication that recaptures the actual sounds [M-0110].
- An independent sound-alike does not infringe the sound recording copyright. The musical work is a separate copyright, so (analysis) a sound-alike still needs a composition licence [M-0111].
- 114(d)(2) puts three kinds of audio transmission under a statutory licence if the listed conditions are met: subscription, eligible nonsubscription and preexisting satellite digital audio radio [M-0114, M-0298].
- The transmission must not be part of an interactive service [M-0115, M-0298].
- An interactive service lets a member of the public receive a program made for the recipient or, on request, a particular sound recording [M-0113, M-0299].
- An eligible nonsubscription transmission is a noninteractive, nonsubscription digital audio transmission made as part of an audio programming service [M-0300].
- A digital audio transmission embodies a sound recording and does not include transmission of any audiovisual work [M-0112, M-0297].
- An interactive service may not publicly perform a sound recording unless the musical work performance is licensed [M-0301]. (analysis) That licence may come from a performing rights society or the copyright owner [M-0313].

#### Rates and who sets them (US federal statute and regulation)
- The Copyright Royalty Judges (three, appointed by the Librarian) set 112(e) and 114 rates [M-0169, M-0170].
- The standard for 114(d)(2) rates is what a willing buyer and willing seller would agree in the marketplace [M-0167].
- Rates run for 5 years unless another period is agreed, and bind all affected owners and performers [M-0168].
- The Judges may adopt a settlement among some or all participants, and decline for non-parties only on an objection and a record showing no reasonable basis [M-0171].
- Web V (37 CFR 380) set webcasting rates for 2021 to 2025 [M-0157, M-0158, M-0306]. That period ended 2025-12-31 [M-0157].
- Web V commercial webcaster rates for 2025: $0.0032 per performance (subscription) and $0.0025 (nonsubscription) [M-0154, M-0307]. Minimum fee $1,000 per channel or station per year [M-0155]. Credit split 5 percent to ephemeral recordings and 95 percent to section 114 [M-0156].
- Web VI began by Federal Register notice on 2024-01-05 [M-0184]. Final rules for commercial broadcasters, Educational Media Foundation, noncommercial educational webcasters and certain public radio stations took effect 2026-03-10 for 2026 to 2030 [M-0010].
- Web VI commercial broadcasters (settlement between SoundExchange and NAB, adopted as proposed) [M-0162, M-0185]: nonsubscription rate $0.0028 per performance in 2026 rising to $0.0032 in 2030 [M-0159]. Minimum fee $1,100 (2026) to $1,250 (2029, 2030) [M-0160].
- A Commercial Broadcaster is a webcaster with a material business in FCC licensed AM or FM stations, so a non-broadcaster app is outside that subpart [M-0161].
- Web VI other licensees: Educational Media Foundation $7,125,000 for 2026 [M-0163]; noncommercial educational minimum fee $800 in 2026 [M-0164].
- NSS V (2026 to 2030) covers new subscription services delivered as part of a cable or satellite TV bundle [M-0166]. Stand-alone monthly per-subscriber base is $0.0234 (2025 rate, then adjusted) [M-0165]. Bundled base is $0.0390 [M-0507].
- Preexisting subscription services deliver Reports of Use to the Collective within 45 days after each month [M-0178]. A Collective is the organization the Judges designate for a statutory licence [M-0305].

#### SoundExchange and the money (US federal)
- SoundExchange says it is the sole organization the US government designated to administer the 114 licence [M-0294]. That is its own description, captured 2026-11-10.
- It says it collects from services such as Pandora, SiriusXM and iHeartRadio [M-0295]. Naming a service is not a statement of its current licence status.
- A nonprofit collective picked by the Judges distributes 114 receipts [M-0304]. Split: 50 percent to the sound recording copyright owner [M-0302], 45 percent to featured recording artists [M-0303].

#### 112 ephemeral copies (US federal statute)
- 112(a)(1) excludes motion pictures and other audiovisual works [M-0117].
- 112(e)(1) gives a transmitting organization entitled to transmit under 114(d)(1)(C)(iv) or a 114(f) licence a statutory licence for no more than 1 ephemeral phonorecord, if conditions are met [M-0116].

#### Pending bills (not law)
- AMFA: H.R. 861 would give sound recordings a public performance right by audio transmission, reaching terrestrial broadcast, and its audio transmission definition excludes audiovisual works [M-0480]. S. 326 was introduced 2025-01-30 and referred to Senate Judiciary [M-0504]. Neither is law.

### Gotchas
- Web V rates are 2025 only [M-0157, M-0307]. Web VI is not fully codified: none is in the saved sources for a commercial non-broadcaster as of 2026-11-10 [M-0010, M-0161] (unverified, M-0182). Do not state a Web VI rate for a commercial non-broadcaster. The Web VI rates above are for broadcasters and other named classes only.
- NSS V 2026 amounts are adjusted bases. The saved text has placeholders for the 2026 figures [M-0165]. Do not quote a 2026 dollar amount.
- "114 licence" does not mean a platform may host a song. It covers audio transmissions only [M-0112].
- The sound recording has no general public performance right [M-0296]. Composition performance is a separate right, see M05 for PROs.
- Statutory licence terms depend on listed conditions [M-0114]. Do not assume a service qualifies.
- AMFA is a bill [M-0480, M-0504]. Do not say terrestrial radio pays sound recording owners.
- SoundExchange sources here are self-description and may change [M-0294, M-0295].

### Open questions for counsel
- US federal: does any platform feature (audio only previews, live audio streams, playlists) fall within a 114(d)(2) noninteractive service, or is every product interactive or audiovisual?
- US federal: for audio only live streams with background music, which licences are needed and who grants them?
- US federal: does a platform's re-encoding of a user's audio create any reproduction or performance exposure for the platform as a service (M-0317 is unverified)?
- US federal: what is the status of the Web VI commercial non-broadcaster determination (docket 24-CRB-0001-W)?
- US federal: should the Web V and NSS V rate figures be rechecked before any rate quote, since the NSS V 2026 figures are adjusted amounts not in the saved text?
- US federal: is there any reason to register with SoundExchange as a service at all?

## M07 Sync and master use licensing for video
- Law last checked: 2026-11-10. Volatility: high.
- Use for questions like: Does the MLC blanket licence or any statutory licence cover songs in a mix posted with video; What licences does a user need to put a commercial song in a video mix; Does a TikTok or Meta sound licence carry over to another platform; Does a platform processing a user's audio need a music licence

### Bottom line
- US federal: no statutory licence covers a song placed in a video. Sections 114 and 115 stop at audio, so a video with music needs two direct licences: sync from the composition owner (publisher) and master use from the recording owner (label or distributor) [M-0342, M-0112, M-0179].
- The MLC blanket licence is a mechanical licence for audio deliveries. It does not reach sounds accompanying an audiovisual work [M-0122, M-0340].
- Platform sound collections are often tied to one platform. Do not assume any of them covers another platform [M-0386].
- Nothing here says any song is cleared. Name the missing licence and who grants it.

### Rules
#### The two copyrights (US federal)
- A recorded song carries two copyrights: the musical work (composition, usually publisher or PRO side) and the sound recording (master, usually label or distributor) (analysis).
- Both carry the reproduction right [M-0108, M-0334]. Musical works also carry public performance [M-0106, M-0335]. Sound recordings carry public performance only by digital audio transmission [M-0107, M-0336].
- A sound recording has no general public performance right under 106(4) [M-0109, M-0296]. Its reproduction right covers only duplication that recaptures the actual sounds [M-0110].
- A sound alike made as an independent fixation does not infringe the master. The composition is a separate copyright, so (analysis) a sound alike still needs a composition licence [M-0111].

#### Why 115 does not cover video (statute)
- Section 115 makes the 106(1) and 106(3) rights to make and distribute phonorecords of nondramatic musical works subject to compulsory licensing [M-0339].
- The compulsory licence is limited to phonorecords whose primary purpose is distribution to the public for private use [M-0120]. Section 101 excludes sounds accompanying an audiovisual work from "phonorecords", so (analysis) 115 does not license music in video [M-0179].
- A digital phonorecord delivery does not include the digital transmission of sounds accompanying a motion picture or other audiovisual work [M-0340, M-0124]. Sync and master use licences are therefore needed (analysis) [M-0342].
- 1976 House Report (legislative history, not binding): the compulsory licence does not reach sound tracks accompanying a motion picture or other audiovisual work [M-0121].
- The MLC administers blanket licences, notices of licence and usage reports, and collects and distributes royalties [M-0128, M-0129]. The blanket covers digital phonorecord deliveries of musical works for covered activities [M-0122, M-0123, M-0125]. It includes incidental reproductions reasonable and necessary for those activities [M-0126]. That is audio delivery, not video.
- The Copyright Office (2015 report, regulator view, not binding) said consumer audiovisual (sync) uses should stay in the free market, with no compulsory licence [M-0140]. The 2018 MMA did not add audiovisual [M-0140, M-0120]. Sync is an industry term for reproduction (and possibly derivative) rights in a musical work synchronized to visual content [M-0141].

#### Why 114 does not cover video (statute)
- A "digital audio transmission" does not include the transmission of any audiovisual work [M-0112, M-0297]. The 114(d)(2) licence therefore does not extend to a video with music [M-0112].
- The licence reaches subscription transmissions, eligible nonsubscription transmissions and preexisting satellite DARS, and the transmission must not be part of an interactive service [M-0114, M-0115, M-0298]. An interactive service lets a member of the public receive on request a transmission of a particular sound recording [M-0113, M-0299]. Eligible nonsubscription means noninteractive digital audio programming [M-0300].
- (analysis) The 114 licence does not cover short videos on a user upload platform, because they are audiovisual [M-0312, M-0180]. If such a platform were an interactive service, it would still need a licence for the public performance of each musical work in the recording [M-0301, M-0313].
- Rate standard and period for the statutory licence are willing buyer and willing seller, set for five year periods [M-0167, M-0168]. Receipts go 50 percent to the recording owner, 45 percent to featured artists, via a designated nonprofit collective [M-0302, M-0303, M-0304]. This is background only. It does not license video.

#### Who grants sync and master use (industry practice)
- Publishers act as owner or administrator of compositions and earn mechanical, performance, sync and other income [M-0079]. Sync is use of the composition combined with visual images [M-0081].
- Each sync licence is generally negotiated with the prospective licensee, and publishers pay songwriters or heirs a contractual share [M-0080, M-0100]. These are company statements in SEC filings, not law.
- Independent publishers license for film, television, advertising and digital platforms including social media and background music [M-0102].
- Master side: labels license recordings under multi year, worldwide, non automatic deals with audit rights [M-0083, M-0084]. Streaming services also license independents and aggregators [M-0085].
- Even a streaming service holding audio licences needed separate direct licences for audiovisual rights: Spotify says it recently signed direct US publisher deals for audiovisual and other rights [M-0087]. Audio-only US mechanicals run through 115 and the blanket licence [M-0086].
- Public performance of compositions comes through PROs under blanket licences [M-0088]. A sync licence is not a performance licence, and PRO coverage is separate [M-0183].
- Chain of title can be messy: label deals often treat artist services as work made for hire, with termination risk if a court disagreed [M-0052, M-0053, M-0099]. Artist deals are recoupable, option based, sometimes 360 [M-0075, M-0076, M-0077, M-0078].
- Licensors in general include labels, aggregators, artists, publishers and PROs, and losing a licence is a stated business risk for services [M-0089].

#### Libraries and platform sound collections (platform terms)
Library and platform terms, as captured 2026-11-10. Terms change, so re-check before relying.
- Epidemic Sound standard licence: personal use only, so corporate or third party content needs other licences [M-0404]; no sublicensing to third parties [M-0405].
- Musicbed: licence is per single audiovisual Project, and excludes public performance where a PRO licence is available [M-0408].
- Artlist: the saved text is site terms only; the music licence itself is not saved, so nothing is confirmed [M-0410].
- YouTube Audio Library: described as copyright safe and not claimed through Content ID [M-0411]. Creative Commons tracks need credit in the description [M-0412]. YouTube disclaims responsibility for music from other libraries [M-0413].
- TikTok Commercial Music Library (CML) User Terms: for Commercial Uses, Commercial Sounds may be posted only within TikTok [M-0382]. Posting on third party platforms needs separate rights holder licences [M-0383]. Sounds may not be used with content violating TikTok's terms or Community Guidelines [M-0384]. (analysis) This gives no rights for use on another platform [M-0386].
- Meta Sound Collection (2022 terms, 2023 archive copy): limited to use on Meta products only [M-0385]. Current page not obtained.
- Content ID is a matching system, not a licence. It scans uploads against owner files with outcomes block, monetize or track [M-0378]. It is for owners with exclusive rights to a substantial body of frequently uploaded material [M-0379].

### Gotchas
- "It is on the MLC" or "it is licensed for streaming" does not mean it is licensed for video. Mechanical audio is not sync [M-0340, M-0342].
- Library licences are often per project, per licensee and non sublicensable. A creator licence may not pass to a platform or to a third party buyer [M-0404, M-0405, M-0408].
- Platform sound licences are platform bound. TikTok commercial sounds stay in TikTok [M-0382, M-0383].
- Content ID matching is not a clearance [M-0378].
- Artlist music licence, TikTok Community Guidelines and the Meta Sound Collection current terms are needs source gaps. Meta's saved text is a 2023 archive [M-0385, M-0386, M-0410].
- Statutory text is stable. Library and platform terms are volatile: they were captured 2026-11-10 and can change without notice [M-0386, M-0408, M-0410].
- Filings (WMG, Spotify, Reservoir) are company statements about practice. They show how deals work, not what the law requires [M-0080, M-0087].

### Open questions for counsel
1. US federal: does placing a creator video re-encoded by a separate tool on a hosting platform create any separate licence need for the tool, or does exposure sit with the creator and the host [M-0317] (unverified)?
2. US federal: what direct licence structure (sync plus master use, or a blanket publisher and label deal) fits a short video app with creator uploaded music, and will majors license that use at all?
3. US federal: do live streams with music need a different set of composition and master licences than recorded uploads?
4. What notice and takedown posture should a platform take for music in creator videos, given licences are missing (see M08)?

# Music law knowledge pack: Platform liability
- File: 02-platform-liability.md, part of the music law knowledge pack (remix edition).
- Contains: M08 DMCA 512 safe harbor for a platform that hosts user mixes; M09 Secondary liability after Cox; M10 Content ID systems and platform sound libraries. Each card is followed by the claims it cites, with source, pinpoint and verbatim quote.
- Law last checked: 2026-11-10.
- Research tool, not legal advice. Have a licensed music attorney confirm anything before you act on it.
- Claim ids are M- plus four digits in square brackets. VERIFIED claims were checked against the saved source text. Claims tagged (unverified) were not confirmed; say so when you rely on one.

## M08 DMCA 512 safe harbor for a platform that hosts user mixes
- Law last checked: 2026-11-10. Volatility: medium.
- Use for questions like: Does the safe harbor protect a platform when users upload mixes of commercial songs; What must a platform do to qualify for 512(c); Does a platform need a designated agent and when does it expire; What is a repeat infringer policy and what must it say; What happens after a counter notice; Does processing or re-encoding user audio change the answer

### Bottom line
US federal law: 17 U.S.C. 512(c) can shield a platform from copyright damages for user uploaded videos that carry someone else's song, but only if the platform meets every condition [M-0343, M-0344, M-0345, M-0346, M-0347, M-0348, M-0357]. The safe harbor can apply to claims on both the composition and the master copyright (analysis), because it limits liability for the infringement claim itself, not a licence. It is not a licence and not a defence for the platform's own conduct. Section 230 does not add anything for copyright [M-0401, M-0402].
- Core conditions: no actual or red flag knowledge, prompt removal, no direct financial benefit with the right and ability to control, a designated agent, and a real repeat infringer policy [M-0344, M-0345, M-0346, M-0347, M-0349, M-0357].

### Rules
#### Statute (17 U.S.C. 512)
- 512(c) covers infringement by reason of storage at the direction of a user on the provider's system [M-0343].
- Knowledge: the provider must lack actual knowledge of infringement [M-0344]. Without actual knowledge it must not be aware of facts or circumstances making infringement apparent, called red flag knowledge [M-0345].
- On gaining knowledge or awareness the provider must act expeditiously to remove or disable access [M-0346].
- Financial benefit: the provider must not receive a financial benefit directly attributable to the infringement where it has the right and ability to control it [M-0347].
- Notice: on a compliant notice the provider must respond expeditiously to remove or disable the claimed material [M-0348].
- Designated agent: the safe harbor applies only if an agent is designated, made available on the service including its website, and provided to the Copyright Office [M-0349].
- Notice contents: an effective notice needs the signature of a person authorized to act for the owner of an exclusive right [M-0350]. It also needs a statement under penalty of perjury that the sender is authorized to act for the owner [M-0351]. The perjury statement attaches to authority, not to the claim that the use infringes [M-0351].
- Repeat infringers: the provider must have adopted, reasonably implemented and told subscribers about a policy to terminate repeat infringers in appropriate circumstances. The limitations apply only if it did [M-0357].
- Monitoring: the safe harbor is not conditioned on monitoring the service or seeking out infringement, except as consistent with a standard technical measure [M-0358]. This does not switch off red flag knowledge (analysis, from the row note).
- Counter notice: a counter notification needs a statement under penalty of perjury that the user believes the material was removed by mistake or misidentification [M-0356]. The provider restores the material not less than 10 nor more than 14 business days after receipt, unless the notifier first tells the agent it has gone to court [M-0355].
- Misrepresentation: a person who knowingly materially misrepresents that material is infringing is liable for damages, costs and attorneys' fees [M-0359].

#### Agent designation (regulation, 37 CFR 201.38)
- The designation gives the provider's full legal name and physical street address [M-0352]. Parent and subsidiary are separate entities and need separate designations [M-0353].
- A designation expires three years after registration unless renewed by amending or resubmitting it [M-0354]. The source is a saved eCFR copy dated 2026-10-26; check the live eCFR before relying on it [M-0352].

#### Court decisions on knowledge and control
- Viacom v. YouTube (2d Cir. 2012): the knowledge conditions mean knowledge or awareness of specific infringing activity [M-0362]. Right and ability to control needs something more than the ability to remove or block access [M-0363]. Willful blindness can apply in the 512(c) knowledge analysis [M-0364].
- Capitol v. Vimeo (2d Cir. 2016): an employee viewing a video with a recognizable copyrighted song does not alone prove red flag knowledge [M-0365]. The test is an ordinary person without specialized music or copyright knowledge [M-0366].
- UMG v. Shelter, the Veoh case (9th Cir. 2013): the label skipped the notice protocol, which stripped it of the most powerful evidence of knowledge [M-0367].
- Ventura v. Motherless (9th Cir. 2018), a UGC site: summary judgment for the site on 512(c) was affirmed [M-0370]. Apparent knowledge and red flag are used interchangeably, and infringement must be obvious to a reasonable person [M-0371]. The site's repeat infringer handling was informal, and the court still found the safe harbor. Do not copy that as a model [M-0372]. No holding on music (row note).
- Mavrix v. LiveJournal (9th Cir. 2017): common law agency decides whether moderators' acts count as the site's own, which can undercut "storage at the direction of a user" [M-0368]. Fact disputes about volunteer moderators as agents led to reversal of summary judgment for the site [M-0369].
- Lenz v. Universal (9th Cir. 2016, amended): a rightsholder must consider fair use before sending a takedown or risk 512(f) damages [M-0360]. The test is subjective good faith [M-0361].
- Fourth Circuit reading of "repeat infringer" as repeat alleged infringer is described in the Copyright Office report [M-0376]. Cox v. Sony (U.S. 2026) addressed contributory liability, not the 512(i) reading (row note on M-0376). Contributory liability now needs inducement or a service tailored to infringement [M-0001, M-0252]. This sits outside the safe harbor and is covered in card M09.

#### Policy view (regulator report, not law)
- The Copyright Office 2020 report recommends no wholesale change to 512, only fine tuning [M-0373]. It says courts' readings of the knowledge requirements may be narrower than Congress intended [M-0374]. It says willful blindness needs deliberate avoidance of specific infringements [M-0375]. It says notice and staydown needs more study [M-0377].

### Gotchas
- 512 is not a licence. A takedown or a counter notice does not clear a song, and winning on safe harbor does not mean the music was licensed.
- "The notice was sloppy" is not a reason to ignore it. Missing signature or authority makes a notice defective, but do not just ignore it. Take it to counsel; needs source for 512(c)(3)(B) [M-0350, M-0351].
- Sending takedowns carelessly is risky for the sender too: knowing misrepresentation carries damages, and Lenz requires fair use consideration [M-0359, M-0360]. Takedown notices a platform sends itself need counsel review.
- Agent designations lapse after three years. A lapsed designation can cost the safe harbor [M-0349, M-0354].
- The safe harbor is not conditioned on monitoring [M-0358], but knowledge, red flags and willful blindness can still defeat it [M-0345, M-0364].
- Informal repeat infringer handling surviving in Ventura is not a safe rule [M-0372]. The Copyright Office noted a Fourth Circuit reading of repeat alleged infringer [M-0376].
- Blurring, muting or re-encoding audio is not a licence and does not erase prior infringement.
- Currency (as of 2026-11-10): the 37 CFR 201.38 text is a saved eCFR copy dated 2026-10-26 [M-0352]. The Copyright Office report is a report, not law [M-0373]. Cox v. Sony was decided 2026-03-25 and is limited to contributory liability [M-0001, M-0252]. Vicarious liability was not decided [M-0252].
- Contested gloss: the "right and ability to control" case law is not fully covered by the ledger [M-0347].

### Open questions for counsel
- US federal: does 512(c) protect a platform's live streams where music is streamed in real time, or only stored uploads?
- US federal: does a separate re-encoding service's processing of user audio, on device or on a server, create its own reproduction outside 512(c), and does that service need its own agent designation?
- Ninth Circuit: given Mavrix, how should a platform structure moderation and featuring so staff acts are not treated as the site's own?
- US federal: what repeat infringer policy text, strike count and reinstatement rules should a platform adopt, given the Fourth Circuit reading of "repeat" [M-0376]?
- US federal: after Cox v. Sony, what does a platform's exposure look like if a song is flagged and it keeps promoting the clip?
- Needs source: Grande remand outcome and any 2026 512 decisions are not in the ledger. No row addresses live streaming under 512 or fingerprint filtering as a standard technical measure.

### Sources
- usc17-512: 17 U.S.C. 512 limitations on liability relating to material online (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/512)
- usc47-230: 47 U.S.C. 230 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/47/230)
- cfr37-201-38: 37 CFR 201.38 designation of agent (eCFR as of 2026-10-26)
- ca2-viacom-youtube-2012: Viacom v. YouTube, 676 F.3d 19 (2d Cir. 2012)

- ca9-umg-shelter-2013: UMG v. Shelter Capital, 718 F.3d 1006 (9th Cir. 2013)

## M09 Secondary liability after Cox
- Law last checked: 2026-11-10. Volatility: high.
- Use for questions like: Is a mixing platform liable if a user uploads a mix with songs they do not own; Does knowing users infringe make a platform contributorily liable after Cox; What is vicarious liability and does Cox change it; Does a platform still need a repeat infringer policy; Does the DMCA safe harbour still matter; Which pre-2026 cases are overtaken

### Bottom line
US federal law, as of 2026-11-10: after Cox v. Sony (U.S. 2026), a service provider is contributorily liable for a user's infringement only if it intended the service be used to infringe, shown by inducement or by a service tailored to infringement. Knowing that some users infringe is not enough [M-0001, M-0221, M-0222, M-0223]. This helps platforms, but it does not touch direct liability, vicarious liability or the section 512 safe harbour, and it gives no licence for music in uploads [M-0252].

### Rules
#### The Supreme Court decision (US federal, court decision)
- The Court decided Cox Communications v. Sony Music (No. 24-171) on March 25, 2026, reversing and remanding [M-0001, M-0226].
- Held: a provider is "contributorily liable for a user's infringement only if it intended that the provided service be used for infringement" [M-0221].
- Mere knowledge that a service will be used to infringe is insufficient to show that intent [M-0222].
- Intent can be shown two ways: inducement, or a service tailored to infringement (not capable of substantial or commercially significant noninfringing uses) [M-0223].
- The Fourth Circuit's knowledge plus insufficient action rule went beyond those two bases and conflicted with the Court's precedent [M-0224].
- Justice Sotomayor, concurring in the judgment, said other common law theories such as aiding and abetting could apply in copyright. That is a concurrence, not the holding [M-0225].
- Cox is an internet access provider case, but the holding is stated for any "provider of a service" [M-0252]. Applying it to an app is (analysis) a fair reading, not a ruling on apps.
- Only contributory liability was before the Court. Vicarious liability is a separate theory the Court did not decide [M-0252]. Direct infringement is not addressed in the syllabus [M-0252]. The section 512 safe harbour was not decided [M-0252].

#### Baseline liability (US federal, statute)
- Anyone who violates an exclusive right of the copyright owner is an infringer [M-0220]. A platform that itself copies, performs or distributes music is a direct infringer, whatever Cox says (analysis).

#### Overtaken or vacated lower decisions (court decisions)
- Fourth Circuit (2024) affirmed willful contributory liability and reversed vicarious liability for lack of profit from subscribers' infringement [M-0228]. The contributory holding was reversed by the Supreme Court [M-0226]. Cite as history only.
- Fifth Circuit (2024, Grande) affirmed contributory liability but vacated the damages award [M-0229]. The Supreme Court granted Grande's petition on April 6, 2026, vacated and remanded in light of Cox [M-0002, M-0227]. The remand outcome is not in our sources. Needs source.
- BMG v. Cox (4th Cir. 2018) held the "knew or should have known" contributory standard is negligence and too low [M-0232]. That standard is overtaken because Cox 2026 requires more than knowledge [M-0224].

#### The DMCA safe harbour still stands apart (court decisions)
- BMG v. Cox (4th Cir. 2018): to use the section 512 safe harbour a provider must have adopted and reasonably implemented a policy to terminate repeat infringers [M-0230]. The 2018 holding on 512(i) is not disturbed by Cox 2026 [M-0230].
- BMG held the safe harbour was lost because the repeat infringer policy was not applied consistently or meaningfully [M-0231, M-0253]. The provider bears the burden of proof on the defence [M-0233].
- Copyright Office 2020 report (regulator report, not law) notes the Fourth Circuit reads "repeat infringer" as repeat alleged infringer [M-0376]. Cox 2026 did not address that 512(i) reading [M-0376].
- Viacom v. YouTube (2d Cir. 2012): 512(c) needs knowledge or awareness of specific infringing activity [M-0362]. "Right and ability to control" needs something more than the ability to remove or block [M-0363]. Willful blindness may apply in the 512(c) knowledge context [M-0364].
- Capitol v. Vimeo (2d Cir. 2016): an employee viewing a video with a recognizable song does not alone create red flag knowledge [M-0365]. The red flag test uses an ordinary person without specialized music or copyright knowledge [M-0366].
- Ventura v. Motherless (9th Cir. 2018, UGC site): summary judgment for the site on 512(c) was affirmed [M-0370]. Apparent knowledge and red flag mean infringement must be obvious to a reasonable person [M-0371]. The site's informal repeat infringer handling still passed on those facts, so do not treat it as a model [M-0372].
- Mavrix v. LiveJournal (9th Cir. 2017): common law agency decides whether moderators' acts are the site's own, which can undercut "storage at the direction of a user"; fact disputes over volunteer moderators led to reversal of summary judgment for the site [M-0368, M-0369].
- The Copyright Office 2020 report recommends no wholesale change to section 512 [M-0373]. It says courts may read knowledge requirements more narrowly than Congress intended [M-0374], and that willful blindness needs deliberate avoidance of specific infringements [M-0375]. Notice and staydown needs more study [M-0377].

### Gotchas
- "Knowledge is not enough" is not "we are safe." Inducement, tailored service, direct liability, vicarious liability and the 512 conditions all remain [M-0222, M-0252].
- Lower court cases that rely on "knew or should have known" or knowledge plus failure to act are overtaken [M-0224, M-0232]. Re-check any other circuit's secondary liability case before citing.
- The BMG repeat infringer holding is a separate 512(i) point and is not disturbed [M-0230]. Do not drop the repeat infringer policy because of Cox.
- Grande: only the April 6, 2026 vacatur is in our sources [M-0227]. The remand result is unknown. Needs source.
- Sotomayor's aiding and abetting remark is a concurrence [M-0225]. Plaintiffs may plead it, so do not call it dead.
- Cox is an ISP case. Whether courts apply it identically to hosting platforms is not settled in our sources (analysis).
- Currency: as of 2026-11-10, post-Cox lower court case law is not in the ledger. Volatility is high.

### Open questions for counsel
- US federal: given our sound features, does any product copy or marketing risk "inducement" under Cox?
- US federal: with Cox silent on vicarious liability, what is a platform's exposure from ad or subscription revenue on videos with unlicensed music?
- US federal: does a platform's server side re-encoding of user audio make it a direct actor, and does 512(c) or 512(a) fit?
- Ninth and Second Circuits: how have courts applied Cox to hosting platforms since March 2026, and what happened on the Grande remand in the Fifth Circuit?
- Does our repeat infringer policy meet BMG v. Cox, and how should it treat creators with multiple unproven notices?
- Should a platform's designated agent and notice workflow be reviewed against current Copyright Office filings?
