## M10 Content ID systems and platform sound libraries
- Law last checked: 2026-11-10. Volatility: high.
- Use for questions like: Can a mixing platform use TikTok or Meta library music; Does a library licence from Epidemic Sound or Musicbed cover mixes on a platform; Does a mixing platform need to build Content ID style filtering; What must a platform do when a rightsholder sends a takedown; What would EU Article 17 require of a platform that hosts user mixes; Is YouTube Audio Library music safe to use in mixes

### Bottom line
- No saved platform or library licence is shown to cover music on a third party platform. TikTok's Commercial Music Library grants no rights outside TikTok [M-0382, M-0383, M-0386], and Meta Sound Collection is limited to Meta products (2023 archive copy) [M-0385].
- A Content ID style filter is a product choice in the US, not a legal duty: the DMCA safe harbor is not conditioned on monitoring [M-0358]. In the EU, Article 17 can require upload filtering style duties (EU law).
- These tools and libraries touch the composition and the master only by licence or claim. A library licence is a direct sync and master licence from the library, and only if its terms fit the use (analysis).

### Rules
#### Content ID style systems (platform terms)
- YouTube Content ID scans each upload against files that owners submit. A match leads to block, monetize or track [M-0378]. It is open only to owners with exclusive rights to a substantial body of frequently uploaded original material [M-0379]. Edition captured 2026-11-10.
- YouTube Audio Library music is described as copyright safe and not claimed through Content ID [M-0411]. The page states no licence scope outside YouTube [M-0411]. Some tracks need credit under a Creative Commons licence [M-0412]. YouTube disclaims responsibility for music from other libraries [M-0413].

#### US federal: DMCA 512(c) (statute)
- The 512(c) safe harbor covers infringement by reason of storage at a user's direction [M-0343].
- Conditions: no actual knowledge [M-0344]; no awareness of facts making infringement apparent, called red flag knowledge [M-0345]; act expeditiously to remove once aware [M-0346]; no direct financial benefit from infringement where the provider can control it [M-0347]; act expeditiously on a compliant notice [M-0348].
- The provider must designate an agent on its service and with the Copyright Office [M-0349].
- A repeat infringer policy must be adopted, reasonably implemented and told to subscribers, or the limitations do not apply [M-0357].
- The safe harbor is not conditioned on monitoring or seeking out infringement, except where a standard technical measure applies [M-0358].
- A valid notice needs an authorised signature [M-0350] and a statement under penalty of perjury that the sender is authorised to act for the owner [M-0351].
- Counter notice: the uploader states under penalty of perjury a good faith belief of mistake or misidentification [M-0356]. The provider restores the material not less than 10 nor more than 14 business days after receipt, unless the notifier first reports a court action [M-0355].
- Knowing material misrepresentation in a notice or counter notice makes the sender liable for damages and fees [M-0359]. In the Ninth Circuit a rightsholder must consider fair use before sending a takedown [M-0360]. The test is subjective good faith [M-0361] (Lenz v. Universal, court decision).
- The Copyright Office 2020 report (a report, not law) recommends only fine tuning of 512 [M-0373]. It says courts may read knowledge requirements more narrowly than Congress meant [M-0374], that willful blindness needs deliberate avoidance of specific infringements [M-0375], and that the Fourth Circuit reads repeat infringer as repeat alleged infringer [M-0376]. It says notice and staydown needs further study [M-0377].

#### EU: Directive 2019/790 Article 17 (foreign law)
- A content sharing service provider communicates to the public when it gives access to user uploads, and needs authorisation [M-0387]. The Article 14(1) hosting safe harbor does not apply to these situations [M-0388].
- Without authorisation the provider is liable unless it made best efforts to get one [M-0389], best efforts to high industry standards to make identified works unavailable [M-0390], and acted expeditiously on notice and made best efforts to prevent re-upload [M-0391].
- Providers under three years old with turnover under EUR 10 million face a lighter regime [M-0392].
- Users may rely on quotation, criticism, review, caricature, parody or pastiche [M-0393]. There is no general monitoring duty [M-0394]. Complaints get human review of disable or remove decisions [M-0395].
- CJEU Poland v Parliament (C-401/19, 26 April 2022) upheld Article 17 [M-0396]. Providers cannot be required to filter content whose unlawfulness needs an independent assessment of context and exceptions [M-0397].
- Commission 2021 guidance (non-binding) says automated blocking at upload should in principle cover only manifestly infringing uploads [M-0398].
- Text and data mining exceptions (CDSM Arts 3 and 4) are an AI topic, not a Content ID rule: Art 3 for research bodies [M-0399], Art 4 unless rightholders reserved use in machine readable form [M-0400, M-0442]. National transposition varies [M-0442].

#### Platform sound libraries and library licences (platform terms)
- TikTok Commercial Music Library: a user engaging in Commercial Uses may post videos with Commercial Sounds only within TikTok [M-0382]. Posting on third party platforms needs separate rights-holder licences [M-0383]. Sounds may not be used with content that breaks TikTok's Terms or Community Guidelines [M-0384]. Edition 2026-11-10.
- Meta Sound Collection: licence limited to Meta products [M-0385]. This is a 2022 terms copy archived 2023-08-18. The current copy was not obtained.
- Epidemic Sound: the personal licence is for the licensee's own personal use [M-0404] and does not allow sublicensing [M-0405]. Edition SingleTrackLicensesV8.
- Musicbed: the licence is per single audiovisual project and excludes public performance where a PRO licence is available [M-0408].
- Artlist: the saved text is only the site terms of use, and the music licence is not in it [M-0410].

### Gotchas
- Absence findings (Artlist site terms, YouTube Audio Library page) mean nothing was found in one saved page [M-0410, M-0411]. They do not prove permission.
- Gap, needs source: TikTok Community Guidelines are unchecked, and the current Meta Sound Collection terms were not obtained [M-0385, M-0384]. The Artlist music licence is not saved [M-0410].
- Library terms change. All editions here were captured 2026-11-10 except Meta (2023-08-18) and Pond5 (archive capture, October 2026). Recheck before relying.
- Content ID is not a licence. A claim or monetize outcome is a platform rule between owner and platform, not a grant to any other platform [M-0378] (analysis).
- A takedown sender who ignores fair use can face 512(f) damages in the Ninth Circuit [M-0360, M-0359], but a counter notice sent in bad faith carries perjury and misrepresentation risk too [M-0356, M-0359].
- Copyright Office report views are not law [M-0373, M-0376]. Commission guidance is non-binding [M-0398].
- 512(c)(1)(B) has a contested case law gloss on "right and ability to control" not covered by the ledger [M-0347].

### Open questions for counsel
- US: does a platform's live streaming fit 512(c) storage at a user's direction, or is it outside the safe harbor?
- US: is an in-app sound picker backed by a library licence a direct licence to the platform, or only to the creator, and do the use limits in that licence bind?
- US: does a re-encode or audio processing tool qualify as a service provider under 512, or does it face direct liability for copying audio?
- US and EU: should a platform adopt audio fingerprinting now, and if it does, does acting on matches create knowledge that cuts against the safe harbor?
- EU: is a user upload platform an online content sharing service provider under Article 17, and does the three year startup tier apply [M-0392]?

==== FILE: 03-sampling-infringement-ownership.md ====

# Music law knowledge pack: Sampling, infringement, ownership and deals
- File: 03-sampling-infringement-ownership.md, part of the music law knowledge pack (remix edition).
- Contains: M11 Sampling and interpolation; M12 Infringement, fair use, registration, damages, limitations; M13 Work for hire, transfers, termination; M14 Deal terms. Each card is followed by the claims it cites, with source, pinpoint and verbatim quote.
- Law last checked: 2026-11-10.
- Research tool, not legal advice. Have a licensed music attorney confirm anything before you act on it.
- Claim ids are M- plus four digits in square brackets. VERIFIED claims were checked against the saved source text. Claims tagged (unverified) were not confirmed; say so when you rely on one.

## M11 Sampling and interpolation
- Law last checked: 2026-11-10. Volatility: medium.
- Use for questions like: Can a user put a short sample of a song or beat in a mix; Is a tiny or unrecognizable sample safe (de minimis); Does re-recording a riff or a sound-alike avoid the recording owner; If a platform licenses the recording does it also need the composition; Does fair use cover a few seconds of a sample; Does splitting or re-encoding user audio create sampling risk

### Bottom line
- US federal law: an unlicensed sample needs a licence from the recording owner (master) and, if the composition is recognizably used, from the composition owner (publisher). Which of two circuits you are in decides whether "too small to matter" works as a defence [M-0249, M-0021]. The two-licence point rests on [M-0108, M-0193].
- Re-recording a riff (interpolation) or a sound-alike avoids the master owner only. The composition is still a separate copyright and still needs a licence [M-0111].
- No statute gives a safe number of seconds, and fair use is argued case by case [M-0203, M-0251].
- The section 114 statutory licence does not cover samples in video, so direct sync and master licences are needed [M-0112, M-0312]. (analysis) We have no saved row on section 115.

### Rules
- Two copyrights exist in a recording: the sound recording (master) and the musical work (composition). Both carry the reproduction right [M-0108].
- Recording owners hold only the 106(1), (2), (3) and (6) rights, and the recording's reproduction right covers only duplication that recaptures the actual sounds [M-0296, M-0110].
- Sound-alikes: an independent fixation of other sounds that imitates the recording does not infringe the sound recording copyright, per 114(b) [M-0111]. Narrow: it must be wholly new sounds, not recaptured ones.
- The musical work remains separate, so (analysis) a sound-alike or replayed interpolation still needs a musical work licence [M-0111]. Right of publicity and false endorsement are not covered here (see M17).
- Sixth Circuit (court decision): for sampling a sound recording the rule is "Get a license or do not sample", with no de minimis inquiry [M-0186].
- Ninth Circuit (court decision, VMG Salsoul, 2016): the de minimis exception applies to sound recording sampling, and the court disagrees with the Sixth Circuit [M-0188, M-0189, M-0021].
- The Ninth Circuit reads the statute and history as keeping de minimis for recordings [M-0190].
- Ninth Circuit test: a taking is de minimis only if the average audience would not recognize the appropriation [M-0191]. A three-note sample of a composition (licensed recording) was de minimis in Newton v. Diamond [M-0192].
- Other circuits are not settled in the saved set. Venue matters and a plaintiff may choose a forum (analysis, inference) [M-0249].
- Grand Upright (S.D.N.Y. 1991, district court): preliminary injunction against unlicensed sampling, with a referral to the US Attorney for possible prosecution under 17 U.S.C. 506(a) and 18 U.S.C. 2319.
- A licence for one copyright does not clear the other. In Estate of Smith v. Cash Money (S.D.N.Y. 2017) the defendants had a licence for the recording but not the composition, and that gap created the composition claim [M-0193, M-0250].
- Same case: a 35-second sample was held a fair use on its facts (district court) [M-0212]. Fair use is an affirmative defence, and the party asserting it bears the burden [M-0211]. This case is an adverse example for "licence one, skip the other" only in that fair use happened to win; it is not a safe harbour [M-0250].
- Fair use: 17 U.S.C. 107 sets a four factor, non-exhaustive test and states no number of seconds [M-0203]. The fourth factor is market effect [M-0204]. Background music in a monetised video must be argued on its facts (analysis) [M-0251].
- Proving a sample or copy claim for compositions: the Ninth Circuit en banc rejected the inverse ratio rule [M-0194]. In the Fifth Circuit even overwhelming proof of access does not establish factual copying without probative similarity [M-0195], and copying can be inferred without access only if works are strikingly similar [M-0196]. Batiste affirmed summary judgment for defendants on no evidence of copying [M-0197].
- Interpolation claims turn on protectable expression. Commonplace elements without an original combination are not protected (Ninth Circuit, Gray v. Hudson) [M-0200]. Sheeran (2d Cir. 2024): a selection and arrangement claim built on a four chord progression and syncopated harmonic rhythm failed as a matter of law [M-0202]. For pre-1978 works the 1909 Act protects the composition as defined by the deposited sheet music [M-0201].
- Williams v. Gaye (9th Cir. 2018): the Blurred Lines verdict stood because there was not an absolute absence of evidence of similarity [M-0198, M-0199].
- Statutory licences do not reach a short video: a "digital audio transmission" excludes any audiovisual work [M-0112, M-0297], and the 114(d)(2) licence also requires a non-interactive service [M-0115, M-0298]. 114 would in any case not clear the composition [M-0313].

### Gotchas
- "Sampling is fair use" is wrong as a rule. Estate of Smith found fair use on its own facts, in a district court, and we have no saved row on any later Second Circuit decision (needs source) [M-0212].
- "Licensing the recording clears the song" is wrong. The case behind it was sued on the composition [M-0193].
- The Sixth versus Ninth Circuit split is as of the saved opinions. Later Supreme Court review of the split is not in the saved set (as of 2026-11-10).
- Sound-alike safety is only for the master, only for wholly independent fixation [M-0111].
- Grand Upright and Estate of Smith are district court decisions. Grand Upright was a preliminary injunction, not a final judgment [M-0187].
- Pre-1978 works: composition rights follow the deposited sheet music in the Second Circuit [M-0201].
- Pending bills and AI sound-alike issues are in M15 to M17, not here.

### Open questions for counsel
- US federal, Second, Sixth, Ninth Circuits: which de minimis rule would a court apply to an unlicensed sample in a video hosted by a platform, and where could a plaintiff sue?
- US federal: if a platform is a host under 512 (see M08), does a sample claim change its safe harbour position?
- US federal: what clearance wording should a platform require when a creator says a sample is "cleared"?
- US federal: does a platform's server-side re-encoding and storage of a user's audio create reproduction, performance or host-style exposure for the platform, especially without terms of use or a DMCA contact?
- US federal: what is the current status of Estate of Smith on appeal (a 2d Cir. 2020 summary order is mentioned in some reports but we have no row for it), and does it support a fair use position on short samples?

## M12 Infringement, fair use, registration, damages, limitations
- Law last checked: 2026-11-10. Volatility: medium.
- Use for questions like: Is a 15 second clip of a song in a monetised mix fair use; How much can a copyright owner recover from a platform or a user; Does an owner have to register before suing; How long after an upload can a music claim be brought; How does a plaintiff prove a song was copied; Does a mix that uses many songs multiply the damages

### Bottom line
US federal law: using a song in a video without a licence can infringe whichever copyright is used, unless a defence such as fair use applies, the composition, the recording, or both [M-0220, M-0028, M-0029]. Fair use is a case by case defence with no safe number of seconds [M-0203, M-0251]. Statutory damages run $750 to $30,000 per work, up to $150,000 if willful, but only for works registered in time [M-0215, M-0217, M-0214]. The suit deadline is three years from accrual, and a timely claim can reach old infringements (discovery rule assumed) [M-0218, M-0219].

### Rules
#### Infringement and proof (US federal unless stated)
- Anyone who violates an exclusive right of the copyright owner is an infringer [M-0220].
- Musical works, including accompanying words, are protected [M-0028]. Sound recordings are a separate category [M-0029, M-0105]. One song is therefore two works (analysis, M-0254).
- Ninth Circuit en banc (court decision, 2020): the inverse ratio rule is rejected, so strong proof of access does not lower the similarity showing [M-0194].
- Fifth Circuit (court decision, 2020): even with overwhelming proof of access, factual copying needs some probative similarity [M-0195]. Without proof of access, copying can be inferred only if the works are strikingly similar [M-0196]. Summary judgment for the defendants was affirmed for lack of evidence of copying [M-0197].
- Ninth Circuit (court decision, 2018, Blurred Lines): the verdict stood because evidence of extrinsic and intrinsic similarity was not absent [M-0199]. The panel affirmed in part and reversed in part: damages and a running royalty were proper, while the vicarious liability finding and one party's verdict were reversed [M-0198].
- Ninth Circuit (court decision, 2022, Dark Horse): commonplace musical elements, without an original combination, are not protected, so the verdict was set aside [M-0200].
- Second Circuit (court decision, 2024, Thinking Out Loud): a pre 1978 work under the 1909 Act is protected only as to the composition as defined by the deposited sheet music [M-0201]. A selection and arrangement claim built on a four chord progression and syncopated harmonic rhythm failed as a matter of law [M-0202].

#### Fair use
- Section 107 is a four factor, non exhaustive test and states no number of seconds [M-0203]. Factor four is the effect on the potential market for or value of the work [M-0204].
- Campbell (Supreme Court, 1994): fair use is case by case and bright line rules do not fit [M-0205]. Factor one asks whether the new work merely supersedes the original or adds new expression, meaning or message [M-0206]. The more transformative the use, the less weight commercialism carries [M-0207].
- Warhol (Supreme Court, 2023): factor one asks whether the use has a further purpose or different character, a matter of degree weighed against commercialism [M-0208]. The court looked at the specific use alleged to infringe, there the licensing, not the work in the abstract [M-0210]. Licensing the image to a magazine did not favour fair use [M-0209].
- Analysis: fair use is decided on the facts, including commercial nature and amount used, so background music in a monetised video must be argued case by case [M-0251].

#### Registration, damages, limitations
- Subject to exceptions in section 411, no civil action for infringement of a US work may start until preregistration or registration has been made [M-0213].
- No statutory damages or fees for infringement of a published work that began before registration, unless registered within three months of publication [M-0214].
- Statutory damages: $750 to $30,000 per work, at the owner's election [M-0215]. They are assessed per work for all infringements in the action and may be elected any time before final judgment [M-0216]. Willful infringement raises the maximum to $150,000 per work [M-0217].
- Analysis: exposure is per work, not per view or per video, and a song can be two works, composition and recording [M-0254].
- Civil limitations period: three years after the claim accrued [M-0218].
- Nealy (Supreme Court, 2024): assuming without deciding that the discovery rule applies, a timely claim can recover damages for any infringement, with no separate three year damages bar [M-0024, M-0219].

#### Safe harbour link (court decision)
- Fourth Circuit, BMG v. Cox (2018): a provider needs a repeat infringer policy adopted and reasonably implemented to use the section 512 safe harbour [M-0230]. Cox lost it by not enforcing the policy meaningfully [M-0231, M-0253]. The provider bears the burden of proof [M-0233].
- BMG's "knew or should have known" contributory standard was called negligence and too low [M-0232]. The Supreme Court in Cox (2026) later held contributory liability cannot rest only on knowledge plus insufficient action [M-0224].

### Gotchas
- No seconds rule, no "non commercial" rule, no "credit the artist" rule. The four factors decide [M-0203, M-0205].
- Transformative is a matter of degree and is judged on the specific use; licensing or monetising weighs against it [M-0208, M-0209, M-0210].
- Nealy assumed the discovery rule without deciding it [M-0024]. Do not say the Supreme Court adopted it.
- Fifth and Ninth Circuit similarity rules differ in detail; name the circuit [M-0195, M-0194]. Batiste is a Fifth Circuit rule on access, not nationwide [M-0196].
- Sheeran concerns a pre 1978 work and the 1909 Act only [M-0201].
- Williams v. Gaye is mixed: verdict stood, vicarious liability reversed [M-0198].
- BMG v. Cox on contributory liability is overtaken by Cox 2026 [M-0232, M-0224]. Its repeat infringer point on section 512(i) stands [M-0230].
- Statutory damage figures are those in the saved text as of 2026-11-10 [M-0215].
- State publicity claims and Section 230 differ by circuit: Third Circuit Hepp (2021) held 230 does not preclude them, while the Ninth Circuit reads the carve out as federal IP only [M-0485, M-0486]. Extension to voice clones is inference; see M16 and M17.
- Currency: Grande remand outcome is a needs source gap; do not guess.

### Open questions for counsel
- US federal: for a monetised video with 20 seconds of a commercial track under a creator's own edit, what is the realistic fair use position under Campbell and Warhol?
- US federal: which of a platform's catalogue risks are registered works, and does section 412 limit statutory damages for newly registered music?
- Ninth Circuit: does accrual under section 507(b) follow the discovery rule for continuing uploads, given Nealy only assumed it?
- US federal: does a live stream performance of a track create separate infringements per stream for damages purposes?
- US federal: does a platform's re-encoding of user audio expose the platform itself to a direct or secondary claim?

## M13 Work for hire, transfers, termination
- Law last checked: 2026-11-10. Volatility: medium.
- Use for questions like: Who owns a song or recording a creator made for a label or publisher; Does a user who mixes others' music own the mix; Can a songwriter or artist take back a music grant years later; Does a licence signed before termination survive it; Does a transfer need to be in writing; Who owns music made for the platform by a contractor

### Bottom line
US federal law: the first owner of a copyright is the author, unless the work is made for hire, in which case the employer or commissioning party is the author [M-0037, M-0048]. A transfer of ownership needs a signed writing [M-0040]. Authors (not work-for-hire employers) can usually terminate grants decades later, and no contract can waive that right [M-0055, M-0059]. For a platform this decides who can sign a sync licence (composition) or a master use licence (recording): you must trace title from the author through every transfer, and no ownership claim by a creator, label or publisher proves a song is cleared.

This is not legal advice. A licensed music attorney must confirm chain of title, work for hire clauses and termination notices before anyone relies on this card.

### Rules
#### Who is the author (US federal, 17 U.S.C. 101 and 201)
- Copyright vests initially in the author; authors of a joint work are co-owners [M-0037]. A joint work is made by two or more authors who intend their contributions to merge into a unitary whole [M-0036].
- A work made for hire is either work by an employee within the scope of employment, or a commissioned work in one of nine listed categories with a signed written agreement [M-0045].
- For commissioned works the categories include a contribution to a collective work, part of a motion picture or other audiovisual work, and a compilation, and the parties must expressly agree in a signed writing [M-0046].
- The employer or commissioning party is the author and owns all rights unless the parties agree otherwise in a signed writing [M-0048].
- The category list does not name sound recordings. Whether a recording is made for hire turns on the employee prong or on fitting a category such as compilation or part of an audiovisual work (analysis) [M-0047].
- Courts apply the 1909 Act "instance and expense" test to older works when deciding work made for hire under Section 304(c): Marvel v. Kirby (2d Cir. 2013) (court decision) [M-0054]. The saved quote is PARTIAL (line numbers interleave), so rely on the claim, not a block quote.
- Waite v. UMG (S.D.N.Y. 31 March 2020, motion to dismiss) (court decision): the court did not decide whether the recordings were made for hire, because the label raised it only on limitations. It found the label's authority for treating albums as compilations unpersuasive [M-0049]. It also noted that the industry frequently inserts work-for-hire language into recording contracts [M-0050]. The artists had asked for a declaration that recordings cannot be made for hire; that is a pleading, not a holding [M-0051].
- Ray Charles Foundation v. Robinson (9th Cir. 2015) (court decision): the foundation could challenge whether works were made for hire, and so not terminable. It was a real party in interest and had standing. The merits were not decided [M-0069, M-0070].

#### Transfers (US federal, 17 U.S.C. 201, 204, 205)
- Ownership can be transferred in whole or part by any means of conveyance or by operation of law [M-0038]. Each exclusive right, and any subdivision, can be owned separately [M-0039].
- A transfer of ownership, other than by operation of law, is not valid unless in a writing signed by the owner or the owner's authorized agent [M-0040].
- "Transfer of copyright ownership" covers an assignment or exclusive licence but not a nonexclusive licence [M-0034]. So a nonexclusive licence is not caught by the Section 204(a) writing rule as a transfer (analysis, narrow).
- A signed transfer can be recorded in the Copyright Office, with a real signature or a sworn or official certification of a true copy [M-0041].
- Between two conflicting transfers, the first executed wins if recorded within one month (two months abroad) or before the later one is recorded [M-0042]. The statute has a further rule for the later transfer (see 17 U.S.C. 205(d)); it is not covered by a ledger row here.
- A nonexclusive licence, recorded or not, beats a conflicting transfer if it is in a signed written instrument and was taken before the transfer or in good faith before its recordation and without notice [M-0043].

#### Which copyright, which grant
- A recording and the underlying composition are separate works with separate copyrights [M-0025]. The Office treats a recording as a derivative work of the composition [M-0026, M-0035]. Authors differ: composition by composers, lyricists and songwriters; recording by performers, producers and sound engineers as the circular lists them [M-0027].
- Section 101 excludes sounds accompanying a motion picture or other audiovisual work from "sound recordings" and "phonorecords" [M-0030, M-0031, M-0118, M-0119, M-0337, M-0338]. A music track embedded in a short video is still treated as keeping its own composition and recording copyrights, but that is an inference (unverified) [M-0032].
- Performing rights societies license public performance of nondramatic musical works for owners [M-0341]. They are not the source of a sync or master grant.

#### Duration (US federal)
- Works from 1 January 1978 on: life of the author plus 70 years, with exceptions for joint, anonymous, pseudonymous and made-for-hire works [M-0044].

#### Termination of grants (US federal)
- Section 203 applies to grants by an author executed on or after 1 January 1978, other than works made for hire and other than by will [M-0055]. Window: five years starting 35 years after execution (or after publication, or 40 years after execution, whichever ends earlier, if the grant covers publication) [M-0056].
- Notice is served two to ten years before the effective date [M-0057]. A copy must be recorded before the effective date or termination does not take effect [M-0058].
- It works notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary [M-0059]. Unless terminated, a grant lasts for the term of copyright unless it says otherwise [M-0061].
- Derivative works exception: a derivative work made under the grant before termination may continue to be used under the grant's terms, but no new derivative works may be made afterwards [M-0060].
- A further grant of terminated rights is valid only if made after the effective date, except that the original grantee or its successor can agree a further grant after notice is served [M-0062].
- Section 304(c) covers pre-1978 grants of the renewal term, other than works made for hire [M-0063]. Window: five years starting 56 years after copyright was first secured, or 1 January 1978, whichever is later [M-0064]. Notice is again two to ten years ahead, with a copy recorded [M-0065]. Same derivative works exception [M-0066].
- Mills Music v. Snyder (U.S. Supreme Court 1985) (court decision): a publisher keeps its contractual share of royalties from pre-termination recordings under the 304(c)(6)(A) exception, because the recordings are derivative works used under the grant [M-0067, M-0068].
- Copyright Office final rule, 89 FR 56586 (regulation, effective 8 August 2024): the exception does not apply to any blanket licence, so nobody is treated as owner or royalty payee of a work used under the blanket licence because of that exception [M-0071, M-0073]. It also does not apply to individual download licences, and not to voluntary licences unless the MLC is directed otherwise [M-0072]. The Office issued it because the MLC's termination dispute policy conflicted with Office guidance [M-0074].

### Gotchas
- A "work for hire" label in a contract is not self proving. Statute needs employee status or a listed category plus a signed writing [M-0045, M-0046].
- Recordings: the categories do not name sound recordings, and no case in this card decides the point [M-0047, M-0049].
- Termination cannot be contracted away [M-0059]. Work made for hire is outside it [M-0055, M-0063], so the work for hire fight is also the termination fight [M-0070].
- Termination timing: Section 203 grants made from 1978 open their window 35 years later, so the earliest windows are already open (analysis, arithmetic from [M-0056]). The 304(c) window uses 56 years [M-0064].
- Termination needs recorded notice. An unrecorded notice does not take effect [M-0058].
- Mills Music (1985) still stands in the saved record, but the 2024 Office rule bars the exception for the MLC blanket licence [M-0067, M-0071]. Do not state the 2024 rule as limiting voluntary licences without the MLC direction clause [M-0072].
- Ray Charles decided standing, not whether the works were for hire [M-0069].
- Waite (S.D.N.Y.), Marvel (2d Cir.) and Ray Charles (9th Cir.) are lower court decisions, not Supreme Court rulings, and bind only their own court or circuit. Other courts may differ (analysis).
- Waite is a motion to dismiss ruling (31 March 2020). It decided nothing on the merits of work for hire [M-0049]. Later history is not in the ledger.
- Marvel v. Kirby: the quote is PARTIAL, and later history of the judgment against two defendants is not in the saved source [M-0054].
- M-0032 is an inference about the audio of a short video and stays unverified. Say so in any answer.
- Not in the ledger: foreign termination or work for hire rules (UK and EU are other cards), state law on assignments, the Estate of Smith (2d Cir. 2020) text, any Grande or later history. Say "not checked", never guess.

### Open questions for counsel
- US: does this creator agreement (attach it) make a commissioned recording a work made for hire, or is a separate written assignment needed?
- US: for this track, what is the chain of title for the composition and the recording, and can the grantor sign a sync and master licence on the grant date?
- US: has a Section 203 or 304(c) notice been served or recorded against this catalogue, and does the derivative works exception reach new videos?
- US: does a platform's creator licence, as written, cover music a creator claims to own, and what warranty and indemnity should it contain?
- US: are a platform's terms of use enough where a user uploads audio they do not own?
- US: after the 2024 Office rule, how should a licensor and payee be identified where an MLC blanket licence and a terminated grant overlap?

## M14 Deal terms
- Law last checked: 2026-11-10. Volatility: medium.
- Use for questions like: Who owns a song after a record deal or publishing deal; Does a transfer of music rights need a signed writing; Can an artist terminate a label grant and what happens to mixes already made; Who can license a song for sync in a video, and is that negotiated each time; Does the Spotify or label deal cover use in a user mix; Can a performer's digital replica be licensed in a services contract

### Bottom line
- US federal: a transfer of copyright ownership needs a writing signed by the owner [M-0040]. A nonexclusive licence is not a transfer, but a signed written licence can beat a later transfer [M-0043]. Sync (the composition) and master use (the recording) are negotiated directly with the rights holders [M-0080, M-0140].
- Label and publisher deals decide who controls each copyright. Public company filings say most label artist deals are work made for hire, with royalties, recoupable advances and options [M-0052, M-0075, M-0076]. These are company statements, not law.
- A streaming service's licences do not cover another platform. They are the service's own contracts [M-0083, M-0084]. A platform needs its own direct licences for music in video.
- Termination rights (17 U.S.C. 203) can reopen grants after 35 years, but a derivative work made before termination may keep being used [M-0056, M-0060]. Never promise that a song is cleared; ask the holder.

### Rules
#### Transfers and records (US federal, statute)
- A transfer of ownership, other than by operation of law, is not valid unless in a writing signed by the owner or the owner's authorized agent [M-0040]. Plain English: a handshake or a text thread does not move ownership. An exclusive licence is a transfer of ownership, so it also needs the signed writing (analysis).
- A transfer or other document may be recorded in the Copyright Office if signed, or certified as a true copy of the signed original [M-0041].
- Of two conflicting transfers, the first executed wins if recorded within one month after signing in the US (two abroad) or before the later transfer is recorded [M-0042].
- A signed written nonexclusive licence, recorded or not, prevails over a conflicting transfer if taken before the transfer or in good faith before its recordation and without notice [M-0043].

#### Work made for hire and the label practice (court decision, industry)
- Warner Music Group says virtually all its agreements with artists since 1971 provide that artists render services as work made for hire [M-0052]. Reservoir Media says the same of its recording artist agreements and says a termination right exists for compositions not made for hire [M-0099]. Both are the companies' own statements about their practice, not rules.
- WMG warns that if a recording were found not to be made for hire, artists or heirs could terminate US rights in a window starting 35 years after release for post 1977 grants [M-0053]. The statute counts from execution of the grant, see below.
- Waite v. UMG (S.D.N.Y. 31 March 2020, motion to dismiss): the court did not decide whether the recordings were works made for hire, because the label raised it only on limitations [M-0049]. It said the label's limitations argument was weakened by the industry habit of inserting work made for hire language, which would force artists to sue within three years or lose the Section 203 right [M-0050]. The artists sought a declaration that sound recordings cannot be works made for hire; the court called authorship a close issue on limitations [M-0051]. This is a pleading stage ruling, not a final holding.
- Ray Charles Foundation v. Robinson (9th Cir. 2015): the estate's sole beneficiary had standing to challenge termination notices [M-0069] and could challenge whether the works were made for hire and so not terminable [M-0070]. Standing only; the merits were not decided [M-0069].

#### Termination, 17 U.S.C. 203 (statute)
- Section 203 applies to grants by an author executed on or after 1 January 1978, other than works made for hire and wills [M-0055].
- The window is five years starting 35 years after execution of the grant (or 35 years after publication or 40 after execution, whichever ends earlier, if the grant covers publication) [M-0056].
- Notice must be served two to ten years before the effective date [M-0057], and a copy must be recorded before that date to take effect [M-0058].
- Termination works notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary [M-0059]. Unless terminated, a grant lasts for the term of copyright [M-0061].
- A derivative work made under the grant before termination may keep being used on the grant's terms. No new derivative works may be made after termination [M-0060]. A further grant is valid only after the effective date, except that the original grantee may agree to one after notice is served [M-0062].
- Copyright Office 2024 final rule (regulation, effective 8 August 2024): the derivative works exception does not apply to any blanket licence [M-0071], nor to any individual download licence, nor to any voluntary licence unless the MLC is directed otherwise [M-0072]. The Office acted because the MLC's termination dispute policy conflicted with Office guidance [M-0074]. Four listed sections applied immediately; MLC compliance with the rest waited for a later payee snapshot, and the Office may extend deadlines [M-0073].

#### How the deals are built (industry practice, company filings)
- Artist deals: royalties on sales and other uses, advances recoupable from future royalties, recording costs typically recoupable [M-0075]. A typical new artist contract requires delivery of an EP or album and gives the label a series of options [M-0076]. Many deals are expanded rights (360) deals sharing touring, merchandising, sponsorship and other income [M-0077, M-0078].
- Publishing: WMG's publisher owns or administers compositions and earns mechanical, performance, sync, digital and other income [M-0079]. Each sync licence is generally negotiated with the prospective licensee, and the publisher pays a contractual share of sync income to songwriters or heirs [M-0080]. Reservoir says the same, with co-publishers also sharing [M-0100]. WMG defines sync as use of the composition in combination with visual images [M-0081].
- The Copyright Office said in 2015 that consumer audiovisual (sync) uses should stay in the free market, with no compulsory licence recommended [M-0140]. Sync is an industry term for reproduction (and possibly derivative) rights in a work synchronized to visual content [M-0141]. This is a regulator report, not binding.
- Reservoir licenses sync to film, television, advertising and digital platforms from social media to fitness; sync was 13% of revenue for the year ended 31 March 2026 [M-0102]. Such social media sync deals are direct licences (analysis).
- Reservoir licenses digital music services itself or through a distributor, with fees set licence by licence [M-0104]. It treats its songwriters and artists as independent contractors and flags reclassification risk [M-0103]. It also owns or acquires label, catalogue and income participation interests [M-0101].
- Distribution deals end by contract: WMG's ADA unit distributed BMG's recordings until the agreement ended in September 2023 [M-0082].

#### What a streaming licence looks like (company filing)
- Spotify takes sound recording and audiovisual licences from the three major label groups and Merlin, with royalties, marketing commitments and operating rules, audit and termination rights [M-0083]. They are generally multi-year, not automatically renewable, worldwide, and terminable for non-payment, material breach or change of control [M-0084]. It also licenses independent labels and aggregators such as CD Baby, DistroKid and TuneCore [M-0085].
- For compositions, Spotify generally gets mechanical, performance and lyric rights. For audio only use in the US, mechanicals run through the Section 115 licence and the MLC blanket licence since January 2021 [M-0086]. That statutory route is audio only, not video.
- Spotify has recently entered direct licences with some US publishers for audiovisual and other rights [M-0087]. US performance rights come through ASCAP, BMI, GMR and SESAC blanket licences with usage reporting and one to four year terms [M-0088]. Failing to obtain or keep licences is a stated business risk [M-0089].

#### UK (foreign law)
- The author is first owner [M-0090]. An employee's musical work or film belongs first to the employer, subject to contrary agreement [M-0091]. The author of a sound recording is the producer [M-0092]. So (analysis) a UK sound recording's first owner is the producer, as the employer rule does not list sound recordings [M-0093].
- An assignment must be in writing signed by or for the assignor [M-0096]. An exclusive licence must be in writing signed by or for the owner [M-0097]. An agreement to assign future copyright, signed by the prospective owner, takes effect as an assignment when the copyright arises [M-0098].
- The owner has exclusive rights to copy, issue, rent, lend, perform, communicate to the public and adapt [M-0234]. Infringement includes authorising another to do a restricted act [M-0235]. Communication to the public covers musical works and recordings [M-0236], including on demand availability [M-0237]. (Analysis) a UK facing platform may face direct or authorising liability [M-0255].

#### Digital replicas in deals (California, statute)
- Digital replica means a computer generated, highly realistic representation readily identifiable as a person's voice or visual likeness [M-0447].
- Producing or making available a deceased personality's digital replica in an expressive audiovisual work or sound recording without consent carries the greater of $10,000 or actual damages, subject to listed exceptions [M-0448].
- A contract term letting a digital replica replace in person work is unenforceable for new performances from 1 January 2025 if it lacks a reasonably specific description of uses and the individual had no representation [M-0449].

### Gotchas
- WMG and Reservoir lines describe each company's contracts. Courts have not all agreed that recordings are works made for hire (analysis from M-0049, M-0051). Waite is a motion to dismiss ruling only.
- WMG says the window is 35 years from release; the statute counts from execution, or publication for grants covering it [M-0053, M-0056].
- Termination cannot be waived by contract [M-0059], so a deal clause saying otherwise does not stop it.
- Filings are dated: WMG fiscal year ended 30 September 2025, Spotify year ended 31 December 2025, Reservoir year ended 31 March 2026. Terms and licence lengths change.
- The Spotify direct publisher AV deals are narrow: some US publishers only [M-0087]. Do not read them as a general video licence.
- The M-0086 statutory route is audio only. A mechanical licence is not sync.
- California digital replica rows are statutes as captured 2026-11-10. California Civil Code 3344.1 covers deceased personalities, not living ones [M-0448].
- UK rules above are English law under the CDPA, not a UK guide to platform liability. UK platform case law is not in the ledger [M-0255].
- Blurring, muting or low audio quality is not a licence, and "the creator said it was theirs" is not a signed writing.

### Open questions for counsel
- US: does an uploader's licence from a distributor or aggregator ever include sync or master use for short video, or only audio distribution?
- US: if a creator's deal is a 360 or expanded rights deal, can the label claim a share of platform earnings from a video using the label's master?
- US: what warranty and indemnity should a platform require from creators who say they hold sync and master rights?
- US: does a platform's re-encoding of creator audio count as a covered use under common creator side licences, or does it need its own terms?
- US: for a catalogue song where the grant was terminated, who now grants sync, and how does a platform video made before termination continue [M-0060]?
- UK: does a platform need a UK licence structure if UK users can stream uploads, and who is the first owner of a creator made recording?
- California: do a platform's creator terms need a reasonably specific description of uses to survive Lab. Code 927 for voice or likeness [M-0449]?
- What currency check is due on the open gaps: Artlist licence terms, TikTok Community Guidelines and current Meta Sound Collection terms?

- Source: California Civil Code s.3344.1 Deceased personality's name, voice, likeness; digital replicas, as amended by AB 1836 (2024) (public.law mirror) (https://california.public.law/codes/civil_code_section_3344.1), source id ca-civ-3344-1
- Pinpoint: 3344.1(a)(2)(A)(i)
- Quote: "shall be liable to any injured party in an amount equal to the greater of ten thousand dollars ($10,000) or the actual damages suffered"
- Checked: 2026-11-10

#### [M-0449] VERIFIED
- Claim: Cal. Lab. Code 927: a contract term allowing a digital replica of voice or likeness in place of in-person work is unenforceable for new performances from Jan. 1, 2025 if it lacks a reasonably specific description of uses and the individual lacked representation.
- Jurisdiction: US-CA
- Source: California Labor Code s.927 Digital replica contract provisions, AB 2602 (2024) (public.law mirror) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_927), source id ca-lab-927
- Pinpoint: Lab. Code 927(a)
- Quote: "is unenforceable only as it relates to a new performance, fixed on or after January 1, 2025, by a digital replica"
- Checked: 2026-11-10


==== FILE: 04-ai-voice-publicity.md ====

# Music law knowledge pack: AI, voice clones and publicity
- File: 04-ai-voice-publicity.md, part of the music law knowledge pack (remix edition).
- Contains: M15 AI training and outputs; M16 Voice clones and digital replicas; M17 Publicity and false endorsement. Each card is followed by the claims it cites, with source, pinpoint and verbatim quote.
- Law last checked: 2026-11-10.
- Research tool, not legal advice. Have a licensed music attorney confirm anything before you act on it.
- Claim ids are M- plus four digits in square brackets. VERIFIED claims were checked against the saved source text. Claims tagged (unverified) were not confirmed; say so when you rely on one.

## M15 AI training and outputs
- Law last checked: 2026-11-10. Volatility: high.
- Use for questions like: Can a user put AI generated music in a mix; Who owns AI generated music; Is training an AI model on songs fair use; Does the TRAIN Act or any AI music bill apply today; Does the EU or UK let AI companies train on music; Can a platform process audio a user made with AI

### Bottom line
US federal law has no AI training rule in a statute. Whether training on recordings and songs is fair use is undecided for music: the fair use test is case by case, and the only US training rulings saved are about books, not music [M-0203, M-0421]. Purely AI-generated material is not copyrightable in the Copyright Office's view, so a creator who prompts a generator may own little or nothing in the track [M-0415, M-0416]. AI output can still copy a real song, so a licence or consent question remains for both copyrights, the composition and the master. As of 2026-11-10 the TRAIN Act is a bill, not law [M-0006].

### Rules
#### US federal: training
- Section 107 makes fair use a four factor, non exhaustive test, and the statute states no number of seconds or safe length [M-0203]. Factor four is the effect on the market for or value of the work [M-0204].
- Copyright Office, Part 3 report (regulator guidance, pre-publication version of May 2025, persuasive not binding): the Office expects some training uses will be fair use and some will not [M-0418, M-0020]. As of 2026-11-10 no final Part 3 is published [M-0020].
- The same report says fairness depends on which works were used, from what source, for what purpose, and with what controls on outputs [M-0419]. It treats lost licensing revenue as part of market harm [M-0420].
- Bartz v. Anthropic (court decision, N.D. Cal., 23 June 2025, district court, books not music): training on lawfully acquired books was fair use, described as exceedingly transformative [M-0421]. Downloading and keeping pirated copies for a central library was not excused, and the court set a trial on those copies [M-0422]. Later settlement and appeals are not in the saved sources.
- Kadrey v. Meta (court decision, N.D. Cal., 25 June 2025): the judge said in many circumstances it will be illegal to copy protected works to train generative AI without permission [M-0423]. That is dicta in a market dilution discussion; the same order gave Meta summary judgment on that record. Do not cite it as a holding that training is illegal.
- Music cases are pleadings and procedure so far. UMG, Capitol and Sony sued Suno in D. Mass. in June 2024 (No. 1:24-cv-11611) alleging copying of recordings to train its model [M-0424] (pleading, not a finding). The UMG complaint against Udio pleaded that unlicensed AI services could saturate the market and compete with genuine recordings [M-0430] (allegation only).
- UMG dismissed its claims against Udio on 3 November 2025 and Warner dismissed on 25 November 2025, without prejudice [M-0011, M-0429]. Warner and Suno stipulated to dismissal of Warner's claims against Suno on 9 December 2025; settlement terms are not in the saved text [M-0012].
- The Suno case continues for the other labels. On 18 August 2026 the court found the labels' 17 U.S.C. 1201(a)(1) stream ripping claim plausible and allowed amendment [M-0013]. That is a pleading ruling, not a merits ruling. Amended complaint filed 25 August 2026 [M-0014]. Suno argued the YouTube measure limits copying but does not control access; the court described that argument and still found the claim plausible [M-0427].
- Section 1201(a)(1)(A) bars circumventing a measure that controls access to a work [M-0489]. Section 1201(a)(2) bars trafficking in circumvention tools [M-0490]. Section 1201 does not affect fair use or other infringement defences [M-0491].
- Concord v. Anthropic (court decision, N.D. Cal., 6 Oct 2025): the court denied dismissal of contributory, vicarious and DMCA 1202(b) claims over lyrics output [M-0492]. Pleading stage, lyrics not audio. Its contributory test predates Cox v. Sony (2026), so do not use it for the current contributory standard (see M09).

#### US federal: outputs and authorship
- Musical works and sound recordings are separate categories of copyrightable work [M-0028, M-0029].
- Copyright Office, Part 2 (regulator guidance, persuasive not binding): copyright does not extend to purely AI-generated material or to material with insufficient human control over expressive elements [M-0415].
- Prompts alone do not give enough control to make the user the author, given current generally available technology [M-0416]. This is tied to today's technology and may change.
- The Office does not recommend legislation on copyrightability and expects courts to give more guidance [M-0417].

#### US federal: pending bill
- TRAIN Act (pending bill, not law): S. 2455, introduced 24 July 2025 by Sen. Welch, referred to Senate Judiciary [M-0478]. H.R. 7209, an identical House bill, introduced 22 January 2026 by Rep. Dean, referred to House Judiciary [M-0505]. Neither is law [M-0006].
- If passed, S. 2455 would let a copyright owner with a good faith belief ask a district court clerk for a subpoena to a generative AI developer for records sufficient to identify the owner's works used in training. It targets the developer, with no host duty [M-0479]. Status files are dated 2026-08-10 (S. 2455) and 2026-08-20 (H.R. 7209) [M-0006].

#### EU
- CDSM Art. 3: text and data mining exception for research organisations and cultural heritage institutions, for scientific research [M-0399].
- CDSM Art. 4: general mining exception for lawfully accessible works, unless the rightholder has reserved use in an appropriate manner [M-0400]. Art. 4(3) limits it to uses not expressly reserved, for online content by machine readable means [M-0442]. National transposition varies.
- AI Act Art. 53(1)(c): providers of general purpose AI models need a copyright policy that identifies and honours Art. 4(3) reservations [M-0439]. Art. 53(1)(d): they must publish a sufficiently detailed training content summary on the AI Office template [M-0440]. These duties apply from 2 August 2025 [M-0441]. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 was read as not amending Art. 53 or 113(b) per the ledger notes, but that regulation text is not saved (needs source).
- The EU GPAI Code of Practice copyright chapter (voluntary, binds signatories only): Measure 1.3(1) commits signatories to comply with machine readable rights reservations when crawling [M-0493]. Measure 1.4(1)(a) commits them to technical safeguards against infringing reproduction in outputs [M-0494].
- GEMA v. OpenAI (foreign court decision, LG Munich I, 11 Nov 2025, 42 O 14139/24, first instance, lyrics not audio): memorising works in a language model is a reproduction [M-0431]. The mining exception covers copies made to build training data but not training the model itself [M-0432]. Model operators, not users, were liable for infringing outputs from simple prompts [M-0433]. Appeal to OLG Munich pending per the source header; later status unchecked.
- CDSM Art. 17 makes an online content sharing service responsible for user uploads and removes the hosting safe harbour for it [M-0387, M-0388]. See M08 and M19 for the upload regime.

#### UK
- CDPA s.29A allows copies for text and data analysis only for non commercial research by a person with lawful access, with acknowledgement [M-0239]. It does not cover commercial training.
- Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 s.135 required an economic impact assessment and s.136 a report, each within nine months of the Act [M-0434, M-0435].
- The s.136 report (March 2026, policy statement not law) says a broad exception with opt out is no longer the preferred option [M-0436, M-0015]. No AI training exception is enacted [M-0436].
- The report proposes removing protection for wholly computer generated works (CDPA s.9(3) type) while keeping protection for AI assisted works [M-0437, M-0016]. Proposal only.
- It says a digital replica or personality right is under further consideration. Exploration only [M-0438]. See M16.
- CDPA s.30A fair dealing for caricature, parody or pastiche exists, and a contract term restricting a permitted act is unenforceable [M-0240, M-0241].

### Gotchas
- "Training is fair use" is not settled for music. The US training rulings saved are about books and are district court orders [M-0421, M-0423]. Kadrey's illegality line is dicta [M-0423].
- Do not call the Udio or Suno dismissals a ruling that AI music is lawful. They are stipulated dismissals with no terms in the saved text [M-0011, M-0012, M-0429].
- Pleadings are not findings [M-0424, M-0430]. The Suno 1201 order is a leave to amend ruling [M-0013].
- The Copyright Office Part 3 is a pre-publication version and persuasive only [M-0418, M-0020]. Part 2 is persuasive, not binding [M-0415].
- The TRAIN Act, and any digital replica bill, are not law [M-0006]. A subpoena right would not itself make training lawful or unlawful [M-0479].
- GEMA v. OpenAI concerns lyrics, first instance, with an appeal pending [M-0431].
- Removing, muting or editing audio is not a licence and does not clear a track. Where the track is protected, the missing licence is sync for the composition and master use for the recording, from the publisher and the label; see M07.
- Currency: Part 3 final, appeals in GEMA, Bartz settlement, the UK policy path and Suno case history all move. Last checked 2026-11-10.

### Open questions for counsel
- US: does a creator who prompts a music generator and edits the result hold a copyright in the output that they can license to a platform?
- US: do a platform's creator terms need an AI disclosure and a warranty that AI music does not copy a protected song?
- US: what Suno or Udio terms, if any, allow commercial use on a user upload platform?
- US: does a platform's processing of creator audio need an express no training clause in its terms and vendor contracts?
- EU: if a platform serves EU users and offers an AI feature, does it count as a general purpose model provider under AI Act Art. 53, or only a downstream deployer?
- EU and UK: what does a reasonable machine readable rights reservation look like for creator uploads on a platform?
- US: has the TRAIN Act moved since 2026-08-20, and is any music AI case on appeal?

## M16 Voice clones and digital replicas
- Law last checked: 2026-11-10. Volatility: high.
- Use for questions like: Can a user put an AI clone of a famous singer's voice in a mix; Is a platform liable for a user mix that contains a voice clone; Does the NO FAKES Act apply to a mixing platform or a processing tool; Which states protect voice; Does a soundalike need a licence; What does the UK protect

### Bottom line
- Jurisdiction first: US federal law has no digital replica statute today. The NO FAKES Act (S. 4591, H.R. 8915) is a bill, not law. As of the saved status file (updated 2026-08-10, last listed action 2026-06-24) S. 4591 was reported and on the Senate calendar, with no floor vote in the file [M-0003, M-0004, M-0465]. H.R. 8915 was referred to committee with no later action in a file updated 2026-10-23 [M-0466].
- Today the rules are state law (Tennessee, California, New York, Illinois), the Lanham Act false endorsement claim, and older voice cases from the Ninth Circuit [M-0443, M-0446, M-0450, M-0456, M-0458, M-0462].
- A voice clone is its own right, apart from the composition and the master. A licence to a song does not clear a clone of a singer's voice. The person whose voice is copied (or an heir, or a label or union holding the right by contract) grants consent. Nobody here can promise a voice is cleared. (analysis)
- Whether any state or bill rule applies to a given platform or tool is a question for a licensed attorney. This card is not legal advice.
- For a platform that hosts user uploads, the main US risks are state voice claims against the person who made the clone and, under some statutes, against those who distribute it knowing it is unauthorized [M-0443, M-0456]. A tool that only re-encodes a user's own file privately likely sits outside the bill's online service definition (unverified) [M-0488].

### Rules
#### US federal (pending bills, not law)
- S. 1367 and H.R. 2794 (2025) were introduced 2025-04-09 and went no further than committee referral [M-0005, M-0463, M-0464]. S. 4591 and H.R. 8915 (2026) were introduced 2026-05-20 [M-0003].
- S. 4591 was reported with a substitute on 2026-06-24 and placed on the calendar (Calendar No. 446). Status file updated 2026-08-10, last listed action 2026-06-24, and may have moved [M-0004, M-0465].
- (pending bill) S. 4591 as reported defines online service to include a site or app that predominantly gives public access to user uploaded material. A UGC short-video platform would appear to fit (analysis) [M-0467, M-0487].
- (pending bill) Safe harbor conditions for a UGC service: remove or disable access to a noticed replica as soon as feasible [M-0469]; also remove later uploads that match the replica's fingerprint, called stay down [M-0470]; register a designated agent with the Copyright Office [M-0471]. The repeat violator policy condition is written for a different provider prong, not the UGC prong [M-0468, M-0487].
- (pending bill) Without the safe harbor, a UGC service is liable only if its agent received a compliant notice or court order, or it willfully avoided one [M-0472]. Voluntary use of removal tools does not alone give actual knowledge [M-0477].
- (pending bill) The extra exclusions (news, documentary, commentary, parody, fleeting use) do not apply to a replica used to depict sexually explicit conduct [M-0473].
- (pending bill) Section 230 would not shield a platform, because the right is treated as intellectual property [M-0475]. The Copyright Office recommended the same carve out in 2024 [M-0484].
- (pending bill) Preemption: state claims over replicas in expressive works are preempted, but state laws existing on 2025-01-02 and state laws on sexually explicit or election replicas are saved [M-0474]. The Office's 2024 recommendation was a federal floor with no full preemption [M-0483].
- (pending bill) The right lasts 10 years after death, renewable in 5 year periods on proof of use, and ends 70 years after death [M-0476].
- (regulator guidance) The Copyright Office report (July 2024) recommended a federal replica law with a notice safe harbor, and liability only on actual knowledge [M-0481, M-0482]. A recommendation, not law.
- The 2025 text differs from 2026: failure to register an agent was conclusive proof of no good faith in S. 1367, but a rebuttable presumption after 90 days in S. 4591 and H.R. 8915 [M-0499, M-0503, M-0471]. S. 1367 as introduced has the same UGC definition and stay down duty [M-0495, M-0497]. H.R. 2794 matches S. 1367 on definition, takedown and stay down [M-0500].
- H.R. 8915 has the same takedown and stay down conditions as S. 4591 [M-0501, M-0502].

#### US federal (law in force)
- Lanham Act 43(a)(1)(A) bars false or misleading statements likely to cause confusion about affiliation, sponsorship or approval. It is the base for a false endorsement claim when a cloned voice suggests a singer backs a product [M-0462].
- (court decision) Midler v. Ford (9th Cir. 1988): deliberately imitating a widely known singer's distinctive voice to sell a product is a California tort. Narrow: distinctive, widely known, deliberate, to sell [M-0458].
- (court decision) Waits v. Frito-Lay (9th Cir. 1992) affirmed voice misappropriation and Lanham Act false endorsement over a soundalike ad, but vacated the Lanham damages award as duplicative [M-0459].
- (court decision) Lehrman v. Lovo (S.D.N.Y., 2025-07-10), motion to dismiss stage: voice clone claims mostly failed under federal trademark and copyright law but could proceed under N.Y. Civil Rights Law 50 and 51. Copyright claims on use of an original recording, contract and consumer claims survived. Later history unchecked [M-0460, M-0461].

#### Tennessee
- (state statute) The ELVIS Act (Pub. Ch. 588, 2024) protects an individual's voice, including a simulation of the voice [M-0019, M-0444]. Effective 2024-07-01 [M-0443].
- Liability: publishing, performing, distributing or making available a voice or likeness knowing it was not authorized [M-0443].
- It also reaches distributors of a tool whose primary purpose is producing a particular person's voice or likeness, with knowledge it was unauthorized [M-0445].

#### California
- (state statute) Civ. Code 3344: knowing use of another's name, voice, signature, photograph or likeness on goods or to advertise or sell, without prior consent, is actionable [M-0446].
- Civ. Code 3344.1 defines digital replica as a computer generated, highly realistic representation readily identifiable as a person's voice or visual likeness. It excludes authorized sampling, remixing and mastering [M-0447].
- For a deceased personality, producing or making available a replica in an expressive audiovisual work or sound recording without consent carries the greater of $10,000 or actual damages, subject to listed exceptions [M-0448].

#### New York
- (state statute) Civil Rights Law 50 makes use of a living person's name, portrait, picture, likeness or voice for advertising or trade without written consent a misdemeanor. Section 51 gives an injunction and damages for knowing use [M-0450, M-0451].
- Section 50-f: using a deceased performer's replica in an audiovisual work, sound recording or live musical performance, knowing it was unauthorized, creates liability. The right ends 40 years after death [M-0452, M-0453].
- Section 50-f(9) exempts owners and employees of an advertising medium, including streaming services, unless they had actual knowledge by prior notice. Scope is advertising media and does not obviously cover a UGC host (analysis) [M-0454].
- General Obligations Law 5-302(1) voids a services contract clause that allows a replica in place of in person work, if it lacks a reasonably specific description of uses and meets the other conditions. All conditions are needed [M-0455].

#### Illinois
- (state statute) Right of Publicity Act s.30(b): no person may knowingly distribute or make available a sound recording or audiovisual work with actual knowledge it contains an unauthorized digital replica [M-0456].
- Public Act 103-0836 added digital replica provisions to that Act [M-0506]. The claimed effective date of 2025-01-01 is (unverified) [M-0017]. State no date as fact.
- The Digital Voice and Likeness Protection Act (P.A. 103-830) voids services contract clauses that allow a replica in place of work without a reasonably specific description, where the person also lacked counsel or union representation [M-0457]. P.A. 104-0282 amended it, effective 2026-01-01 [M-0018].

#### United Kingdom (foreign law)
- A performer's consent is needed to record a live performance or broadcast it live (CDPA s.182) [M-0243], to copy a recording of it (s.182A) [M-0244], and to make it available on demand (s.182CA) [M-0245].
- Showing, playing or communicating a performance by means of a recording the person knows or has reason to believe was made without consent infringes (s.183) [M-0247].
- Equitable remuneration is owed to the performer from the copyright owner when a published recording is played in public or communicated to the public, other than on demand (s.182D) [M-0246].
- Section 191HA lets a performer recover rights after 50 years if the producer does not issue or offer the recording. Rarely relevant to a short-video app [M-0248].
- These rights protect the performance itself. The ledger holds no UK row on whether an AI voice clone is a protected performance. Do not state that it is.

### Gotchas
- NO FAKES is not law. Every S. 4591, S. 1367, H.R. 2794 and H.R. 8915 statement is a bill description. Status is as of the status file updated 2026-08-10 for S. 4591 and the 2026-10-23 file for H.R. 8915 [M-0465, M-0466].
- Bill text changed between 2025 and 2026. Check which version a source describes [M-0499, M-0503].
- A US federal voice or likeness right does not exist yet. Lanham Act false endorsement needs confusion about sponsorship [M-0462].
- Lehrman v. Lovo is an early motion ruling. Do not read it as a final merits holding [M-0460].
- Soundalikes are not free. Midler and Waits turned on deliberate imitation of a famous voice to sell a product [M-0458, M-0459]. Whether a creator video that is not an ad fits those cases is open (analysis).
- A song licence, a library licence or a platform sound licence covers music, not a person's voice cloned to perform it (analysis). Do not tell a creator a library covers a platform without the saved terms text.
- State death periods differ: New York 40 years [M-0453], the bill 70 years at most [M-0476].
- The Illinois effective date is not confirmed (unverified) [M-0017].
- Needs source: Lehrman v. Lovo later history, live streaming under replica laws, and UK law on AI clones.

### Open questions for counsel
- US federal: does a UGC video app with creator uploads fit prong (i) of S. 4591 (online service), and does an agent registration plus stay down plan fit its file pipeline?
- Tennessee and Illinois: what counts as actual knowledge of an unauthorized clone for a host, a notice, or a pattern of reports?
- California and New York: do 3344 and 50 and 51 reach a non ad creator video on a UGC app, and does 50-f(9) cover a short-video host?
- Is a voice changing or voice cloning feature in a platform a tool within the Tennessee distributor rule [M-0445]?
- UK: does an AI clone of a performer's voice infringe CDPA performer rights, and who is liable if a platform serves UK users?
- What wording should a platform use in creator terms to require consent for any cloned voice and to allow quick removal?

## M17 Publicity and false endorsement
- Law last checked: 2026-11-10. Volatility: high.
- Use for questions like: Can a user put a pop star's voice or a soundalike in a mix; Does an AI voice clone of a singer in an uploaded mix create liability for the platform; Does the ELVIS Act or California law reach a platform that hosts the mix; Would NO FAKES make a platform set up takedown and stay down; Does a processing tool face any digital replica duty when it processes user audio

### Bottom line
US state publicity law and the federal Lanham Act protect a person's voice and likeness separately from copyright in the song [M-0462, M-0019] (analysis). A licence for the composition and the master does not clear a singer's voice, a soundalike or an AI clone (analysis). Tennessee, California, New York and Illinois each have statutes on voice or digital replicas [M-0019, M-0446, M-0450, M-0456]. Federal NO FAKES (S. 4591, H.R. 8915) is a bill, not law, as of the 2026-08-10 and 2026-10-23 status captures [M-0465, M-0466].

### Rules
#### Federal false endorsement (US federal)
- Lanham Act 43(a)(1)(A) bars false or misleading representations likely to cause confusion about affiliation, sponsorship or approval [M-0462].
- Midler v. Ford (9th Cir. 1988) (court decision, Ninth Circuit only): deliberately imitating a widely known professional singer's distinctive voice to sell a product is a tort in California. It is limited to that fact pattern [M-0458].
- Waits v. Frito-Lay (9th Cir. 1992) (court decision, Ninth Circuit only): the Ninth Circuit affirmed judgment for voice misappropriation and Lanham Act false endorsement over a soundalike ad, but vacated the Lanham Act damages as duplicative [M-0459].
- Lehrman v. Lovo (S.D.N.Y. 2025-07-10) (court decision): at the motion to dismiss stage, voice clone claims mostly failed under federal trademark and copyright law but could proceed under N.Y. Civil Rights Law 50 and 51 [M-0460]. The motion was denied for the original voice recording copyright claim, contract, NY Civil Rights Law and GBL claims [M-0461]. Later history is unchecked.

#### Tennessee
- The ELVIS Act (Pub. Ch. 588, 2024) adds an individual's voice to the protected rights of publicity [M-0019]. Voice includes a simulation of the voice [M-0444].
- Liability attaches to publishing, performing, distributing or making available a voice or likeness knowing it was not authorized [M-0443]. Effective 2024-07-01 per the same row.
- It also reaches distributors of a tool whose primary purpose is producing a particular identifiable person's voice or likeness, with knowledge it was unauthorized [M-0445].

#### California
- Cal. Civ. Code 3344(a)(1): knowing use of another's name, voice, signature, photograph or likeness on goods, or to advertise or sell, without prior consent is actionable [M-0446].
- Section 3344.1 defines a digital replica as a computer generated, highly realistic representation readily identifiable as a person's voice or visual likeness. Authorized sampling, remixing and mastering are carved out of the definition [M-0447].
- For a deceased personality, producing or distributing a digital replica in an expressive audiovisual work or sound recording without prior consent carries the greater of $10,000 or actual damages, subject to the listed exceptions [M-0448].

#### New York
- Civil Rights Law 50: using a living person's name, portrait, picture, likeness or voice for advertising or trade without written consent is a misdemeanor [M-0450]. Section 51 allows an injunction and damages [M-0451].
- Section 50-f: using a deceased performer's digital replica in an audiovisual work, sound recording or live musical performance with knowledge it was unauthorized creates liability [M-0452]. The post mortem right ends forty years after death [M-0453].
- Section 50-f(9) exempts owners or employees of an advertising medium (including streaming services) unless they had actual knowledge by prior notification. The row notes it does not obviously cover user content hosts [M-0454].

#### Illinois
- 765 ILCS 1075/30(b): no person may knowingly distribute or make available to the public a sound recording or audiovisual work with actual knowledge it contains an unauthorized digital replica [M-0456].
- Public Act 103-0836 added a digital replica definition to the Right of Publicity Act [M-0506]. The January 1, 2025 effective date is unconfirmed; saved text has no effective date line [M-0017] (unverified). The compiled statute row also describes it as effective 1-1-25, not rechecked [M-0456].

#### Pending federal bills (not law)
- NO FAKES was reintroduced 2026-05-20 as S. 4591 and H.R. 8915 [M-0003]. S. 4591 was reported with a substitute on 2026-06-24 and placed on the Senate calendar [M-0004, M-0465]. H.R. 8915 was referred to House Judiciary with no later action [M-0466]. Status captures: S. 4591 2026-08-10, H.R. 8915 2026-10-23.
- The 2025 bills, S. 1367 and H.R. 2794, did not advance past committee referral [M-0005, M-0463, M-0464].
- As reported, S. 4591 defines online service to include a site or app that predominantly provides public access to user uploaded material [M-0467]. S. 1367 had the same definition [M-0495].
- Safe harbor conditions in S. 4591 as reported: act on compliant notices and remove or disable access as soon as feasible [M-0468, M-0469]. A UGC service must also remove later uploads matching the fingerprint of the noticed replica (stay down) [M-0470]. The same conditions appear in H.R. 8915 [M-0501, M-0502] and in the 2025 text [M-0496, M-0497, M-0500].
- The repeat violator termination policy condition is written for the prong (iii) services, not the UGC prong [M-0498, M-0487]. That is the S. 1367 text; the S. 4591 equivalent is not separately cited here.
- UGC services must register a designated agent with the Copyright Office. Failure raises a presumption of no good faith effort after 90 days [M-0471, M-0503]. The 2025 text made it conclusive with no grace period [M-0499].
- An online service is liable only if its agent got a compliant notice or court order, or it willfully avoided one [M-0472]. Voluntary tool use to remove content does not alone confer actual knowledge [M-0477].
- The extra exclusions (news, documentary, commentary or parody, fleeting use) do not apply where the replica depicts sexually explicit conduct [M-0473].
- It would treat the right as intellectual property law, so Section 230 would not shield platforms [M-0475].
- State law: it preempts state claims over digital replicas in expressive works but saves state laws in force by 2025-01-02 and state laws specifically on sexually explicit replicas [M-0474].
- Term: 10 years after death, renewable in 5 year periods on proof of use, ending at 70 years after death [M-0476].
- Copyright Office Part 1 (July 2024) (regulator guidance, recommendations only) urged a federal replica law with a notice safe harbor, an actual knowledge standard, no full preemption and no Section 230 shield [M-0481, M-0482, M-0483, M-0484].

### Gotchas
- Needs a licensed attorney: every application point above and the open questions below.
- A song licence is not a voice licence. Composition, master and the singer's voice are three separate permissions (analysis).
- Muting, pitch shifting or calling something a "tribute" is not consent (analysis). A soundalike can still be actionable [M-0458, M-0459]. Both cases are Ninth Circuit only.
- NO FAKES is not law. Do not tell a creator it applies or that it protects a platform. As of the 2026-08-10 capture, S. 4591 is on the Senate calendar and later action is unchecked [M-0004, M-0465].
- Several rows rest on mirror texts. Lehrman v. Lovo is a motion to dismiss ruling and later history is unchecked [M-0460].
- The Illinois effective date is not confirmed by saved source text (unverified) [M-0017, M-0506].
- Tennessee, California and New York have different consent forms: written consent in New York, prior consent in California [M-0450, M-0446].
- Post mortem terms differ: New York 40 years [M-0453]; S. 4591 would use a 10 to 70 year structure [M-0476].
- Currency: state replica laws and NO FAKES change fast. Re-check before relying after 2027-02-08 (90 days).

### Open questions for counsel
- Tennessee and Illinois: does a UGC host with no knowledge, but a takedown process, face liability for a user's voice clone under the ELVIS Act or 765 ILCS 1075/30(b)?
- New York: does 50-f(9) shield a short video app as an advertising medium, or only paid ad channels?
- California: does 3344 reach user posted soundalikes in non advertising videos hosted by a platform?
- Federal: if S. 4591 passes as reported, what notice and stay down build does a platform need, and who is its designated agent?
- Illinois: what is the confirmed effective date of Public Act 103-0836?
- Processing tools: on current facts, is a tool that only re-encodes a user's own file privately an online service under any prong of S. 4591?
- Section 230: do state publicity claims against a UGC host survive under the intellectual property carve out in each circuit that matters to the platform?
