# Music law knowledge pack: UK and EU
- File: 05-uk-eu.md, part of the music law knowledge pack (remix edition).
- Contains: M18 UK music copyright; M19 EU music law for an upload platform. Each card is followed by the claims it cites, with source, pinpoint and verbatim quote.
- Law last checked: 2026-11-10.
- Research tool, not legal advice. Have a licensed music attorney confirm anything before you act on it.
- Claim ids are M- plus four digits in square brackets. VERIFIED claims were checked against the saved source text. Claims tagged (unverified) were not confirmed; say so when you rely on one.

## M18 UK music copyright
- Law last checked: 2026-11-10. Volatility: high.
- Use for questions like: Do UK users need separate licences for the song and the recording; Is a mixing platform liable in the UK if a user uploads a mix with songs; Does the UK have a fair use rule or a parody exception a platform can rely on; Can a platform train or tune AI on UK music; Who owns a UK recording made by a producer or an employee; Do UK performers have rights over a recording used in a mix

### Bottom line
UK law, as of 2026-11-10: a recorded song has two separate copyrights, the musical work (composition) and the sound recording (master), and using both in a video needs permission for each [M-0238]. Putting a video with music online for UK viewers is a restricted act (communication to the public, including on demand) that needs a licence from the rights holders, and a platform can be liable for authorising it [M-0236, M-0237, M-0235, M-0255]. UK law has no US style statutory licence for sync, and no general fair use. The AI and copyright rules are under review and are not settled [M-0436].

### Rules
#### What is protected and who owns it (UK, statute)
- Copyright subsists in original musical works and in sound recordings as separate works [M-0238].
- A sound recording is a recording of sounds from which they may be reproduced, or a recording of a literary, dramatic or musical work from which sounds reproducing it may be produced [M-0094].
- No new copyright arises in a sound recording to the extent it is a copy taken from a previous sound recording [M-0095].
- The author of a work is its first owner, subject to the exceptions in s.11 [M-0090].
- Where an employee makes a literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work or film in the course of employment, the employer is first owner, subject to contrary agreement [M-0091].
- The author of a sound recording is the producer [M-0092]. (analysis) Because s.11(2) does not list sound recordings, the first owner of a recording is the producer unless assigned or agreed otherwise [M-0093]. This is an inference from the statute text.
- Assignment must be in writing signed by or on behalf of the assignor [M-0096]. An exclusive licence must also be in writing signed by or on behalf of the owner [M-0097].
- An agreement to assign future copyright, signed by the prospective owner, takes effect as an assignment when the copyright comes into existence [M-0098].

#### What the owner controls (UK, statute)
- The owner has the exclusive right to copy, issue copies, rent or lend, perform in public, communicate to the public and adapt [M-0234].
- Copyright is infringed by a person who, without licence, does or authorises another to do a restricted act [M-0235].
- Communication to the public covers a musical work, sound recording, film or broadcast [M-0236]. It includes making a work available on demand at a time and place individually chosen [M-0237].
- The High Court can grant an injunction against a service provider with actual knowledge of another person using its service to infringe (s.97A) [M-0242].

#### Performers (UK, statute)
- Performers have their own rights, separate from copyright. Recording a live performance, or broadcasting it live, without consent infringes them [M-0243].
- Copying a recording of a performance without consent infringes [M-0244]. Making a recording available on demand without consent infringes [M-0245].
- Showing, playing in public or communicating a performance by means of a recording the person knows or has reason to believe was made without consent infringes [M-0247].
- A performer is entitled to equitable remuneration from the copyright owner when a commercially published recording is played in public or communicated to the public, other than on demand under s.182CA [M-0246]. It is a payment right, not a bar to use, and is assignable only to a collecting society [M-0246].
- A performer who assigned rights to a producer can serve notice to terminate if the producer, after 50 years, fails to issue copies or make the recording available on demand [M-0248]. Rarely relevant to a short video app.

#### Exceptions (UK, statute)
- Fair dealing for caricature, parody or pastiche does not infringe [M-0240]. A contract term that restricts an act permitted by that exception is unenforceable [M-0241].
- The text and data analysis exception covers copies made only for non-commercial research by a person with lawful access, with acknowledgement [M-0239]. It does not cover commercial AI training.

#### AI and policy (UK, regulator report, not law)
- The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 required an economic impact assessment of four policy options within 9 months [M-0434] and a report on copyright works in developing AI systems [M-0435].
- The government report of March 2026 says a broad exception with opt-out is no longer its preferred way forward [M-0436, M-0015]. This is a policy statement, not law, and no AI training exception has been enacted [M-0436].
- The report proposes removing protection for wholly computer generated works (the s.9(3) type) while keeping it for works made with AI assistance [M-0437, M-0016]. Proposal only.
- The government is considering whether to introduce a new digital replica or personality right [M-0438]. Exploration only, not law.

#### Market context (UK, regulator report)
- The CMA music streaming report records an argument that, because about 90% of Content ID claims are monetised rather than taken down, rightsholders do not see YouTube streams as cannibalising streaming revenue [M-0381]. That is an argument put to the CMA, not a CMA finding.

### Gotchas
- The UK has no fair use. Fair dealing exceptions are specific and narrow [M-0240, M-0239].
- "Producer" is the author of a recording, which can differ from the artist or the label [M-0092, M-0093].
- An assignment or exclusive licence not in signed writing fails the statute test [M-0096, M-0097].
- The 2026 AI report is a policy statement. Do not say the UK allows or bans AI training on music on this basis [M-0436].
- Cases on secondary liability from the US (BMG v. Cox 2018 and Cox v. Sony 2026) do not apply in the UK. See M09 for the US position.
- Currency, as of 2026-11-10: the March 2026 AI report and its proposals can change at any time. Volatility is high. Check the legislation.gov.uk text before relying on any section, since amendments may follow.
- Not in our sources: UK collecting society licence terms, UK case law on platform liability, UK moral rights, and UK term of protection. Needs source.

### Open questions for counsel
- UK: which societies or direct licences does a UK facing short video app need for composition and for recording?
- UK: is a platform liable for authorising infringement when creators upload videos with unlicensed music, and does a UK notice and takedown practice reduce that risk?
- UK: does a live stream playing a commercial recording need separate performance licences, and who pays performers' equitable remuneration?
- UK: does a platform's server side re-encoding of user audio make it a direct infringer?
- UK: can the parody or pastiche exception ever cover a short video using part of a track, and what are the limits?
- UK: what is the current status of the AI copyright and digital replica proposals after the March 2026 report?

#### [M-0238] VERIFIED

#### [M-0236] VERIFIED

## M19 EU music law for an upload platform
- Law last checked: 2026-11-10. Volatility: high.
- Use for questions like: Would a platform that hosts user mixes be an online content sharing service provider in the EU; Does the EU hosting safe harbor protect a platform for user mixes with music; Who licenses music in the EU and on what terms; Can users rely on parody or quotation when uploading a mix; Does EU law let rightholders block AI training on their music; What does the AI Act require of model providers about copyright

### Bottom line
- EU law (foreign law): if a platform is an online content sharing service provider, it performs an act of communication to the public when users upload and must get authorisation, and the usual hosting safe harbor does not apply [M-0387, M-0388]. Without authorisation it is liable unless it meets the best efforts tests [M-0389, M-0390, M-0391].
- Authorisation means licences for both copyrights: the composition (usually publisher or a collective management organisation) and the master (label or distributor) (analysis). Collective bodies must license on objective and non-discriminatory terms [M-0310].
- Editing, muting or re-encoding a file is not a licence (analysis).
- Whether a given platform is in scope, and which national law applies, needs an EU licensed attorney. Nothing here says any song is cleared.

### Rules
#### Article 17 of Directive (EU) 2019/790 (foreign law, EU directive)
- Article 17(1): a provider performs an act of communication to the public when it gives access to user uploads, and must get authorisation [M-0387].
- Article 17(3): the Article 14(1) e-Commerce hosting safe harbor does not apply to these situations [M-0388].
- Article 17(4)(a): without authorisation the provider is liable unless it made best efforts to obtain one [M-0389].
- Article 17(4)(b): best efforts, to high industry standards of professional diligence, to make unavailable works for which rightholders gave relevant and necessary information [M-0390].
- Article 17(4)(c): act expeditiously on a notice and make best efforts to prevent future uploads, called notice and stay down [M-0391].
- Article 17(6): a lighter regime for services available in the Union under three years with turnover under EUR 10 million [M-0392]. Check the full conditions of the Article with counsel before relying on this.
- Article 17(7): users can rely on quotation, criticism, review, caricature, parody or pastiche when uploading [M-0393].
- Article 17(8): no general monitoring obligation [M-0394].
- Article 17(9): complaints are processed without undue delay, and decisions to disable or remove get human review [M-0395].

#### Courts and the Commission
- CJEU Grand Chamber, Poland v Parliament and Council, C-401/19, 26 April 2022 (court decision): the Court dismissed the annulment action and upheld Article 17 [M-0396]. Its holding on Article 17(4)(b) and (c) depends on safeguards (see the ledger note on M-0396).
- Same case, para 90: providers cannot be required to filter content whose unlawfulness would need an independent assessment of context and exceptions [M-0397].
- Commission 2021 guidance (regulator guidance, non-binding): automated blocking at upload should in principle be limited to manifestly infringing uploads [M-0398].

#### Collective management of music (Directive 2014/26/EU, foreign law)
- Rightholders may authorise a collective management organisation of their choice for the rights and territories of their choice [M-0308].
- Organisations and users must negotiate licences in good faith and share necessary information [M-0309].
- Licensing terms must rest on objective and non-discriminatory criteria [M-0310].

#### AI and music in the EU (foreign law, court decision, voluntary code)
- CDSM Art 3: a text and data mining exception for research organisations and cultural heritage institutions, for scientific research [M-0399].
- CDSM Art 4(1), (3): a general mining exception for lawfully accessible works, unless the rightholder reserved use in an appropriate manner, such as machine readable means for content online [M-0400, M-0442]. National transposition varies [M-0442].
- AI Act Art 53(1)(c): providers of general purpose AI models need a copyright policy that identifies and honours Article 4(3) reservations [M-0439]. Art 53(1)(d): they must publish a training content summary using the AI Office template [M-0440]. These obligations apply from 2 August 2025 [M-0441].
- EU GPAI Code of Practice, copyright chapter (voluntary, binds signatories only): Measure 1.3(1) commits to honour machine readable reservations when crawling for mining [M-0493]. Measure 1.4(1)(a) commits to technical safeguards against outputs that reproduce protected training content [M-0494].
- GEMA v OpenAI, LG Munich I, 11 Nov 2025, 42 O 14139/24 (German first instance court decision, lyrics only, not audio): memorising works in a language model is a reproduction under UrhG s.16 [M-0431]. The s.44b mining exception covers copies made to build training data, not training the model [M-0432]. Model operators, not users, are liable for infringing outputs from simple prompts [M-0433]. Appeal pending per the source header; later status unchecked.

### Gotchas
- This is EU level text. Each Member State transposed the directives; national law and national courts decide details [M-0442].
- Article 17(7) exceptions are user rights, not a way for a platform to treat all uploads as exempt. Parody of a track does not make a full song under a video safe (analysis).
- The Article 17(6) lighter regime has an age and turnover test [M-0392]. It lapses as a platform ages (analysis).
- "No general monitoring" [M-0394] sits beside "best efforts to make unavailable" [M-0390]. The CJEU reconciles them with safeguards [M-0397].
- GEMA v OpenAI is one first instance German court on lyrics. It is not an EU wide rule and not about audio [M-0431].
- AI Act dates: Art 113(b) is unchanged by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 per the ledger note on M-0441, which says the source file for that regulation is still needed.
- The GPAI Code is voluntary and its text was captured 2026-11-10 without a check for later Commission updates [M-0494].
- Open gaps: no saved row on live streaming under Article 17 or on any national transposition. Status as of 2026-11-10.

### Open questions for counsel
- EU: would a platform serving EU users with user uploaded short video be an online content sharing service provider under Article 17, and under which Member State law?
- EU: does a live stream count as upload and making available under Article 17(1)?
- EU: does a tool that re-encodes a creator's own file fall inside Article 17 if it never publishes the file?
- EU: which collective management organisations would license composition rights for EU launch?
- EU: does the Article 17(6) lighter regime fit a platform today and when does it end?
- EU and Germany: how should we treat the pending GEMA v OpenAI appeal before using AI features trained on music?

# Music law knowledge pack: Remixes, covers, stem tools and DJ mixes
- File: 06-remixes-covers-dj-mixes.md, part of the music law knowledge pack (remix edition).
- Contains: M21 Remixes and derivative works; M22 Covers and the compulsory mechanical licence; M23 Stem tools and DJ mixes. Each card is followed by the claims it cites, with source, pinpoint and verbatim quote.
- Law last checked: 2026-11-13.
- Research tool, not legal advice. Have a licensed music attorney confirm anything before you act on it.
- Claim ids are M- plus four digits in square brackets. VERIFIED claims were checked against the saved source text. Claims tagged (unverified) were not confirmed; say so when you rely on one.

## M21 Remixes and derivative works
- Law last checked: 2026-11-13. Volatility: medium.
- Use for questions like: Who has to give permission for a remix; Who owns a remix; Can I protect a remix I made without permission; Does changing a song enough make it mine; Is a re-played version safer than using the original recording; Can a remix or mashup be fair use

### Bottom line
- US federal law. A remix of a released track touches two copyrights: the song (composition) and the recording (master). They are separate works [M-0025]. Each owner holds its own right to make derivative works and to let others make them [M-0522]. So a remix built from the original audio needs a yes from both sides (analysis).
- Who usually says yes: the publisher or songwriter for the composition, the label or distributor for the master (industry practice, see card M01).
- The statute names remixing. The master owner's derivative right covers works in which the actual recorded sounds are "rearranged, remixed, or otherwise altered in sequence or quality" [M-0523].
- A remix made without permission gets no copyright protection in any part that uses the borrowed material unlawfully [M-0528]. Changing the song a lot does not fix that [M-0534, M-0552].
- A remix made with permission: the remixer can own only the new material added, never the underlying song or recording [M-0529].

### Rules
- US federal, 17 U.S.C. 101: a derivative work is a work based on one or more earlier works. The examples include a musical arrangement and a sound recording, and "any other form in which a work may be recast, transformed, or adapted" [M-0521, M-0035].
- US federal, 17 U.S.C. 106(2): the copyright owner has the exclusive right to prepare derivative works and to authorise others to do so [M-0522, M-0565].
- US federal (regulator guidance, Copyright Office Circular 56A): a sound recording is a separate work from the composition under it [M-0025]. The Office treats the recording as a derivative work of the composition [M-0026].
- US federal, 17 U.S.C. 114(b): the master owner's derivative right is limited to works where the actual sounds fixed in the recording are rearranged, remixed or otherwise altered in sequence or quality [M-0523]. The 1976 House Report says the wording was added to make that scope clear [M-0524].
- US federal, 17 U.S.C. 114(b): the master owner's reproduction right covers only copying that recaptures the actual sounds [M-0110]. A new recording made wholly of independently recorded sounds does not infringe the master, even if it imitates it. The composition is still a separate copyright (analysis in the row) [M-0111].
- US federal, 17 U.S.C. 103(a): protection for a work that uses earlier copyrighted material does not extend to any part where that material was used unlawfully [M-0528]. The Copyright Office says the same and adds that unauthorised adaptation may be infringement (regulator guidance) [M-0527].
- US federal (legislative history): the House Report says an unauthorised translation of a novel could not be copyrighted at all, while a use that is not unlawful, for example a fair use, leaves the new work copyrightable [M-0530].
- US federal, 17 U.S.C. 103(b): copyright in a derivative work or compilation covers only the new material the author added. It gives no right in the earlier material [M-0529]. Copyright Office Circular 14 says the same (regulator guidance) [M-0531].
- Seventh Circuit (court decision, Pickett v. Prince, 2000): section 103(a) does not let a stranger make a derivative work. The court read it, at least so far as that case went, to mean only that the right to make one does not authorise using material that infringes someone else's copyright [M-0532].
- Seventh Circuit (court decision, Pickett): the court found it very difficult to see how a derivative work not made by the owner of the original could fail to infringe it [M-0533]. It rejected the idea that a stranger may make one as long as the original does not pervade the new work [M-0534].
- Second Circuit (court decision, Keeling v. Hars, 2015): the maker of an unauthorised work that stays within fair use and adds enough originality may claim protection for her own original contributions [M-0535]. The facts were a parody stage show, not music, and a jury had found fair use [M-0536].
- US federal, 17 U.S.C. 501(a): anyone who violates an exclusive right of the copyright owner is an infringer [M-0220]. That sentence has no carve-out for giving credit or for not charging money (analysis).
- US federal, 17 U.S.C. 107: fair use is a four factor test. The factors are purpose and character, nature of the work, amount used, and market effect [M-0547]. The statute sets no number of seconds [M-0203]. It is judged case by case with no bright-line rules (court decision, Campbell) [M-0205].
- US federal (court decision, Campbell, 1994): parody needs to mimic the original to make its point, so it has some claim to use it. Satire can stand on its own and needs a reason for the borrowing [M-0548]. Commercial use is only one element of factor one [M-0549]. The amount taken is judged against the purpose of the copying [M-0550].
- US federal (court decision, Warhol, 2023): if the original and the new use share the same or a very similar purpose and the use is commercial, factor one is likely to weigh against fair use unless there is another justification [M-0551]. Treating any added new expression as enough would let "transformative use" swallow the owner's derivative right [M-0552]. Commercial nature is relevant but does not decide the matter [M-0553].
- Southern District of New York (court decision, Estate of Smith, 2017): fair use is a defence, and the party who raises it carries the burden [M-0211].
- Ownership of an authorised remix, US federal: a work is made for hire if an employee makes it within the job, or if it is specially commissioned, falls in a listed category and the parties sign a writing that says so [M-0537, M-0046]. The list does not name sound recordings (analysis row) [M-0047]. For a work made for hire the employer or commissioning party is the author [M-0048].
- US federal, 17 U.S.C. 201(d)(2) and 204(a): any exclusive right, or a slice of one, can be transferred and owned separately [M-0539]. A transfer is not valid without a writing signed by the owner of the right [M-0040].
- US federal (policy paper, Commerce Department white paper, January 2016, not law): remixes include mashups and sampling, and in many cases will be derivative works, compilations or collective works [M-0554]. Because remixes often rely on several copyrighted works, they can raise daunting licensing issues [M-0555].
- Same paper: the Task Force found no proven need for a remix exception or a compulsory remix licence. It recommended guidelines, more voluntary licensing and education [M-0556]. It said some remixes will clearly fall on one side of the fair use line and others will be uncertain [M-0557].

### Platform application
- A user blends two hit records. That mix can involve four owners: two compositions and two masters (analysis) [M-0025, M-0522]. Mixing more tracks adds more owners. This is the licensing problem the 2016 paper describes [M-0555].
- Who must authorise: both owners of each track, because the mix rearranges or alters the actual recorded sounds [M-0523] and each owner controls derivative works of its own work [M-0522]. No row in this base lets a platform or a user skip either side.
- Who owns a user's mix: at most, the user owns the new material the user added [M-0529]. If the tracks were used without permission, the unlawful parts get no protection [M-0528]. In the Second Circuit a user could still claim the original additions if the use is a fair use [M-0535]. The Seventh Circuit took a harder line [M-0532]. Other circuits are not in the saved set.
- Platform terms should not tell users "your mix is yours" without limits (analysis). The accurate line is: you own what you add, not the songs or recordings you used [M-0529].
- Official remix projects (an artist or label invites remixes): put the grant in a signed writing [M-0040]. Do not assume a commissioned remix is a work made for hire, since the commissioned categories are a closed list and sound recordings are not named [M-0046, M-0047]. The base has no saved source on standard remix deal terms (gap).
- Re-played versions: if a user re-records a part with new sounds, the master owner drops out but the composition owner does not [M-0111]. A stem pulled from the original recording is not a re-play, because it holds the actual recorded sounds (analysis) [M-0110].
- Fair use is a defence the user or platform would have to prove [M-0211]. A mix that plays songs as songs, for listening, shares the purpose of the originals, which Warhol says weighs against fair use when the use is commercial [M-0551]. The base has no case on whether a DJ mix or mashup is a fair use (gap).
- Risk carriers: the user who makes and shares the remix comes first. The platform carries risk as host, as tool maker and for anything it copies or performs itself (see cards M23 and M25). Claimants are labels and publishers.

### Gotchas
- "Change it enough and it is yours" is wrong. Pickett rejected the idea that a stranger may make a derivative work when the original does not pervade it [M-0534]. Warhol warns that adding new expression is not enough on its own [M-0552].
- "I own my remix because I made it" is at best half right. Protection covers only what you added [M-0529] and drops out where the borrowed material was used unlawfully [M-0528].
- Pickett is one circuit and its own wording is limited to that case [M-0532]. Keeling is not a music case and rested on a fair use finding [M-0536]. Do not present either as the national rule.
- A sound-alike avoids only the master. The composition still needs a licence [M-0111].
- Giving credit and not charging are not defences in the infringement statute (analysis) [M-0220]. Commercial nature is one fair use factor, not the test [M-0549, M-0553].
- The white paper is a 2016 policy paper, not law. As of 2026-11-13 the saved set has no later statute or Copyright Office action on a remix exception. Check before relying on [M-0556].
- Anderson v. Stallone is often quoted on this topic. The base has no primary text for it, so it is not cited here.
- Joint authorship of a remix (two users, or a user and the original artist) is not covered in the base (gap).

### Open questions for counsel
- US federal: when a platform's tool renders the mix, who is the maker of the derivative work, the user or the platform?
- US federal: outside the Second and Seventh Circuits, can a user claim copyright in the new parts of an unauthorised mix?
- US federal: can a transition-only blend, where each track plays mostly unchanged, be a fair use, and does the answer differ for a mashup that layers two tracks?
- US federal: for artist-approved remix projects, what grant wording gives users a safe right to make and share remixes, and who should own the result?
- US federal: has anything since January 2016 changed the white paper position that there is no remix exception or compulsory remix licence?

## M22 Covers and the compulsory mechanical licence
- Law last checked: 2026-11-13. Volatility: medium.
- Use for questions like: What does a cover licence allow; Can I change the arrangement of a song I cover; Does a cover licence cover a remix or mashup; Why does a cover in a video need a sync licence; Does a cover licence let me use the original recording; What do distributors require for a cover

### Bottom line
- US federal law. A cover is your own new recording of someone else's song. Section 115 gives a compulsory "mechanical" licence to make and distribute audio recordings of a song that has already been released, without asking the publisher, if you follow the statute's steps [M-0339, M-0545].
- The licence is for the composition only. It is not a licence of any sound recording [M-0542]. You may not copy the original recording with it [M-0543].
- You may arrange the song to fit your style. You may not change the basic melody or the fundamental character of the work [M-0540].
- It is audio only. It does not cover putting the song in a video. Video needs a sync licence agreed directly with the publisher [M-0544, M-0121, M-0140].
- A remix or mashup built from the original audio is not a cover, and a cover licence does not reach it (analysis from [M-0542, M-0540]).

### Rules
- US federal, 17 U.S.C. 115: the rights to make and to distribute phonorecords (audio copies) of nondramatic musical works are subject to compulsory licensing [M-0339]. The licence is limited to phonorecords made mainly for distribution to the public for private use [M-0120].
- First release belongs to the owner. US federal, 115(a)(1)(A): the compulsory licence is open only if phonorecords of the song were already distributed to the public in the US with the owner's authority. For a digital music provider's digital deliveries there is a second path: the first recording was made with the composition owner's authority and the recording owner authorised the deliveries [M-0545].
- Arrangement limit. US federal, 115(a)(2): the licence includes the privilege of making an arrangement only as far as needed to fit the style or manner of the performance. The arrangement may not change the basic melody or fundamental character of the work [M-0540].
- No new copyright in the arrangement. US federal, 115(a)(2): an arrangement made under the compulsory licence is not protected as a derivative work unless the composition owner gives express consent [M-0541].
- Composition only. US federal, 115(a)(1): the licence is for making and distributing phonorecords of the musical work. It is not a licence of any sound recording [M-0542]. The Copyright Office says you cannot copy a publicly distributed sound recording without permission, cannot change the basic melody, and cannot claim your arrangement as a derivative work (regulator guidance, Circular 73) [M-0543].
- No video. The Copyright Office says a phonorecord does not include sounds that accompany a motion picture or other audiovisual work, so the compulsory licence does not cover a song in video (regulator guidance) [M-0544]. The 1976 House Report says the same about sound tracks [M-0121]. The base's own reading reaches the same result for the blanket licence (analysis row) [M-0179].
- Sync is a free-market licence. The sync right is the industry term for the reproduction right in a song timed to pictures [M-0141]. The Copyright Office recommended in 2015 that consumer audiovisual uses stay in the free market with no compulsory licence (regulator report) [M-0140].
- Notice for physical copies. US federal, 115(b): for non-digital phonorecords, a notice of intention must be served before, or within 30 days after, making the phonorecords and before distributing them. Missing it closes off the compulsory licence and, without a voluntary licence, makes the making and distribution infringement [M-0546].
- Digital services. US federal, 115(d): a digital music provider can get a blanket mechanical licence through the Mechanical Licensing Collective for digital phonorecord deliveries [M-0023, M-0122]. The blanket licence covers the musical works available for compulsory licensing for covered activities [M-0125]. The base has no row on how notices changed over in 2021 (gap). Rates are in card M04 and are not quoted here.
- A cover avoids the master owner only if every sound is newly recorded. US federal, 114(b): an independent recording of other sounds does not infringe the sound recording copyright, even if it imitates the original [M-0111].
- Playing a cover to the public is a different right. Public performance of the song is separate from the reproduction and distribution rights that the mechanical licence covers (analysis row) [M-0183]. See card M05 for performing rights organisations.
- CD Baby (platform terms, help page, web archive copy dated 2026-02-16, captured 2026-11-13): a cover release needs a mechanical licence for digital downloads, which covers the composition but not the original recording [M-0596]. Derivative works such as samples cannot be cleared through its cover song process [M-0597]. Even for streaming-only plans it still requires at least a digital download licence to distribute a cover [M-0598].
- TuneCore (platform terms, help page, web archive copy dated 2020-05-07, captured 2026-11-13, possibly stale): a cover may need permission and possibly a licence from the original copyright holder before release [M-0594]. The same 2020 page says some stores did not accept soundalike covers [M-0595].

### Platform application
- A user records their own performance of a released song, audio only. That is a cover. The composition side can run through the compulsory mechanical licence [M-0339, M-0545]. The master belongs to whoever made the new recording (analysis) [M-0111].
- A user mixes the original recording of a song. That is not a cover. It uses the actual recorded sounds, which sit inside the master owner's rights [M-0110, M-0523], and the cover licence is not a licence of any sound recording [M-0542].
- A user layers the vocal of one song over the instrumental of another. Even on the composition side this is likely past the arrangement privilege, because it goes beyond fitting a style of performance (analysis) [M-0540]. It needs the publishers' direct consent, and the masters' owners too if original audio is used [M-0522].
- A user changes tempo, key or structure of a cover so far that the melody or character changes. That is outside the compulsory licence and needs the publisher's consent (analysis) [M-0540].
- A user makes a video of a cover or a mix. The mechanical licence stops at audio [M-0544]. A sync licence from the publisher is needed, and a master use licence too if the original recording is used [M-0140, M-0141].
- If the platform streams covers on demand, it also needs public performance licences for the compositions (see card M05) [M-0183]. Whether the platform can itself use the blanket mechanical licence depends on whether it qualifies as a digital music provider. That is a question for counsel [M-0122].
- If users send covers to stores through a distributor, the distributor's own rules apply on top of the law. The two saved pages both treat covers and sample-based works differently [M-0597, M-0594].
- Risk carriers: the user who records and releases the cover; the platform if it hosts, streams or distributes it; publishers as claimants. Labels become claimants only when original audio is used.

### Gotchas
- "A cover licence covers a remix" is wrong. The compulsory licence is composition only [M-0542], bars changes to the basic melody or fundamental character [M-0540], and one distributor says in terms that derivative works such as samples cannot go through its cover process [M-0597].
- "I bought a cover licence, so I can post the video" is wrong. No video under the compulsory licence [M-0544].
- "My arrangement is mine" is wrong under the compulsory licence. It is not protected as a derivative work without the owner's express consent [M-0541].
- A song that has never been released with the owner's authority is not open to the compulsory licence [M-0545].
- The TuneCore page is a 2020 archive copy and may be out of date. The CD Baby page is an archive copy dated 2026-02-16. Both were captured 2026-11-13. Re-check live terms before relying on them.
- DistroKid and SoundCloud cover and remix rules were not captured (pages blocked). The base makes no claim about them.
- Outside the US the compulsory mechanical licence in section 115 does not apply. The base has no rows on cover licensing in other countries (gap).

### Open questions for counsel
- US federal: does a platform that hosts and streams user covers qualify as a digital music provider that can use the blanket mechanical licence?
- US federal: where is the line between a permitted arrangement and a change to the "fundamental character" of a song, for tempo changes, key changes and re-ordered sections?
- US federal: how do the notice rules work today for a user who releases a cover as a download or on physical media, given the 2021 change to the blanket licence?
- US federal: what is the least a user needs to post a cover with video on the platform?
- Non-US: which licences replace section 115 for covers in the UK, EU, Canada and Australia?

## M23 Stem tools and DJ mixes
- Law last checked: 2026-11-13. Volatility: high.
- Use for questions like: Is it legal to host or stream DJ mixes of commercial songs; Is the maker of a stem splitter or mixing tool liable for what users do; Does the statutory webcasting licence cover saved or on-demand mixes; How do licensed mix services clear the tracks; What does a live DJ stream need; Is splitting a song into stems a copy

### Bottom line
- US federal law. Nothing in this base lets a platform publish DJ mixes of commercial tracks without licences. Every track in a mix carries two copyrights, the song and the recording [M-0025]. A recorded mix copies both [M-0108]. Playing it to the public performs the songs [M-0106] and, online, the recordings [M-0107].
- The section 114 statutory licence does not fit a library of saved mixes that people play on demand. It bars interactive services [M-0115], archived programs under 5 hours [M-0578] and longer archives kept up more than 2 weeks [M-0579].
- The licensed mix services in the saved set describe direct deals with labels and paying rights holders in each mix. Neither says it relies on the statutory licence (company statements, captured 2026-11-13) [M-0589, M-0593].
- A tool maker is not contributorily liable just because the tool can be misused [M-0560, M-0563]. It is exposed when it promotes or shapes the tool for infringement [M-0562, M-0221]. No saved case applies this to a stem tool, and vicarious liability is a separate question [M-0252].
- Four things are unsettled or missing here: whether splitting stems is itself an infringing copy, whether a mix is a compilation or a derivative work, what a club or venue licence covers, and live-stream terms of services other than Mixcloud. This card says so and does not fill them.

### Rules
- Tool makers, the old baseline. US federal (court decision, Sony v. Universal, 1984): selling copying equipment is not contributory infringement if the product is widely used for legitimate purposes or is merely capable of substantial noninfringing uses [M-0560]. The Court found the video recorder had such uses, in part because private, noncommercial home time-shifting of broadcast television was fair use [M-0561]. That holding is about TV recorders. No saved case applies it to a stem tool (analysis).
- Tool makers, inducement. US federal (court decision, Grokster, 2005): one who distributes a device with the object of promoting its use to infringe, shown by clear expression or other affirmative steps, is liable for the resulting infringement by others [M-0562]. Mere knowledge that a product could be or is used to infringe is not enough, and ordinary product support is not inducement [M-0563].
- Services, the current rule. US federal (court decision, Cox v. Sony, decided March 25, 2026): contributory liability needs intent that the service be used for infringement, shown only by inducement or by a service tailored to infringement [M-0001, M-0221, M-0223]. Mere knowledge that the service will be used to infringe is not enough [M-0222]. The Court rejected the lower court's knowledge plus inaction rule [M-0224].
- What Cox left open. Cox was about contributory liability. Vicarious liability is a separate theory the Court did not decide (analysis row) [M-0252]. One Justice said other common-law theories such as aiding and abetting could apply [M-0225].
- Applying inducement to a stem or mixing tool: the researchers' reading is that a tool maker whose marketing or onboarding steers users to split and mix commercial songs they do not own is exposed through its own statements and design, not through the tool's ability alone (unverified) [M-0564].
- Direct liability. US federal, 17 U.S.C. 501(a): anyone who violates an exclusive right is an infringer [M-0220]. When the platform's own servers copy, split, render or stream music, the question becomes whether the platform itself did the act. The base has no row on that test (gap).
- Hosting user uploads. US federal, 17 U.S.C. 512(c): the safe harbor covers infringement by reason of storage at the direction of a user [M-0343]. Conditions include no actual or red flag knowledge [M-0344, M-0345], fast removal on knowledge or notice [M-0346, M-0348], no direct financial benefit from infringement the provider can control [M-0347], a designated agent [M-0349] and a repeat infringer policy [M-0357]. Card M08 has the detail.
- What a mix is, right by right. Reproduction: both the song and the recording carry it [M-0108]. Derivative works: each owner controls them [M-0522], and for the master that covers rearranging, remixing or altering the actual sounds [M-0523]. Performance: songs have a public performance right [M-0106]; recordings have one only for digital audio transmission [M-0107, M-0296].
- Compilation or derivative work. A compilation is a work formed by collecting and assembling existing materials, selected, coordinated or arranged so the whole is an original work [M-0569]. A derivative work recasts, transforms or adapts earlier works [M-0521]. A government paper says remixes will in many cases be derivative works, compilations or collective works (policy paper, 2016) [M-0554]. No saved authority decides which one a DJ mix is. Unsettled.
- Either way, the mix maker's own copyright covers only what the maker added [M-0529], and not any part where earlier material was used unlawfully [M-0528].
- Stem splitting. The master owner's reproduction right covers copying that recaptures the actual sounds [M-0110]. A stem holds the actual recorded sounds, so it falls within that wording (analysis). No saved case rules on stem separation, private or public. Unsettled.
- Home recording law is narrow. US federal, 17 U.S.C. 1008: no infringement action may be based on making or selling the listed recording devices and media, or on a consumer's noncommercial use of such a device or medium to make musical recordings [M-0572]. The device definition turns on a recording function designed or marketed mainly for making private-use digital audio copies [M-0573].
- Ninth Circuit (court decision, RIAA v. Diamond, 1999): a computer hard drive is outside the Act's definition of a digital music recording, and a player that copies only from a hard drive is not a covered device [M-0574, M-0575]. The court described the Act's purpose as private, noncommercial recording by consumers [M-0576]. Whether software stem splitting on a computer or server is inside this shelter is not decided, and Diamond makes it doubtful (analysis).
- US federal, 17 U.S.C. 117(a) lets the owner of a copy of a computer program make another copy or adaptation of that program on stated conditions. Its text names only computer programs [M-0577]. It gives no stated right to copy or adapt music files (analysis).
- The 114 statutory licence, entry test. It reaches subscription transmissions, eligible nonsubscription transmissions and one satellite category, if the listed conditions are met [M-0114]. The transmission must not be part of an interactive service [M-0115, M-0298]. An interactive service lets a member of the public receive a program made for the recipient or, on request, a particular sound recording [M-0113, M-0299]. Taking requests for the public at large does not alone make a service interactive, within limits [M-0585].
- The 114 licence, archive rules. The transmission may not be part of an archived program of less than 5 hours [M-0578]. An archived program of 5 hours or more may not stay available for more than 2 weeks [M-0579].
- The 114 licence, programming rules. The service may not exceed the sound recording performance complement or publish an advance schedule of the specific recordings [M-0580]. The complement caps, in any 3-hour period on a channel, how many selections come from one record or one featured artist [M-0581].
- The 114 licence, other conditions. The service may take no affirmative steps to cause or induce listeners to make copies [M-0582]. The transmission must be made from a phonorecord lawfully made under the copyright owner's authority [M-0583]. The service must show the title, record and featured artist in text while the recording plays [M-0584].
- What 114 does not do. It is about performing recordings by digital audio transmission [M-0114, M-0107]. An interactive service also needs a licence for each song inside the recordings [M-0301]. A digital audio transmission does not include any audiovisual work, so video of a DJ set is outside it [M-0112, M-0297].
- How licensed mix services clear tracks. Mixcloud (company blog, not terms and not law; blog dated 2024-03-28, page path after redirect dated 2025-01-01, captured 2026-11-13) says a streaming service must hold licences clearing both the composition and the sound recording of every track in a stream [M-0586]. It says it was the first streaming service to clear the copyrights for radio shows and mixes [M-0587]. Its checklist asks whether a platform has direct deals with the labels whose music is played [M-0589]. It says downloading needs an additional licensed right, the mechanical right [M-0588].
- Apple Music (company notice to artists dated 2021-11-16, captured 2026-11-13) says it developed a process to identify and compensate the individual creators in DJ mixes [M-0592], works with major and independent labels, and pays rights holders within DJ mixes directly [M-0593].
- Live sets. Mixcloud describes its live product as a licensed live streaming platform that also archives the stream as a recording (company blog, captured 2026-11-13) [M-0590]. It says that on a platform that has not cleared the music, rights holders can have a mix taken down or muted [M-0591].

### Platform application
- The tool itself. A stem splitter and mixer has lawful uses: a user's own songs, licensed stems, music whose owners agreed (analysis). Under Sony, Grokster and Cox the ability to misuse it is not what creates liability [M-0560, M-0563, M-0222]. What the platform says and builds is. Adverts, tutorials, presets or search features aimed at chart hits are the kind of affirmative steps Grokster describes [M-0562], and a product built around unlicensed hits risks being called tailored to infringement [M-0223].
- Keep the two roles apart. As a tool maker the platform is judged by intent [M-0221]. As a host of user mixes it is judged by the 512(c) conditions [M-0343]. As the party that itself copies, renders or streams, it may be judged as a direct infringer [M-0220]. Each role needs its own answer from counsel.
- Recorded mixes shared with the public. A saved mix that listeners start whenever they like looks like an archived program, and a user mix is almost always under 5 hours (analysis). The 114 licence bars that [M-0578]. So public mix hosting of commercial tracks needs direct master licences, plus licences for the songs [M-0301, M-0106]. This matches what the licensed services say they do [M-0586, M-0589].
- A radio-style channel of mixes could in theory use 114, but only with the complement, no advance track lists, no downloads, track text on screen and lawfully made source copies [M-0580, M-0581, M-0582, M-0583, M-0584]. A user-driven mixing product is a poor fit for those limits (analysis).
- Live mixing to an audience. Online, each track is performed as a song and as a recording [M-0106, M-0107]. The only saved service statement says both must be cleared by the service [M-0586]. If the live set is saved for replay, the archive rules above apply to the replay [M-0578, M-0579].
- Stems. Whether the split happens on the user's device or on the platform's servers changes who made the copy (analysis). Server-side splitting and storage put the platform closer to direct copying [M-0110, M-0220]. This is unsettled and is a lead question for counsel.
- Risk carriers: the user for what the user uploads, mixes and shares; the platform as tool maker, host and possibly direct actor; labels and publishers as claimants; a licensed service partner, if one is used, for what its own licences cover.

### Gotchas
- "DJs do it in clubs, so it is legal online" does not follow. The right to perform a song in public is separate from the right to copy it (analysis row) [M-0183]. The base has no saved text of a club or venue licence, so it makes no claim about what such a licence covers (gap). Online, the one saved service statement says both the song and the recording must be cleared for every track [M-0586].
- "We are just a tool" is not a shield by itself. Sony protects a product with substantial lawful uses [M-0560], but inducement is judged by what the maker says and does [M-0562, M-0221].
- "The webcasting licence covers our mixes" is wrong for on-demand or saved mixes [M-0115, M-0578, M-0579] and for any download feature [M-0582].
- "It is for private use, so home recording law covers it" is not established. The Act is tied to listed devices and media [M-0572], and the Ninth Circuit kept computer hard drives outside it [M-0575].
- The Mixcloud and Apple rows are company statements about their own services. They are not law and not terms of service. Capture date 2026-11-13.
- Live-stream music rules for Twitch, YouTube, Instagram and SoundCloud were not captured. The base makes no claim about them (gap).
- Cox v. Sony is from 2026. Outcomes on remand and any new stem or mixing cases are not tracked here. Re-check before relying.
- Statutory damages are counted per work [M-0216], and a single mix can hold many works (analysis). See card M12.

### Open questions for counsel
- US federal: is a stem split of a lawfully bought track a reproduction under 106(1) and 114(b), and does it matter whether the user's device or the platform's server does it?
- US federal: does the home recording shelter in section 1008 reach software stem splitting at all after RIAA v. Diamond?
- US federal: is a blended DJ mix a derivative work of each song and recording, a compilation, or both, and what turns on the label?
- US federal: when a user streams a live mix through the platform, who performs the works publicly, the user, the platform or both?
- US federal: which exact licences does an on-demand mix library need for masters and for songs, and can any part run through 114, the blanket mechanical licence or the performing rights organisations?
- US federal: does the 512(c) safe harbor cover a mix that the platform's own tool rendered from user-supplied tracks, or only files users upload ready-made?
- US federal: what marketing, onboarding and design choices would a court read as inducement or as tailoring the service to infringement after Cox?
- US federal: what does a club or venue performance licence actually cover, and does any of it carry over to online streaming?

### Claims cited in M23
Each claim below gives its status, source, pinpoint and verbatim quote. In quotes a long dash in the source is shown as --.

#### [M-0025] VERIFIED
- Claim: A sound recording is a separate work from the musical composition; a sound recording copyright is not a substitute for copyright in the underlying composition.
- Jurisdiction: US-federal
- Source: U.S. Copyright Office, Circular 56A: Copyright Registration of Musical Compositions and Sound Recordings (https://www.copyright.gov/circs/circ56a.pdf), source id co-circular-56a
- Pinpoint: Circular 56A p.1
- Quote: "Sound recordings and musical compositions are considered two separate works for copyright purposes. Even though a sound recording is a derivative work of the underlying musical composition, a copyright in a sound recording is not the same as, or a"
- Checked: 2026-11-10

#### [M-0108] VERIFIED
- Claim: Both musical works and sound recordings carry the reproduction right (copies or phonorecords).
- Jurisdiction: US-federal
- Source: 17 U.S.C. 106 exclusive rights in copyrighted works (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/106), source id usc17-106
- Pinpoint: 17 U.S.C. 106(1)
- Quote: "to reproduce the copyrighted work in copies or phonorecords;"
- Checked: 2026-11-10

#### [M-0106] VERIFIED
- Claim: Musical works carry an exclusive right of public performance.
- Jurisdiction: US-federal
- Source: 17 U.S.C. 106 exclusive rights in copyrighted works (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/106), source id usc17-106
- Pinpoint: 17 U.S.C. 106(4)
- Quote: "in the case of literary, musical, dramatic, and choreographic works, pantomimes, and motion pictures and other audiovisual works, to perform the copyrighted work publicly;"
- Checked: 2026-11-10

#### [M-0107] VERIFIED
- Claim: Sound recordings carry a public performance right only by digital audio transmission.
- Jurisdiction: US-federal
- Source: 17 U.S.C. 106 exclusive rights in copyrighted works (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/106), source id usc17-106
- Pinpoint: 17 U.S.C. 106(6)

- Pinpoint: 607 U.S. ___ (2026), syllabus

#### [M-0252] VERIFIED

Sony (U.S. 2026) a service provider is contributorily liable for a user's infringement only if it induced the infringement or the service is tailored to it; knowing that some users infringe is not enough. Vicarious liability is a separate theory that the Court did not decide (cert limited to contributory).
- Jurisdiction: analysis
- Source: Cox Communications, Inc. v. Sony Music Entertainment, No. 24-171, 607 U.S. ___ (Mar. 25, 2026) (https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/24-171_new_3dq3.pdf), source id scotus-cox-sony-2026

- Checked: 2026-11-10

#### [M-0223] VERIFIED

- Jurisdiction: US-federal

- Pinpoint: 607 U.S. ___ (2026), syllabus

#### [M-0222] VERIFIED

#### [M-0225] VERIFIED
- Claim: Cox (2026): Justice Sotomayor, concurring in the judgment, said other common-law theories such as aiding and abetting could apply in copyright.
- Jurisdiction: US-federal

- Claim: Statutory damages are assessed per work for all infringements involved in the action; the owner may elect them any time before final judgment.
- Jurisdiction: US-federal
- Source: 17 U.S.C. 504 remedies, damages and profits (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/504), source id usc17-504
- Pinpoint: 17 U.S.C. 504(c)(1)
- Quote: "an award of statutory damages for all infringements involved in the action, with respect to any one"
- Checked: 2026-11-10


==== FILE: 07-remix-platform-part1.md ====

# Music law knowledge pack: Remix platform, part 1
- File: 07-remix-platform-part1.md, part of the music law knowledge pack (remix edition).
- Contains: M24 Licensed platform models, distributor rules and stem model licences; M25 DJ-mix platform application, feature by feature; playbook Questions for a licensed music attorney. Each card is followed by the claims it cites, with source, pinpoint and verbatim quote.
- Law last checked: 2026-11-13.
- Research tool, not legal advice. Have a licensed music attorney confirm anything before you act on it.
- Claim ids are M- plus four digits in square brackets. VERIFIED claims were checked against the saved source text. Claims tagged (unverified) were not confirmed; say so when you rely on one.

## M24 Licensed platform models, distributor rules and stem model licences
- Law last checked: 2026-11-13. Volatility: high.
- Use for questions like: How do licensed mix platforms clear the music; Will a distributor take a remix or a cover; Can we use an open source stem splitter in a paid product; Is a code licence the same as a licence for the model weights; What does it mean when a model page says nothing about a licence; Which licences would a mix platform need to sign

### Bottom line
- The mix services in the saved set that describe themselves as licensed say they run on licences for both the songs and the recordings of every track, backed by direct deals with labels (company statements, captured 2026-11-13) [M-0586, M-0589, M-0593]. No saved source shows a mix platform running on commercial tracks without such deals.
- Distributors treat a cover and a remix differently. The saved pages offer a route for covers and say sample-based or derivative works cannot use it [M-0596, M-0597, M-0599].
- A stem splitter has two licences to check: one for the code and one for the trained model weights. An MIT licence on the code is not a licence for the weights [M-0600, M-0603]. Where a project says nothing about its weights, that is silence, not a grant [M-0604, M-0607].
- Of the stem models checked on 2026-11-13, none has weights with a stated licence that clearly allows commercial use. One is stated non-commercial [M-0606]. One maintainer says the weights are for personal or research use [M-0603]. The rest are silent [M-0604, M-0607, M-0609, M-0610].

### Rules
- Mixcloud (platform terms: company blog, not terms of service and not law; blog dated 2024-03-28, page path after redirect dated 2025-01-01, captured 2026-11-13): a streaming service must hold licences that clear both the composition and the sound recording of every track in a stream [M-0586]. It says it was the first streaming service to clear the copyrights for radio shows and mixes [M-0587].
- Mixcloud (same blog, same capture date): its checklist for choosing a platform asks whether the platform has direct deals with the labels whose music is played [M-0589]. It says downloading needs an additional licensed right, which it calls the mechanical right [M-0588]. That is the company's short version, not a statement of US law.
- Mixcloud (same blog, same capture date): it describes its live product as a licensed live streaming platform that also archives the stream [M-0590]. On a platform that has not cleared the music, rights holders can have a mix taken down or muted [M-0591].
- Apple Music (platform terms: company notice to artists dated 2021-11-16, captured 2026-11-13): it says it built a process to identify and compensate the individual creators in DJ mixes [M-0592]. It says it works with major and independent labels and pays rights holders within DJ mixes directly [M-0593].
- A large on-demand service's public filing (industry practice, Spotify annual report for fiscal year 2025): in the US, mechanical rights for audio-only use run through the section 115 compulsory licence, with a blanket licence run by the Mechanical Licensing Collective [M-0086]. Public performance rights for compositions come through the performing rights organisations ASCAP, BMI, GMR and SESAC under blanket licences [M-0088].
- US federal, 17 U.S.C. 114: the statutory licence for recordings is closed to interactive services [M-0115] and to archived programs under 5 hours [M-0578]. An interactive service also needs a licence for each song [M-0301]. So an on-demand mix library has to get its master rights by direct deal (analysis).
- US federal (court order, ASCAP consent decree): ASCAP may hold and license only non-exclusive public performance rights [M-0256]. It cannot grant sync rights (analysis row) [M-0311]. The decrees bind only ASCAP and BMI [M-0278]. An ASCAP licence therefore does not cover copying, remixing or video (analysis) [M-0183]. The base has no saved text on the scope of the other organisations' licences.
- CD Baby (platform terms, help page, web archive copy dated 2026-02-16, captured 2026-11-13): a cover release needs a mechanical licence for digital downloads. That licence covers the composition, not the original recording [M-0596]. Derivative works such as samples cannot be cleared through its cover song process [M-0597]. Even a streaming-only release of a cover needs at least a digital download licence under its rules [M-0598].
- CD Baby (platform terms, artist education article, live page, undated, captured 2026-11-13): using a sample of a recording means clearing the master with the label and the composition with the publisher. There is no standard rate, and the deal is negotiated directly [M-0599].
- TuneCore (platform terms, help page, web archive copy dated 2020-05-07, captured 2026-11-13, possibly stale): a cover may need permission and possibly a licence from the original copyright holder [M-0594]. Some stores did not accept soundalike covers, and content hidden by a store was not reversed or refunded [M-0595].
- Demucs (industry, checked 2026-11-13): the code licence file is MIT and says nothing about model weights [M-0600]. The project README says the licence of the weights is "not clear" because the training set includes research-only data [M-0601]. A maintainer says he cannot grant a licence for the weights [M-0602]. A maintainer comment dated 2022-09-29 says the code is free for commercial use under MIT, while the weights are research artefacts for personal or research usage [M-0603].
- Spleeter (industry, checked 2026-11-13): the code is MIT. The README is silent on a licence for the pretrained models: silence, not a grant [M-0604]. Its disclaimer tells users to get authorisation from right owners before using it on copyrighted material [M-0605].
- Open-Unmix (industry, checked 2026-11-13): the umxl weights are licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, which is non-commercial [M-0606]. The umx and umxhq models were trained on the MUSDB18-HQ set, and no weights licence is stated for them: silence, not a grant [M-0607].
- python-audio-separator and the UVR models (industry, checked 2026-11-13): the tool's code is MIT, and it asks users to credit the UVR models. It gives no licence for the model files [M-0608]. Its default BS-Roformer checkpoint and its Mel-Band Roformer checkpoint are listed with no licence [M-0609, M-0610]. A separate BS-RoFormer code project is MIT and is silent on checkpoints [M-0611].
- UVR (industry, checked 2026-11-13): the developers say they trained all the models in the package except the Demucs v3 and v4 4-stem models [M-0612]. The README asks for credit under MIT and has no separate licence text for the models [M-0613].
- Training data (industry, checked 2026-11-13): the MUSDB18 set includes 46 tracks from MedleyDB that are licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 [M-0614]. The dataset page does not state terms for the DSD100 tracks [M-0615].

### Platform application
- Model 1, direct deals for a mix library. The platform signs master licences with labels and distributors, and song licences with publishers and performing rights organisations. Every saved statement from a lawful mix service points to this model [M-0586, M-0589, M-0593]. It is slow and costly, and labels can say no (analysis).
- Model 2, partner with a service that already holds the licences. Mixes are published and streamed only inside the partner. The platform would rely on the partner's licences and terms. The base has only the partner's own public statements, not its contract terms [M-0586, M-0590]. Whether a partner's licences reach mixes made with split stems is unknown (gap).
- Model 3, radio-style streaming under the 114 statutory licence, plus performing rights licences for the songs. It works only for non-interactive listening with the programming limits in card M23 [M-0115, M-0578]. It does not fit saved mixes that users pick and play.
- Model 4, a licensed catalogue. Users mix only tracks or stems the platform has licensed for remixing. This removes the "any music" problem but needs remix-grade grants from owners, which are derivative work grants [M-0522]. The base has no saved terms from stem catalogue or sample pack services (gap).
- Sending user work to stores through a distributor. Covers have a path [M-0596]. Mixes and mashups built from original audio do not go through the cover path and need the master and the composition cleared one by one [M-0597, M-0599].
- Picking a stem model. Treat the code and the weights as two separate licence checks (analysis) [M-0600, M-0603]. For a paid product, do not ship weights that are stated non-commercial [M-0606] or stated research-only [M-0603]. Do not ship weights whose licence is silent without a written grant from whoever can give one [M-0604, M-0609, M-0610].
- Why the weights are a problem at the root: public stem models are commonly trained on a research set that includes non-commercial tracks [M-0614, M-0601]. Whether that limit carries over to trained weights is a legal question the base does not answer (unsettled).
- Clean options for the stem engine (analysis): train on audio the platform owns or has licensed for training, license a commercial stem engine under a written contract, or get a written commercial grant from a model's owner. The base has no saved terms for commercial stem engines (gap).
- A model's licence and the music's copyright are separate questions. A clean model licence does not make it lawful to split a song the user has no rights in [M-0605, M-0110].
- Risk carriers: the platform for the model it ships and for any deal it signs; the user for what goes to stores under the user's name; model owners and dataset owners as possible claimants on the weights; labels and publishers on the music.

### Gotchas
- "The repo is MIT, so we can sell it" is wrong for the weights. The Demucs maintainers say so in terms [M-0603].
- "It does not say we cannot" is not permission. Silence is not a grant [M-0604, M-0607].
- A credit request is not a licence. The UVR pages ask for credit and give no model licence text [M-0608, M-0613].
- The Mixcloud and Apple rows are public statements by the companies about themselves. They do not show the deal terms, the price, or whether stem-based mixes are covered.
- Mixcloud's line that downloads need "the mechanical right" is a simplification. In US law a download of a mix also copies and distributes the recordings (analysis) [M-0108].
- The TuneCore page is a 2020 archive copy. The CD Baby help page is an archive copy dated 2026-02-16. Service terms change. Re-capture before relying on them.
- Not captured: SoundCloud, DistroKid, Beatport, Beatsource, Splice, BandLab, Twitch, YouTube and Instagram terms. The base makes no claim about them.
- Model licences can change with a commit. All stem model rows were checked 2026-11-13. Pin the exact version checked.

### Open questions for counsel
- Which licences does an on-demand mix library need in the US, and from whom: labels, distributors, publishers, the Mechanical Licensing Collective, each performing rights organisation?
- If mixes are published only through a licensed partner service, what must the partner contract say for the platform to rely on its licences, and do those licences cover stem-based blends?
- Does a non-commercial or research-only limit on training data carry over to the trained weights, and who could enforce it?
- Who can grant a commercial licence for weights when the maintainer says he cannot?
- If the platform trains its own stem model, what rights does it need in the training audio? See card M15 for the open AI training questions.
- Can the platform pass distributor rules on to users in its own terms, and what should it check before sending a user's cover to stores?
