## M25 DJ-mix platform application, feature by feature
- Law last checked: 2026-11-13. Volatility: high.
- Use for questions like: Which features of a mixing app need licences; Is private mixing on my own device lower risk than sharing; What happens when users upload commercial tracks; Can users export or download their mixes; Does charging money change the legal risk; Do Canada, Australia, the UK or the EU treat user remixes differently

### Bottom line
- Risk rises in steps: mixing on the user's own device, then saving, then storing on the platform's servers, then sharing with the public, then downloads and paid features. Each step adds rights that need a licence and moves more of the risk from the user to the platform (analysis from the rows below).
- Nothing in the base makes any step fully safe with unlicensed commercial tracks. Private, on-device mixing is the lowest step, but whether it is lawful is unsettled, not cleared [M-0110, M-0575].
- Public sharing of mixes of commercial tracks needs licences for both the songs and the recordings [M-0301, M-0106, M-0107]. The statutory webcasting licence does not cover saved or on-demand mixes [M-0115, M-0578].
- Country rules differ sharply. Canada has a non-commercial user content exception for individuals [M-0616]. The UK and EU have narrow parody and pastiche exceptions [M-0240, M-0631]. Australia's saved sections cover parody or satire only [M-0622]. None of them is a general licence for a mix platform.

### Rules
- US federal: each track is two works, a song and a recording [M-0025]. Both carry a reproduction right [M-0108]. Each owner controls derivative works [M-0522]. For recordings that reaches works where the actual sounds are rearranged, remixed or altered [M-0523].
- US federal: songs carry a public performance right [M-0106]. Recordings carry one only for digital audio transmissions [M-0107]. Anyone who violates an exclusive right is an infringer [M-0220].
- US federal, tool maker tests: a product capable of substantial lawful uses is not contributory infringement by itself (court decision, Sony) [M-0560]. Promoting infringing use by clear words or affirmative steps creates liability (court decision, Grokster) [M-0562]. Contributory liability needs intent, shown by inducement or a service tailored to infringement (court decision, Cox v. Sony, 2026) [M-0221, M-0223].
- US federal, hosting: the 512(c) safe harbor covers storage at the direction of a user [M-0343], on conditions: no actual or red flag knowledge [M-0344, M-0345], fast removal [M-0346, M-0348], no direct financial benefit from infringement the provider can control [M-0347], a designated agent [M-0349], and a repeat infringer policy [M-0357]. The safe harbor is not conditioned on the provider monitoring its service [M-0358].
- US federal, 114 statutory licence: not for interactive services [M-0115], not for archived programs under 5 hours [M-0578], not for longer archives kept more than 2 weeks [M-0579], and not if the service induces listeners to make copies [M-0582].
- US federal, damages: statutory damages run from $750 to $30,000 per work [M-0215], up to $150,000 per work for willful infringement [M-0217], counted per work and not per view (analysis row) [M-0254]. They depend on timely registration [M-0214].
- Canada (foreign law), Copyright Act s.29.21: an individual may use an existing published work to make a new work, and use or share it, if the use is solely for non-commercial purposes [M-0616], the source is mentioned where reasonable [M-0617], the individual had reasonable grounds to believe the source copy was not infringing [M-0618], and the use has no substantial adverse effect on the market for the original, including that it is not a substitute for it [M-0619].
- Canada (foreign law): s.29.21(2) defines an intermediary as a person or entity who regularly provides space or means for works to be enjoyed by the public [M-0620]. The exception protects the individual's acts. Whether and how far it protects a platform is an inference, not saved text. Fair dealing in s.29 lists research, private study, education, parody and satire [M-0621]. The fairness test is case law and is not in the base. Moral rights (s.28.2) were not captured (gap).
- Australia (foreign law), Copyright Act 1968: fair dealing for parody or satire does not infringe copyright in a work [M-0622] or in an audio-visual item [M-0623], which includes a sound recording [M-0624]. Fair dealing for criticism or review needs sufficient acknowledgement [M-0625]. Authors have a right of integrity against derogatory treatment, which for a musical work includes material alteration or distortion that harms honour or reputation [M-0626]. The base holds no Australian user content exception and makes no claim about other parts of the Act.
- UK (foreign law), CDPA 1988: the owner controls copying, communication to the public and adaptation [M-0234]. Communication to the public covers music and recordings and includes on-demand access [M-0236, M-0237]. Fair dealing for caricature, parody or pastiche does not infringe [M-0240], and a contract cannot override it [M-0241].
- UK (foreign law), moral rights: the author of a musical work has the right not to have it subjected to derogatory treatment [M-0627]. Treatment is derogatory if it distorts or mutilates the work or otherwise harms the author's honour or reputation [M-0628]. Communicating a derogatory treatment to the public infringes the right [M-0629]. The exceptions in ss.81 and 82 were not reviewed.
- EU (court decision, Pelham I, 2019): a recognisable sample may be a quotation only if the use is in dialogue with the sampled work and the other conditions are met [M-0630].
- EU (court press release No 50/26, 14 April 2026, on Pelham II; unofficial summary, judgment text not saved): pastiche covers creations that evoke existing works while being noticeably different, including by sampling, in a recognisable artistic dialogue [M-0631]. The test is whether a person familiar with the work would recognise the pastiche, and intent is not required [M-0632]. Pastiche is not a catch-all and does not cover concealed imitation or plagiarism [M-0633]. Confirm against the judgment before relying.
- EU (foreign law), Copyright Directive 2019/790 Art 17: a content-sharing platform itself communicates user uploads to the public and must get authorisation [M-0387]. The hosting safe harbor does not apply to that act [M-0388]. Without authorisation it must show best efforts to license, to keep identified works unavailable, and to take down and keep down on notice [M-0389, M-0390, M-0391]. Providers under 3 years old with turnover under EUR 10 million have a lighter regime [M-0392]. Users may rely on quotation, parody and pastiche [M-0393]. There is no general monitoring duty [M-0394], and complaints need human review [M-0395].

### Platform application
- Feature 1, mixing privately on the user's own device.
  - What happens: the app plays and blends tracks in real time. Nothing is published.
  - Rights touched: playing music privately is outside the public performance right, which is limited to public performance (analysis) [M-0106]. The open points are the copies made on the way (stems are copies of the actual sounds) [M-0110] and whether a private blend "prepares" a derivative work [M-0522]. No saved case decides either. Unsettled.
  - Shelters that do not clearly apply: the home recording statute is tied to listed devices and media [M-0572], and the Ninth Circuit kept computer hard drives outside it [M-0575]. The Sony fair use finding was about home taping of TV [M-0561].
  - Who carries the risk: mainly the user (analysis). The platform is judged as a tool maker, so its marketing and design matter most [M-0562, M-0223]. Keeping all audio on the device keeps the platform's own servers out of the copying (analysis).
- Feature 2, saving a mix.
  - A saved mix is a fixed copy of every song and recording in it [M-0108], with the sounds rearranged or altered [M-0523].
  - Saved only on the user's device: the user made the copy. Saved to the platform's cloud: the platform now stores it. That can fit "storage at the direction of a user" [M-0343], but only if the 512(c) conditions are met, and counsel must confirm the fit when the platform's own tool rendered the file.
  - Who carries the risk: the user first; the platform once the file sits on its servers.
- Feature 3, sharing a mix publicly on the platform.
  - Needs: licences for the recordings and for the songs [M-0301, M-0106, M-0107]. The 114 statutory licence does not fit an on-demand or saved mix [M-0115, M-0578, M-0579]. The licensed services say they use direct deals [M-0589, M-0593].
  - Without licences the platform leans wholly on the 512(c) safe harbor [M-0343]. Red flag knowledge is a live risk on a service whose purpose is mixing well-known tracks (analysis) [M-0345]. A service built around unlicensed hits also risks the "tailored to infringement" label [M-0223].
  - Who carries the risk: the user as uploader; the platform as host and possibly as the party performing the works; labels and publishers are the claimants.
- Feature 4, live mixing to an audience.
  - Each track is publicly performed as a song [M-0106] and, online, as a recording [M-0107]. The one saved service statement says the service must clear both for every track [M-0586].
  - A non-interactive audio stream could in theory use the 114 licence with its programming limits (see card M23). Video is outside 114 [M-0112] and adds sync questions [M-0141]. A replay of the set is an archived program, so the archive limits of the 114 licence apply to it [M-0578, M-0579]. A replay that does not fit them needs direct licences.
  - Who carries the risk: the DJ user and the platform together. How the safe harbor applies to live streams is not covered in the base (gap).
- Feature 5, users uploading commercial tracks to mix.
  - This is the "any music" choice. The upload is storage at the user's direction [M-0343]. The platform needs the full 512(c) kit: a registered agent, renewed every 3 years [M-0349, M-0354], notice and takedown [M-0348], counter notice [M-0355, M-0356], and a repeat infringer policy that is actually applied [M-0357, M-0376].
  - The safe harbor does not require the platform to monitor [M-0358]. It is lost on actual or red flag knowledge without removal [M-0344, M-0345, M-0346].
  - Design matters. Features that invite users to bring chart hits, such as search by hit title or presets named after famous tracks, look like the affirmative steps in Grokster [M-0562].
  - Who carries the risk: the user for the upload; the platform if it loses the safe harbor or is found to induce.
- Feature 6, storing stems.
  - A stem holds the actual recorded sounds, so making and keeping it is within the reproduction wording for recordings (analysis) [M-0110]. No case rules on it. Unsettled.
  - Per-user stems kept at the user's direction are closer to user storage [M-0343]. A shared library of split hits that the platform builds and serves to other users is the platform's own copying and distribution, not user storage (analysis) [M-0220].
  - The stem model's own licence is a separate check (see card M24) [M-0603, M-0606].
  - Who carries the risk: the platform, more than for any other private feature, when the splitting and storage happen on its servers.
- Feature 7, export and download.
  - A download is a new copy that leaves the platform, so it is reproduction and distribution of each song and recording [M-0108]. The 114 licence bars inducing listeners to make copies [M-0582]. One licensed service says downloads need an extra licensed right [M-0588].
  - The compulsory mechanical licence does not cover it: that licence is for the composition only, bars changes to the basic melody or character, and is not a licence of any recording [M-0540, M-0542].
  - Export to other services passes the problem on. The saved distributor pages do not take sample-based works through their cover route [M-0597].
  - Who carries the risk: the user who exports and posts elsewhere; the platform for offering public downloads of other people's mixes.
- Feature 8, charging money.
  - Not charging is not a defence [M-0220]. But charging changes several tests. Commercial use weighs in fair use factor one [M-0549, M-0551, M-0553]. A direct financial benefit from infringement the platform can control costs it the safe harbor, and the benefit need not be large (court decision, Ninth Circuit) [M-0347, M-0515]. Canada's user content exception needs a solely non-commercial purpose on the individual's side [M-0616].
  - Vicarious liability, which turns on financial benefit and control, was left undecided in Cox (analysis row) [M-0252].
  - Lower-risk pricing (analysis): charge for the tool and for storage, not per mix of named commercial tracks, and keep adverts and payouts away from unlicensed mixes. Counsel should confirm. A subscription can still count as a financial benefit if infringing use is what draws users. The base has no row that decides this (gap).
- Country flags for rollout.
  - Canada: the s.29.21 exception may protect an individual user's non-commercial mix if all four conditions hold [M-0616, M-0617, M-0618, M-0619]. A mix that can stand in for the original tracks is at risk on the market condition [M-0619]. The platform's own position is not settled by the saved text [M-0620].
  - Australia: only parody or satire and criticism or review are in the saved set [M-0622, M-0625]. Add the integrity right [M-0626]. Treat as stricter than Canada until counsel says otherwise.
  - UK: pastiche and parody are fair dealing exceptions, not a blanket right [M-0240]. On-demand sharing is communication to the public [M-0237]. Moral rights can be asserted against a distorting mix [M-0628, M-0629].
  - EU: the platform is itself liable for user uploads under Art 17 unless it is licensed or meets the best efforts tests [M-0387, M-0389]. Users may rely on pastiche [M-0393], and the 2026 Pelham II press release reads pastiche to include some sampling [M-0631], but not as a catch-all [M-0633]. A straight DJ blend that plays whole tracks is not shown to qualify.
- Risk carriers overall: the user for what the user uploads, saves, shares and exports; the platform as tool maker, host, possible direct actor and payee; labels and publishers as claimants; authors as moral rights claimants in the UK and Australia.

### Gotchas
- "Private" must be real. Unlisted links, friends lists and "share with followers" are sharing. The base has no row on how many listeners make a performance public (gap). Ask counsel before calling any sharing feature private.
- Private mixing is the lowest-risk step, not a cleared one. The stem copy and the derivative work questions are both open [M-0110, M-0522].
- The safe harbor covers what users store. It does not clearly cover what the platform itself renders, splits, curates or promotes (analysis) [M-0343].
- Cox removed "knowledge plus inaction" as a route to contributory liability [M-0224]. It did not change the safe harbor conditions, and it left vicarious liability open [M-0252].
- Canada's exception is for individuals and needs a non-commercial purpose [M-0616]. It is not a licence for a paid platform.
- The Pelham II rows rest on a press release, not the judgment [M-0631]. EU member states also apply these exceptions through their own national laws, which are not in the base.
- One mix can hold many works, and statutory damages are per work [M-0254].
- Geo-blocking and age of the company change the EU answer [M-0392]. Re-check before an EU launch.

### Open questions for counsel
- US: is on-device stem splitting and real-time blending of a lawfully bought track an infringement by the user, and does the platform's exposure change if no audio ever reaches its servers?
- US: at what point does "sharing with friends" become a public performance or a distribution?
- US: does 512(c) protect the platform for mixes rendered by its own tool from user uploads, and for stems it stores per user?
- US: which pricing models avoid a "direct financial benefit" finding, and how should adverts and creator payouts be handled around unlicensed mixes?
- Canada: does s.29.21 protect the platform as an intermediary when it charges a subscription, and how do courts read "solely non-commercial" and the market effect test for a DJ mix?
- UK and Australia: can a blend or mashup be a derogatory treatment, and can the platform get moral rights waivers that hold?
- EU: after Pelham II, can any DJ mix or mashup count as pastiche, and what does Art 17 require of a new, small platform in its first 3 years?
- All countries: can the platform launch in one country only, and what blocking is enough to keep foreign law out?

- Claim: Ninth Circuit (Mavrix v. LiveJournal, 2017): the 512(c) financial benefit test is a common-sense, fact-based inquiry, and the benefit need not be substantial or a large proportion of revenue.
- Jurisdiction: case-law
- Source: Mavrix Photographs v. LiveJournal, 873 F.3d 1045 (9th Cir. 2017) (https://static.case.law/f3d/873/html/1045-01.html), source id ca9-mavrix-livejournal-2017
- Pinpoint: 512(c)(1)(B) discussion
- Quote: "The financial benefit need not be substantial or a large proportion of the service provider’s revenue."
- Checked: 2026-11-10

#### [M-0252] VERIFIED
- Claim: Analysis: after Cox v. Sony (U.S. 2026) a service provider is contributorily liable for a user's infringement only if it induced the infringement or the service is tailored to it; knowing that some users infringe is not enough. Vicarious liability is a separate theory that the Court did not decide (cert limited to contributory).
- Jurisdiction: analysis
- Source: Cox Communications, Inc. v. Sony Music Entertainment, No. 24-171, 607 U.S. ___ (Mar. 25, 2026) (https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/24-171_new_3dq3.pdf), source id scotus-cox-sony-2026
- Pinpoint: 607 U.S. ___ (2026), syllabus
- Quote: "Held: The provider of a service is contributorily liable for a user’s infringement only if it intended that the provided service be used for infringement,"
- Checked: 2026-11-10

#### [M-0224] VERIFIED
- Claim: Cox (2026): the Fourth Circuit's knowledge-plus-insufficient-action rule went beyond the two recognised bases and conflicted with the Court's precedent.
- Jurisdiction: US-federal
- Source: Cox Communications, Inc. v. Sony Music Entertainment, No. 24-171, 607 U.S. ___ (Mar. 25, 2026) (https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/24-171_new_3dq3.pdf), source id scotus-cox-sony-2026
- Pinpoint: 607 U.S. ___ (2026), Part III
- Quote: "contributory liability cannot rest only on a provider’s knowledge of infringement and insufficient action to prevent it."
- Checked: 2026-11-10

## playbook Questions for a licensed music attorney

Research tool, not legal advice. Law last checked 2026-11-13.

## Questions for a licensed music attorney

How to use this page: hand it to the attorney with the cards M21 to M25. Each question lists the rows that frame it. The rows are verified quotes from statutes, cases and service statements, but they do not answer the question. The attorney's answer does. Rows marked "(analysis)" are the researchers' reasoning.

### A. The stem tool

#### A1. Is splitting a lawfully obtained track into stems a reproduction or the making of a derivative work?
- Why it matters: every feature starts with a stem split. If the split itself infringes, private use is not a safe starting point.
- Rows that frame it: the recording owner's copy right covers copying that recaptures the actual sounds [M-0110]. The derivative right covers sounds rearranged, remixed or altered [M-0523]. Each owner controls derivative works [M-0522].
- Gap: no saved case rules on stem separation.

#### A2. Does it matter whether the split runs on the user's device or on our servers?
- Why it matters: it decides the product's architecture and who made the copy.
- Rows that frame it: anyone who violates an exclusive right is an infringer [M-0220]. The safe harbor covers storage at the direction of a user [M-0343].
- Gap: the base has no row on the test for who "does" the act when a server acts on a user's command.

#### A3. Does the home recording statute or the Sony fair use finding protect private stem splitting and mixing?
- Rows that frame it: section 1008 bars actions over a consumer's noncommercial use of listed devices and media [M-0572, M-0573]. The Ninth Circuit kept computer hard drives outside the Act [M-0574, M-0575] and described its purpose as private, noncommercial use [M-0576]. Sony's fair use finding was about home time-shifting of TV [M-0561]. Section 117 names only computer programs [M-0577].

#### A4. What can we say in marketing, onboarding and the product itself without inducing infringement?
- Why it matters: the tool maker cases turn on the maker's own words and design.
- Rows that frame it: Sony's staple article rule [M-0560]. Grokster's inducement rule [M-0562, M-0563]. Cox's intent rule and the "tailored to infringement" route [M-0221, M-0222, M-0223].
- The researchers' reading that inducement reaches a stem tool promoted for commercial songs is not confirmed by any case (unverified) [M-0564].

#### A5. Which theories did Cox leave open against us?
- Rows that frame it: vicarious liability was not decided (analysis row) [M-0252]. A concurrence pointed to other common-law theories [M-0225]. The Court rejected knowledge plus inaction for contributory liability [M-0224].

#### A6. Can we ship the stem model we want?
- Why it matters: a bad model licence is a problem separate from the music.
- Rows that frame it: code licence silent on weights [M-0600]; maintainer statements that the weights licence is unclear and that he cannot grant one [M-0601, M-0602, M-0603]; non-commercial weights [M-0606]; silent projects [M-0604, M-0607, M-0609, M-0610]; training set with non-commercial tracks [M-0614].
- Ask: does a non-commercial limit on training data bind the weights, who could enforce it, and who can give a commercial grant?

### B. What a mix is

#### B1. Is a DJ mix a derivative work of each track, a compilation, or both? What turns on the answer?
- Rows that frame it: definitions of derivative work [M-0521] and compilation [M-0569]. A 2016 policy paper says remixes are often derivative works, compilations or collective works [M-0554].
- Gap: no saved authority decides it.

#### B2. What, if anything, does a user own in a mix made without permission?
- Rows that frame it: no protection for parts using material unlawfully [M-0528]; protection only for new material [M-0529]; the Seventh Circuit's hard line [M-0532, M-0533]; the Second Circuit's fair use route [M-0535, M-0536].
- Ask: what should our user terms say about ownership?

#### B3. Can any kind of mix be fair use: a transition-only blend, a mashup, a short clip?
- Rows that frame it: the four factors [M-0547]; no bright lines [M-0205]; parody against satire [M-0548]; purpose and commerciality after Warhol [M-0551, M-0552]; burden on the user [M-0211]; the sampling split between circuits [M-0186, M-0188].
- Gap: no saved case on a DJ mix or mashup.

#### B4. For artist-approved remix projects, what should the grant say and who should own the result?
- Rows that frame it: transfers need a signed writing [M-0040]; rights can be split and owned separately [M-0539]; work made for hire is a closed list [M-0537, M-0047].
- Gap: no saved remix deal terms.

### C. Hosting, sharing and streaming

#### C1. Which exact licences does a public, on-demand library of user mixes need, and from whom?
- Rows that frame it: an interactive service needs song licences as well as recording licences [M-0301]; performance rights in songs and recordings [M-0106, M-0107]; the 114 licence bars interactive services and short archives [M-0115, M-0578, M-0579]; a large service's account of mechanical and performance licensing [M-0086, M-0088]; licensed mix services' statements about direct deals (captured 2026-11-13) [M-0586, M-0589, M-0593].

#### C2. Can any part of our service run under the section 114 statutory licence?
- Rows that frame it: eligible classes [M-0114]; interactive service definition and the request rule [M-0113, M-0585]; performance complement [M-0580, M-0581]; no inducing copies [M-0582]; lawful source copy [M-0583]; on-screen track text [M-0584].

#### C3. Does the 512(c) safe harbor cover mixes that our own tool rendered, stems we store per user, and live streams?
- Rows that frame it: storage at user direction [M-0343]; knowledge and red flag conditions [M-0344, M-0345]; removal [M-0346, M-0348]; financial benefit and control [M-0347, M-0515]; no monitoring condition [M-0358]; how one court read red flag knowledge for music in videos [M-0365, M-0366].
- Gap: no saved source on the safe harbor and live streams.

#### C4. What must our takedown system include on day one?
- Rows that frame it: registered agent and renewal [M-0349, M-0354]; notice elements [M-0350, M-0351]; counter notice and put-back timing [M-0355, M-0356]; repeat infringer policy [M-0357, M-0376]; liability for knowingly false notices [M-0359].

#### C5. When does "sharing with friends" become a public performance or distribution?
- Rows that frame it: the public performance right [M-0106]; the reproduction right [M-0108].
- Gap: the base has no row on the meaning of "publicly". Do not label any sharing feature private until this is answered.

#### C6. When a user streams a live mix through us, who performs the works?
- Rows that frame it: performance rights [M-0106, M-0107]; a licensed service's statement that the service must clear both rights (captured 2026-11-13) [M-0586, M-0590]; video is outside 114 [M-0112].

#### C7. What does a club or venue licence actually cover, and does any of it carry over online?
- Rows that frame it: performance is a separate right from reproduction (analysis row) [M-0183]; the consent decrees limit ASCAP to non-exclusive public performance rights [M-0256].
- Gap: no venue licence text is saved.

#### C8. If we publish only through a licensed partner service, what must the contract say?
- Rows that frame it: the partner's public statements (captured 2026-11-13) [M-0586, M-0590, M-0591].
- Gap: no partner contract terms are saved. Ask whether a partner's licences reach stem-based blends.

### D. Downloads, covers and money

#### D1. What rights does a mix download or export need?
- Rows that frame it: reproduction in both works [M-0108]; the compulsory mechanical licence is song only, audio only, and bars changes to the basic melody or character [M-0542, M-0540, M-0544]; a service's statement that downloads need an extra right (captured 2026-11-13) [M-0588].

#### D2. Can we qualify as a digital music provider and use the blanket mechanical licence for user covers?
- Rows that frame it: the blanket licence and who may use it [M-0023, M-0122, M-0125]; first-use rule [M-0545]; notice rule for physical copies [M-0546].
- Gap: no row on how notices changed over in 2021.

#### D3. Where is the line between a permitted cover arrangement and a change to the song's fundamental character?
- Rows that frame it: [M-0540, M-0541, M-0543].

#### D4. Which pricing, advert and payout models avoid a direct financial benefit finding and limit vicarious liability?
- Rows that frame it: safe harbor financial benefit condition [M-0347, M-0515]; vicarious liability left open (analysis row) [M-0252]; commerciality in fair use [M-0549, M-0553].

#### D5. What is our realistic damages exposure, and how does registration timing affect it?
- Rows that frame it: [M-0215, M-0216, M-0217, M-0214, M-0218].

### E. Other countries

#### E1. Canada: does s.29.21 protect our users, and us, when we charge a subscription?
- Rows that frame it: the four conditions [M-0616, M-0617, M-0618, M-0619]; intermediary definition [M-0620]; fair dealing purposes [M-0621].
- Gap: Canadian case law on fairness and moral rights (s.28.2) not captured.

#### E2. UK: can a mix be pastiche, and can it be a derogatory treatment?
- Rows that frame it: s.30A [M-0240, M-0241]; restricted acts and on-demand communication [M-0234, M-0236, M-0237]; moral rights [M-0627, M-0628, M-0629].
- Gap: ss.81 and 82 exceptions not reviewed.

#### E3. EU: after Pelham II, can any DJ mix or mashup count as pastiche, and what does Article 17 require of us in our first three years?
- Rows that frame it: Pelham I on quotation [M-0630]; the Pelham II press release [M-0631, M-0632, M-0633]; Article 17 duties and the lighter regime [M-0387, M-0388, M-0389, M-0390, M-0391, M-0392]; user exceptions and complaints [M-0393, M-0395].
- Note: the Pelham II rows rest on the Court's press release. Ask the attorney to read the judgment.

#### E4. Australia: which exceptions, if any, could a user mix rely on, and how do moral rights apply?
- Rows that frame it: parody or satire [M-0622, M-0623, M-0624]; criticism or review [M-0625]; integrity right [M-0626].
- Gap: the base makes no claim about other parts of the Australian Act.

#### E5. Can we launch in one country only, and what blocking is enough?
- Rows that frame it: none. The base has no rows on jurisdiction or geo-blocking (gap).

### F. Decisions the answers feed
- Private-only against public release: A1, A2, A3, C3, C5.
- Any music against a licensed catalogue: A4, A5, B4, C1, C8.
- Stem engine choice: A6.
- Pricing: D4, D5.
- Country order: E1 to E5.

### Claims cited in attorney-questions
Each claim below gives its status, source, pinpoint and verbatim quote. In quotes a long dash in the source is shown as --.

#### [M-0110] VERIFIED
- Claim: The sound recording reproduction right covers only duplication that recaptures the actual sounds.
- Jurisdiction: US-federal
- Source: 17 U.S.C. 114 scope of exclusive rights in sound recordings (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/114), source id usc17-114
- Pinpoint: 17 U.S.C. 114(b)
- Quote: "is limited to the right to duplicate the sound recording in the form of phonorecords or copies that directly or indirectly recapture the actual sounds fixed in the recording."
- Checked: 2026-11-10

#### [M-0523] VERIFIED
- Claim: The sound recording owner's derivative right (106(2)) is limited to works in which the actual sounds fixed in the recording are rearranged, remixed, or otherwise altered in sequence or quality.
- Jurisdiction: US-federal
- Source: 17 U.S.C. 114 scope of exclusive rights in sound recordings (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/114), source id usc17-114
- Pinpoint: 17 U.S.C. 114(b)
- Quote: "limited to the right to prepare a derivative work in which the actual sounds fixed in the sound recording are rearranged, remixed, or otherwise altered in sequence or quality"
- Checked: 2026-11-13

#### [M-0522] VERIFIED
- Claim: The copyright owner has the exclusive right to prepare derivative works, and to authorize others to do so.
- Jurisdiction: US-federal
- Source: 17 U.S.C. 106 exclusive rights in copyrighted works (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/106), source id usc17-106
- Pinpoint: 17 U.S.C. 106(2)
- Quote: "the owner of copyright under this title has the exclusive rights to do and to authorize any of the following"
- Checked: 2026-11-13

#### [M-0220] VERIFIED

#### [M-0343] VERIFIED

#### [M-0572] VERIFIED
- Claim: The Audio Home Recording Act bars infringement actions based on the manufacture, importation or distribution of a digital audio recording device, digital audio recording medium, analog recording device or analog recording medium, or on a consumer's noncommercial use of such a device or medium for making digital or analog musical recordings.

#### [M-0573] VERIFIED

#### [M-0574] VERIFIED

#### [M-0575] VERIFIED

#### [M-0577] VERIFIED

#### [M-0222] VERIFIED

#### [M-0223] VERIFIED

==== FILE: 07-remix-platform-part2.md ====

# Music law knowledge pack: Remix platform, part 2
- File: 07-remix-platform-part2.md, part of the music law knowledge pack (remix edition).
- Contains: playbook DJ-mix platform playbook; playbook Quick answers for the DJ-mix platform team. Each card is followed by the claims it cites, with source, pinpoint and verbatim quote.
- Law last checked: not stated.
- Research tool, not legal advice. Have a licensed music attorney confirm anything before you act on it.
- Claim ids are M- plus four digits in square brackets. VERIFIED claims were checked against the saved source text. Claims tagged (unverified) were not confirmed; say so when you rely on one.

## playbook DJ-mix platform playbook

Research tool, not legal advice. Law last checked 2026-11-13.

## DJ-mix platform playbook

### What this page is
- A plain-words map for the team building a platform where ordinary people mix existing songs: blends, transitions, mashups, recorded mixes and maybe live mixes, fed by a tool that splits a song into stems.
- It assumes users may feed in anything, including commercial hits.
- It covers US law in depth and flags Canada, Australia, the UK and the EU where they differ sharply.
- Every legal statement carries a row id in square brackets. Rows marked "(analysis)" are reasoning, not quoted law. Where the law is unsettled or the base has no source, the page says so.
- Detail lives in cards M21 (remixes), M22 (covers), M23 (stem tools and DJ mixes), M24 (licensed models, distributors, stem model licences) and M25 (feature by feature).

### The ground rules in six lines
- Every track is two copyrights: the song and the recording [M-0025]. Each owner controls copies and derivative works [M-0108, M-0522].
- Remixing the actual recorded sounds is named in the statute as part of the recording owner's rights [M-0523].
- Playing songs to the public needs a performance licence [M-0106]. Streaming recordings online does too [M-0107].
- No saved source shows a remix exception or a compulsory remix licence in US law. A 2016 government paper looked at both and recommended neither (policy paper, not law) [M-0556].
- A tool maker's contributory liability turns on intent: what it says and what it builds the product to do [M-0562, M-0221, M-0223]. Vicarious and direct liability are separate theories that the 2026 ruling did not decide (analysis row) [M-0252].
- A host of user uploads can use the 512(c) safe harbor only if it meets every condition [M-0343, M-0345, M-0347, M-0349, M-0357].

### What needs no label deal (lowest risk, not cleared)
These are the lowest-risk pieces. None is risk-free. Each has open questions for the attorney.
- A mixing and stem tool that runs on the user's own device, where no commercial audio reaches the platform's servers.
  - Why (analysis): selling a product that is capable of substantial lawful uses is not, by that fact alone, contributory infringement [M-0560], and mere knowledge that some users infringe is not enough for contributory liability [M-0563, M-0222]. No saved case applies these rulings to a stem or mixing tool, and they do not cover direct or vicarious liability [M-0220, M-0252].
  - Condition: marketing, onboarding and design must not steer users to commercial hits [M-0562, M-0223].
  - Open: whether a stem split is an infringing copy, even in private, is unsettled [M-0110]. The home recording statute does not clearly help [M-0572, M-0575].
- Mixing of music where the user owns both the song and the recording, or has written permission from the owners of both.
  - Why: the owner of a work may authorise derivative works [M-0522], and the song and the recording are separate works [M-0025]. Get every permission in a signed writing (good practice; a transfer of ownership is not valid without one) [M-0040].
- An opt-in catalogue: artists and small labels who own both the song and the recording and grant the platform remix rights in writing.
  - Why: this is a direct licence from the owners of both works [M-0025, M-0522]. No major label deal is needed for music the majors do not control (analysis).
  - Condition: the grant must cover copying, stem splitting, derivative works, public performance and any download or export the product offers (analysis) [M-0108, M-0106, M-0107].
- Public sharing of mixes built wholly from that opt-in catalogue, or from music the user owns on both sides, the song and the recording [M-0025]. Condition (analysis): the grants cover public performance and sharing [M-0106, M-0107], and the platform can act when a user's ownership claim turns out to be false [M-0345, M-0348].
- User covers, audio only, where the user records every sound. No label is involved, because no original recording is used (analysis) [M-0111]. Publisher-side licences are still needed: a mechanical licence for each song, which is compulsory only if the statute's steps are followed [M-0339, M-0545], and public performance licences for the songs if the platform streams the covers (see card M05) [M-0183]. Whether the platform itself can use the blanket mechanical licence is an open question for counsel [M-0122]. Limits are in card M22 [M-0540, M-0542].
- The compliance kit, which costs nothing in deals: a registered copyright agent [M-0349], notice and takedown [M-0348], counter notice [M-0355], and a repeat infringer policy [M-0357].
- Needed before any item above: a stem model with a clean licence for its weights. This is a precondition, not something that can launch today. None of the public models checked on 2026-11-13 has weights with a stated licence that clearly allows commercial use [M-0603, M-0606, M-0604]. See card M24.

### What needs deals
- Public sharing of saved mixes that contain commercial tracks.
  - Needs: licences for the recordings and for the songs [M-0301, M-0106, M-0107]. The 114 statutory licence does not fit saved or on-demand mixes [M-0115, M-0578, M-0579].
  - How others do it: one licensed service says it has direct deals with labels, and another says it pays rights holders in each mix directly (company statements, captured 2026-11-13) [M-0589, M-0593].
- Live mixing of commercial tracks to an audience. Both the song and the recording are performed for every track [M-0106, M-0107]. One licensed service says the service must clear both (company blog, captured 2026-11-13) [M-0586].
- Downloads and export of mixes that contain commercial tracks. A download is a copy and a distribution of every work in the mix [M-0108]. One licensed service says downloads need an extra licensed right (company blog, captured 2026-11-13) [M-0588].
- Video of mixes. Video is outside the 114 licence [M-0112] and outside the compulsory mechanical licence [M-0544]. Sync is licensed directly [M-0140].
- An EU launch with public sharing. The platform itself needs authorisation for user uploads, or must meet the best efforts tests [M-0387, M-0389].
- The partner route: publish mixes only inside a service that already holds the licences. This still needs a contract with that service. The base has only such services' public statements, not their contract terms (gap) [M-0586, M-0590].

### What stays off limits
- Marketing or onboarding that invites users to split and mix commercial songs they do not own. This is the conduct Grokster punishes [M-0562].
- Presets, search or templates built around named hit records. This risks the "tailored to infringement" finding in Cox [M-0223].
- A platform-built shared library of stems split from commercial tracks. That is the platform's own copying, not user storage (analysis) [M-0110, M-0220, M-0343].
- Public downloads of mixes that contain unlicensed commercial tracks [M-0108, M-0582].
- Relying on the 114 statutory licence for saved or on-demand mixes [M-0115, M-0578].
- Telling users any of these: that changing a song enough makes it theirs [M-0534, M-0552]; that crediting the artist makes it fine [M-0220]; that a set number of seconds is fair use [M-0203, M-0205]; that a cover licence covers a remix [M-0542, M-0540]; that not selling it makes it legal [M-0220, M-0549].
- Telling users they own their mixes without limits. They own at most what they added [M-0529], and nothing in parts that use others' material unlawfully [M-0528].
- Shipping stem model weights in a paid product when the weights are stated non-commercial or research-only [M-0606, M-0603], or when the licence is silent and no one has given a written grant [M-0604, M-0609].
- Ads or creator payouts tied to mixes of unlicensed tracks. A direct financial benefit from infringement the platform can control costs it the safe harbor [M-0347, M-0515].
- Ignoring takedown notices or repeat infringers [M-0348, M-0357].

### Decision page: the two open choices
Two choices are not yet made. Each path below lists what it needs. The four combinations follow.

#### Choice A: private-only use, or public release
- Path A1, private only. Users mix and save on their own device. Nothing is shared through the platform.
  - Needs: on-device processing where possible; no public links; lawful-use marketing; a stem model with a clean licence; clear user terms.
  - Rights in play: copies and the derivative work question on the user's side [M-0110, M-0522]. No public performance by the platform (analysis) [M-0106].
  - Main risk: tool maker liability if the product is promoted or shaped for infringement [M-0562, M-0223]. The open stem copy question [M-0110].
  - Who carries it: mostly the user (analysis). The platform as tool maker.
  - What it gives up: sharing, audience, most network growth.
- Path A2, public release. Users publish mixes for others to hear.
  - Needs: licences for recordings and songs [M-0301, M-0106, M-0107], or a licensed partner; the full 512(c) kit as a backstop [M-0343]; a plan for the EU [M-0387].
  - Main risk: direct and secondary liability for hosted and streamed mixes; loss of the safe harbor through red flag knowledge or financial benefit [M-0345, M-0347]; statutory damages per work [M-0215, M-0217].
  - Who carries it: the user and the platform together.

#### Choice B: any music, or a licensed catalogue
- Path B1, any music. Users bring any track, including commercial hits.
  - Needs: the full 512(c) kit [M-0343, M-0349, M-0357]; design and marketing that do not induce [M-0562]; a view from counsel on stems stored server-side.
  - Main risk: most uploads will be tracks no one cleared. The safe harbor has knowledge and financial benefit conditions [M-0344, M-0345, M-0347]. Cox narrowed contributory liability but left vicarious liability open [M-0222, M-0252].
- Path B2, licensed catalogue. Users mix only tracks the platform has rights to: opt-in artists, direct deals, or a partner's catalogue.
  - Needs: written grants that cover remixing, since remixing is a derivative work right [M-0522, M-0523], plus the performance and copy rights the features use.
  - Main risk: small catalogue at first; the cost and time of deals. Legal risk is far lower because the owners agreed (analysis).

#### The four combinations
- A1 plus B1, private tool, any music. Launch needs: no label or publisher deals, but a stem model whose weights are licensed for commercial use [M-0603, M-0606], marketing and design that do not steer users to commercial hits [M-0562, M-0223], and counsel's answer on whether a stem split is itself an infringing copy [M-0110]. Risk: unsettled and not rated. No saved case applies the tool maker rulings to a stem or mixing tool [M-0560, M-0562, M-0221], and the home recording statute does not clearly help [M-0575].
- A1 plus B2, private tool, licensed catalogue. Launch needs: opt-in grants. Risk: lowest of the four (analysis), if the grants cover both the song and the recording and the stem model licence is clean.
- A2 plus B2, public release, licensed catalogue. Launch needs: grants that cover public performance and sharing. Risk: low (analysis) if the grants are complete and each grantor really owns both the song and the recording. This is the first public feature to ship.
- A2 plus B1, public release, any music. Launch needs: label and publisher deals or a licensed partner [M-0589, M-0593]. Without them the platform stands on the safe harbor alone [M-0343], in a product whose purpose makes red flag knowledge more likely (analysis) [M-0345]. Risk: highest. Do not ship this without counsel's sign-off.

### Risk register
- Risk 1, inducement by marketing or design.
  - What: the platform is held liable for users' infringement because of its own words or design [M-0562, M-0223]. The researchers' reading that this applies to a stem or mixing tool is their analysis and no case confirms it (unverified) [M-0564].
  - Who carries it: platform.
  - Lower it: lawful-use marketing, no hit-based presets, written review of all launch copy.
- Risk 2, direct liability for server-side copies and streams.
  - What: the platform itself copies, splits, renders or streams works [M-0220, M-0110]. The base has no row on the test for who "does" the act (gap).
  - Who carries it: platform.
  - Lower it: process on the device; store per user only; ask counsel.
- Risk 3, loss of the safe harbor.
  - What: red flag knowledge without removal [M-0345, M-0346], direct financial benefit [M-0347, M-0515], no registered agent or a lapsed one [M-0349, M-0354], no real repeat infringer policy [M-0357].
  - Who carries it: platform.
  - Lower it: run the kit from day one; keep money away from unlicensed mixes.
- Risk 4, statutory damages at scale.
  - What: $750 to $30,000 per work, up to $150,000 if willful [M-0215, M-0217], counted per work (analysis row) [M-0254]. One mix can hold many works.
  - Who carries it: user and platform.
  - Lower it: licensed catalogue; fast takedown; no public downloads.
- Risk 5, the stem copy question.
  - What: a court could hold that splitting a track is an infringing reproduction even in private [M-0110]. Unsettled.
  - Who carries it: user first; platform if the split happens on its servers.
  - Lower it: on-device splitting; attorney opinion before launch.
- Risk 6, stem model licence.
  - What: weights that are non-commercial, research-only or silent [M-0606, M-0603, M-0604], trained on a set with non-commercial tracks [M-0614].
  - Who carries it: platform.
  - Lower it: licensed or self-trained model; written grant.
- Risk 7, wrong statutory licence.
  - What: treating saved mixes as covered by section 114 [M-0115, M-0578, M-0579] or remixes as covered by a cover licence [M-0542].
  - Who carries it: platform.
  - Lower it: use these licences only where card M22 and card M23 say they fit.
- Risk 8, foreign law.
  - What: EU platform liability for uploads [M-0387, M-0388]; UK and Australian moral rights [M-0628, M-0626]; narrow exceptions only [M-0240, M-0622]; Canada's exception limited to non-commercial acts by individuals [M-0616].
  - Who carries it: platform and user.
  - Lower it: launch in one country first; get local advice before each new country.
- Risk 9, user ownership claims.
  - What: users believe they own mixes and try to license or monetise them [M-0529, M-0528].
  - Who carries it: user; platform through support load and disputes.
  - Lower it: plain terms and in-app wording.
- Risk 10, vicarious liability.
  - What: liability based on control plus financial benefit. Cox did not decide it (analysis row) [M-0252].
  - Who carries it: platform.
  - Lower it: pricing that does not earn from infringing mixes; counsel review.

### Rollout order
- Step 0, before building further.
  - Put the attorney questions (the page "Questions for a licensed music attorney") to a licensed music attorney.
  - Pick a stem model with a clean weights licence or get a written grant.
  - Write marketing rules: lawful uses only, no hit names.
- Step 1, private tool. On-device mixing and stem splitting, local save, no sharing. User's own files.
- Step 2, opt-in catalogue. Sign written remix grants with independent artists and labels. Let users mix that catalogue.
- Step 3, public sharing of mixes built wholly from the opt-in catalogue or the user's own music. Launch the 512(c) kit at the same time.
- Step 4, cloud save for private mixes, per user, only after counsel confirms the storage design.
- Step 5, commercial tracks in public mixes, only through direct deals or a licensed partner.
- Step 6, live mixing, on the same licensed footing as Step 5.
- Step 7, downloads and export, only for content whose licences cover downloads.
- Step 8, other countries, one at a time, with local advice. Canada, the UK, the EU and Australia each have their own rules (card M25).

### What this page does not settle
- Whether stem splitting is itself a reproduction. No saved case.
- Whether a DJ mix is a compilation, a derivative work or both. No saved authority decides [M-0569, M-0521].
- What a club or venue licence covers. No venue licence text is saved.
- Live-stream music terms of services other than Mixcloud. Not captured.
- The contract terms and prices of any licensed mix service. Not public in the saved set.

#### [M-0183] VERIFIED

- Checked: 2026-11-13

#### [M-0569] VERIFIED
- Claim: A compilation is a work formed by collecting and assembling preexisting materials selected, coordinated or arranged so the whole is an original work of authorship.
- Jurisdiction: US-federal
- Source: 17 U.S.C. 101 definitions (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/101), source id usc17-101
- Pinpoint: 17 U.S.C. 101 'compilation'
- Quote: "selected, coordinated, or arranged in such a way that the resulting work as a whole constitutes an original work of authorship"
- Checked: 2026-11-13

#### [M-0521] VERIFIED
- Claim: A derivative work is one based on preexisting works; the statute's examples include a musical arrangement and a sound recording, and 'any other form in which a work may be recast, transformed, or adapted'.
- Jurisdiction: US-federal

- Checked: 2026-11-13

## playbook Quick answers for the DJ-mix platform team

Research tool, not legal advice. Law last checked 2026-11-13.

## Quick answers for the DJ-mix platform team

How to read this page: each answer is short and carries claim ids in square brackets. US law unless a country is named. "(analysis)" marks reasoning. "Gap" or "unsettled" means the base has no source that decides the point. Service statements carry their capture date. "The base" means the research behind these pages.

### The myths

#### 1. If I change a song enough, is it mine?
- No. Only the owner may make or authorise works based on the original [M-0522]. One appeals court rejected the idea that a stranger may make one when the original does not pervade the new work [M-0534]. The Supreme Court warned that adding new expression is not enough by itself [M-0552].
- You can own only what you added [M-0529], and not even that in parts where others' material is used unlawfully [M-0528].

#### 2. Is anything under a set number of seconds safe?
- No. The fair use statute has four factors and no number of seconds [M-0203, M-0547]. Courts decide case by case with no bright-line rules [M-0205]. The base's own summary: there is no safe length (analysis row) [M-0251].
- One trial court found a 35-second sample a fair use of the song (the composition) on its facts. That is one case, not a rule, and the base has not checked its later history [M-0212]. One appeals court said of recordings: get a licence or do not sample [M-0186]. Another allows very small uses only if an average listener would not recognise them [M-0188, M-0191].

#### 3. Does crediting the artist make it fine?
- No. Anyone who violates an exclusive right is an infringer [M-0220]. That rule has no credit exception (analysis).
- Credit matters only as one condition inside some foreign exceptions, such as Canada's user content exception [M-0617]. It never works alone.

#### 4. I am not selling it. Is that enough?
- No. Infringement does not depend on a sale [M-0220] (analysis). Commercial use is only one element of one fair use factor [M-0549, M-0553].
- Statutory damages are set per work, not by what you earned [M-0215, M-0254].

#### 5. Does a cover licence cover a remix?
- No. The compulsory cover licence is for the song only and is not a licence of any recording [M-0542]. It bars changes to the basic melody or fundamental character [M-0540].
- One distributor says derivative works such as samples cannot go through its cover process (web archive copy dated 2026-02-16, captured 2026-11-13) [M-0597].

#### 6. DJs do it in clubs, so is it legal online?
- That does not follow. Permission to perform a song in public does not supply the right to copy it (analysis row) [M-0183].
- The base has no saved club or venue licence text, so it makes no claim about what such a licence covers (gap).
- Online, a licensed mix service says both the song and the recording of every track must be cleared by the service (company blog, captured 2026-11-13) [M-0586].

### Rights basics

#### 7. What rights sit in one track?
- Two separate copyrights: the song and the recording [M-0025]. Both carry a right to copy [M-0108]. Songs carry a public performance right [M-0106]. Recordings carry one only for digital audio transmission [M-0107].

#### 8. Who has to say yes to a remix?
- Both owners of each track. Each controls derivative works of its own work [M-0522]. For the recording that covers rearranging, remixing or altering the actual sounds [M-0523].

#### 9. I bought the track. Can I mix it and share the mix?
- Buying a copy is not shown in the base to carry the rights to copy, remix or perform in public. Those rights belong to the owners [M-0108, M-0522, M-0106]. The base has no row on what a download store's terms allow (gap).

#### 10. Who owns a mix I make?
- At most, you own the new material you added [M-0529]. Parts that use others' material unlawfully get no protection [M-0528].
- Courts differ at the edges. The Second Circuit allows a claim to original additions when the use is fair [M-0535]. The Seventh Circuit took a harder line [M-0532].

#### 11. Is re-playing a part myself safer than using the original audio?
- Only if every sound is newly recorded, and then it removes the recording owner only. A new recording of independently made sounds does not infringe the recording, but the song is still a separate copyright [M-0111].

#### 12. Could my mix be fair use?
- Perhaps, but do not plan on it. Fair use is a defence and the user carries the burden [M-0211]. When the new use shares the purpose of the original and is commercial, factor one likely weighs against it [M-0551].
- The base has no case on whether a DJ mix or mashup is fair use (gap).

#### 13. Is a mashup a parody?
- Only if it comments on the original. Parody needs to mimic the original to make its point. Satire that uses a song to comment on something else needs its own justification [M-0548]. Applying this to a mashup is analysis.

#### 14. Is there a remix exception or a compulsory remix licence in the US?
- No saved source shows one. A 2016 government paper found no proven need for either (policy paper, not law) [M-0556].

### Covers and video

#### 15. What does a cover licence allow?
- Making and distributing your own audio recording of a song that was already released [M-0339, M-0545], with an arrangement that fits your style [M-0540]. Nothing more.

#### 16. Can I post a video of my cover or mix?
- Not under the cover licence. It does not reach audiovisual works [M-0544]. Video needs a sync licence agreed directly with the publisher [M-0140], plus the recording owner's licence if original audio is used (analysis) [M-0522].

#### 17. Will a distributor release my remix or mashup?
- The saved pages give covers a route [M-0596] and say sample-based works need the master cleared with the label and the song with the publisher, by direct deal [M-0599]. Captured 2026-11-13. Other distributors were not captured.

### The tool and the platform

#### 18. Is it illegal to make a stem splitter?
- Not by itself on the contributory liability cases (analysis; no saved case is about a stem or mixing tool). Selling a product capable of substantial lawful uses is not contributory infringement [M-0560], and mere knowledge of misuse is not enough [M-0563]. Vicarious and direct liability are separate questions [M-0252].
- It becomes a problem when the maker promotes infringing use or tailors the product to it [M-0562, M-0223].

#### 19. Is splitting a song into stems an infringing copy?
- Unsettled. A stem holds the actual recorded sounds, which is what the recording owner's copy right covers [M-0110] (analysis). No saved case rules on stem splitting, in private or in public.

#### 20. Does home recording law cover private mixing?
- Doubtful. The statute protects consumers' noncommercial use of listed recording devices and media [M-0572]. An appeals court kept computer hard drives outside the Act [M-0575]. No case applies it to stem software.

#### 21. Can our marketing get us into trouble?
- Yes. Liability for inducement turns on clear expression or other affirmative steps to foster infringement [M-0562].
- The researchers read this as reaching a tool maker whose marketing steers users to commercial songs they do not own. That reading is not confirmed by any case (unverified) [M-0564].

#### 22. Did Cox v. Sony make platforms safe?
- No. It held that contributory liability needs intent, and mere knowledge is not enough [M-0221, M-0222]. It did not decide vicarious liability (analysis row) [M-0252], and one Justice said other theories could apply [M-0225].

#### 23. Does the DMCA safe harbor protect us when users upload hits?
- Only if every condition is met: user-directed storage [M-0343], no actual or red flag knowledge [M-0344, M-0345], fast removal [M-0348], no direct financial benefit from infringement you can control [M-0347], a registered agent [M-0349], and a repeat infringer policy [M-0357].
- Whether it covers files the platform's own tool rendered is a question for counsel.

#### 24. Do we have to scan every upload?
- Not for the US safe harbor. It is not conditioned on monitoring [M-0358]. Actual knowledge that material is infringing, or awareness of facts that make it apparent, still removes the protection [M-0344, M-0345].
- The EU differs. A platform must make best efforts to keep identified works unavailable [M-0390], though there is no general monitoring duty [M-0394].

#### 25. Can we host saved mixes under the webcasting licence?
- No. The section 114 licence bars interactive services [M-0115], archived programs under 5 hours [M-0578], and longer archives kept up more than 2 weeks [M-0579].

#### 26. Could a radio-style stream of mixes use that licence?
- In theory, with strict limits: caps on tracks per record and per artist in any 3 hours [M-0581], no advance track list [M-0580], track details on screen [M-0584], no help with copying [M-0582], lawfully made source copies [M-0583]. The songs need their own performance licences [M-0106].

#### 27. What does a live DJ stream need?
- Each track is performed as a song and as a recording [M-0106, M-0107]. One licensed service says the service must clear both (company blog, captured 2026-11-13) [M-0586]. Video is outside the 114 licence [M-0112].
- Other services' live-stream terms were not captured (gap).

#### 28. How do the licensed mix services do it?
- By their own account, with direct label deals and a way to pay rights holders inside each mix [M-0589, M-0592, M-0593]. Mixcloud statements captured 2026-11-13. Apple notice dated 2021-11-16, captured 2026-11-13. These are company statements, not law.

#### 29. Can users download or export mixes?
- That adds copying and distribution of every work in the mix [M-0108]. The 114 licence bars inducing copies [M-0582]. One licensed service says downloads need an extra licensed right (captured 2026-11-13) [M-0588].

#### 30. Does charging money change the risk?
- Yes, in several tests. A direct financial benefit from infringement can cost the safe harbor, and it need not be large [M-0347, M-0515]. Commercial use weighs in fair use [M-0551]. Canada's user exception needs a solely non-commercial purpose [M-0616].

#### 31. How large can damages be?
- Statutory damages run $750 to $30,000 per work [M-0215], up to $150,000 per work if willful [M-0217], counted per work, not per view (analysis row) [M-0254]. They depend on timely registration [M-0214].

### Stem models

#### 32. The stem model's code is MIT. Can we ship it in a paid app?
- The code, yes on its face. The weights are a separate question. For Demucs the licence file is silent on weights [M-0600] and a maintainer says the weights are for personal or research usage [M-0603]. Checked 2026-11-13.

#### 33. The model page says nothing about a licence. Is that permission?
- No. Silence is not a grant [M-0604, M-0607, M-0609]. Get a written grant from someone able to give it.

#### 34. Which of the checked models are clearly fine for commercial use?
- None, on their stated weights terms as checked 2026-11-13. One is non-commercial [M-0606]. One is described as research or personal use [M-0603]. The others are silent [M-0604, M-0609, M-0610].

### Other countries

#### 35. Does Canada's user content exception make mixes legal there?
- It can protect an individual, not clearly a platform. Conditions: solely non-commercial [M-0616], source named where reasonable [M-0617], reasonable belief the source copy was lawful [M-0618], and no substantial harm to the market for the original [M-0619]. The platform's own position rests on inference [M-0620].

#### 36. Do the UK and EU pastiche rules cover mixes?
- Not as a general rule. The UK has a fair dealing exception for caricature, parody or pastiche [M-0240]. The EU court's 2026 press release reads pastiche to include some sampling in artistic dialogue [M-0631], and says it is not a catch-all [M-0633]. That row rests on a press release, not the judgment.

#### 37. Is the platform itself liable for uploads in the EU?
- Yes, if the service counts as an online content-sharing service provider, unless it is licensed or meets the best efforts tests. A content-sharing platform communicates user uploads to the public and must get authorisation [M-0387, M-0389]. New, small providers have a lighter regime [M-0392].

#### 38. What about Australia?
- The saved sections cover parody or satire [M-0622, M-0623] and criticism or review with acknowledgement [M-0625]. Authors also have an integrity right [M-0626]. The base holds no Australian user content exception and makes no claim about the rest of the Act.
